  1052	\subsection{Generalized Pauli observables}
  1053	\label{sec:generalized-pauli}
  1054	
  1055	
  1056	For prime number $p$, the generalized Pauli operators over $\Fp$ are a
  1057	collection of observables indexed by a basis setting $X$ or $Z$ and an element
  1058	$a$ or $b$ of $\Fp$, with eigenvalues that are $p$-th roots of unity.
  1059	They are given by
  1060	\begin{equation}
  1061	  \label{eq:pauli-fp}
  1062	  \sigma^X(a) = \sum_{j \in \Fp} \ket{j + a} \bra{j}\qquad \text{and} \qquad
  1063	  \sigma^Z(b) = \sum_{j \in \Fp} \omega^{bj} \ket{j} \bra{j}\;,
  1064	\end{equation}
  1065	where $\omega = e^{\frac{2\pi i}{p}}$, and addition and multiplication are over
  1066	$\Fp$.
  1067	These observables obey the ``twisted commutation'' relations
  1068	\begin{equation}
  1069	  \label{eq:twisted-fp}
  1070	  \forall a,b\in\Fp\;,\qquad \sigma^X(a)\, \sigma^Z(b) =
  1071	  \omega^{-ab} \,\sigma^Z(b)\,\sigma^X(a)\;.
  1072	\end{equation}
  1073	Similarly, over a field $\Fq$ with $q$ a power of $p$, we can consider a set of generalized Pauli
  1074	operators, indexed by a basis setting $X$ or $Z$ and an element of $\Fq$ and
  1075	with eigenvalues that are $p$-th roots of unity.
  1076	For $a, b\in\Fq$ they are given by
  1077	\begin{equation*}
  1078	  \qp^X(a) = \sum_{j \in \Fq} \ket{j+a}\bra{j} \qquad \text{and} \qquad
  1079	  \qp^Z(b)= \sum_{j \in \Fq} \omega^{\tr(b j)} \ket{j}\bra{j}\;,
  1080	\end{equation*}
  1081	where addition and multiplication are over $\Fq$.
  1082	For all $W \in \{X,Z\}$, $a, a' \in \Fq$, and $b \in \Fp$, powers of these
  1083	observables obey the relations
  1084	\begin{equation*}\label{eq:pauli-product-power}
  1085	  \bigl(\qp^W(a)\qp^W(a')\bigr) = \qp^W(a+a') \qquad \text{and}
  1086	  \qquad \bigl( \qp^W(a) \bigr)^b = \qp^W(a b) \;.
  1087	\end{equation*}
  1088	In particular, since $pa=0$ for any $a\in \Fq$ we get that that $(\qp^W(a))^p =
  1089	I$ for any $a\in\Fq$.
  1090	The observables obey analogous ``twisted commutation'' relations
  1091	to~\eqref{eq:twisted-fp},
  1092	\begin{equation}
  1093	  \label{eq:twisted-fq}
  1094	  \forall a, b \in \Fq\;, \qquad \qp^X(a)\, \qp^Z(b) =
  1095	  \omega^{-\tr(a b)} \, \qp^Z(b)\, \qp^X(a)\;.
  1096	\end{equation}
  1097	It is clear from the definition that all of the $\qp^X$ operators commute with
  1098	each other, and similarly all the $\qp^Z$ operators commute with each other.
  1099	Thus, it is meaningful to speak of a common eigenbasis for all $\qp^X$
  1100	operators, and a common eigenbasis for all $\qp^Z$ operators.
  1101	The common eigenbasis for the $\qp^Z$ operators is the computational
  1102	basis $\{\ket{j}\}_{j \in \F_q}$.
  1103	To map this basis to the common eigenbasis of the $\qp^X$ operators, one can
  1104	apply the Fourier transform
  1105	\begin{equation}
  1106	  \label{eq:fourier-f}
  1107	  F \,=\, \frac{1}{\sqrt{q}} \sum_{a, b\in \Fq} \omega^{-\tr(ab)}
  1108	  \ket{a}\bra{b}\;.
  1109	\end{equation}
  1110	Explicitly, the eigenbases consist of the vectors $\ket{e_W}$ labeled by an
  1111	element $e \in \Fq$ and $W \in \{X, Z\}$, given by
  1112	\begin{equation*}
  1113	  \ket{e_X} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{q}} \sum_j \omega^{- \tr(e j)} \ket{j}\;, \qquad
  1114	  \ket{e_Z}   = \ket{e}\;.
  1115	\end{equation*}
  1116	We denote the POVM whose elements are projectors onto basis vectors of the
  1117	eigenbasis associated with the observables $\qp^W$ by $\{\qp^W_e\}_e$.
  1118	Then for all $W \in \{X,Z\}$ and $a\in \Fq$, the observables $\qp^W(a)$ can be
  1119	written as
  1120	\begin{equation}\label{eq:pauli-obs-proj-single}
  1121	  \qp^W(a) = \sum_{b \in \Fq} \omega^{\tr(a b)} \qp^W_b\;.
  1122	\end{equation}
  1123	
  1124	To invert this relation, we first quote the following useful Fourier fact.
  1125	\begin{lemma}[Fact 3.2 of \cite{NW19}]
  1126	  \label{lem:cancellation}
  1127	  Let $V$ be a subspace of $\F^k$. For all $v \not\in V^\perp$, 
  1128	  \begin{equation*}
  1129	    \E_{u \sim V} \omega^{\tr(u \cdot v)} = 0\;,
  1130	  \end{equation*}
  1131	  where the expectation is over a uniformly random vector $u$ from $V$.
  1132	\end{lemma}
  1133	
  1134	We may now invert~\Cref{eq:pauli-obs-proj-single}:
  1135	\begin{equation}\label{eq:pauli-inversion-0-single}
  1136	  \E_{a\in \F_q} \omega^{-\tr(ab)} \qp^W(a) = \sum_{b'\in \F_q} \E_{a\in \F_q}
  1137	  \omega^{\tr(a(b'-b))} \qp^W_{b'} = \qp^W_b\;,
  1138	\end{equation}
  1139	where the second step follows from Lemma~\ref{lem:cancellation}.
  1140	
  1141	For systems with many qudits, we will consider tensor products of the operators
  1142	$\qp^W$.
  1143	Slightly abusing notation, for $W \in \{X, Z\}$ and $a \in \Fq^n$ we denote by
  1144	$\qp^W(a)$ the tensor product $\qp^W(a_1) \ot \dots \ot \qp^W(a_n)$.
  1145	These obey the twisted commutation relations
  1146	\begin{equation*}
  1147	  \forall a,b\in \Fq^n,\qquad \qp^X(a)\, \qp^Z(b) \,=\, \omega^{-\tr (a \cdot
  1148	    b)}\, \qp^Z(b)\, \qp^X(a)\;,

  1178	  and between $(\C^2)^{\ot L k} \ot (C^2)^{\ot Lk}$ and $(\C^2 \ot

    17	`def:graph-distribution` in `blueprint/src/chapter/ch12_qpbt_games.tex:441-535`.
    18	The paper origin is `references/qpbt-paper/05_conditionally_linear_functions.tex:35-57`
    19	and `references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:964-1010`.

    22	open scoped BigOperators
    23	
    24	namespace MIPStarRE.QPBT
    25	
    26	open MIPStarRE.LDT
    27	
    28	variable {K ι : Type*} [Field K] [Fintype ι] [DecidableEq ι]
    29	
    30	/--
    31	The source definition is recursive in the residual map.  A direct inductive
    32	predicate with that recursive occurrence under a dependent finite-set index is
    33	rejected by Lean's strict-positivity checker.  We therefore expose the same
    34	public predicate through a positive syntax tree (`CondLinearTerm`), together
    35	with its support invariant and evaluation function.  This is a representation
    36	deviation forced by Lean, not an additional mathematical hypothesis.  It encodes
    37	`def:cl-func`, blueprint `blueprint/src/chapter/ch12_qpbt_games.tex:441-463`,
    38	paper origin `references/qpbt-paper/05_conditionally_linear_functions.tex:35-57`.
    39	-/
    40	inductive CondLinearTerm (K : Type*) [Field K] {ι : Type*} [Fintype ι]
    41	    [DecidableEq ι] : ℕ → Type _ where
    42	  | zero : CondLinearTerm K (ι := ι) 0
    43	  | succ {ell : ℕ}
    44	      (S₁ : Finset ι)
    45	      (L₁ : (ι → K) →ₗ[K] (ι → K))
    46	      (hSupport : ∀ x i, i ∉ S₁ → L₁ x i = 0)
    47	      (rest : (ι → K) → CondLinearTerm K (ι := ι) ell) :
    48	      CondLinearTerm K (ι := ι) (ell + 1)
    49	
    50	/-- Restrict a coordinate vector to a register, zeroing the complementary
    51	coordinates.  This is Lean-only support for the projections in `def:cl-func`,
    52	blueprint `blueprint/src/chapter/ch12_qpbt_games.tex:441-463`, paper origin
    53	`references/qpbt-paper/05_conditionally_linear_functions.tex:35-57`.
    54	-/
    55	def coordinateRestriction (S : Finset ι) (x : ι → K) : ι → K :=
    56	  fun i => if i ∈ S then x i else 0
    57	
    58	/-- Evaluation of a conditionally-linear syntax term.  Lean-only support for
    59	`def:cl-func`, blueprint `ch12_qpbt_games.tex:453-463`, paper origin
    60	`references/qpbt-paper/05_conditionally_linear_functions.tex:35-57`.
    61	-/
    62	def CondLinearTerm.eval {ι : Type*} [Fintype ι] [DecidableEq ι]
    63	    {K : Type*} [Field K] :
    64	    {ell : ℕ} → CondLinearTerm K (ι := ι) ell → (ι → K) → (ι → K)
    65	  | _, .zero => fun _ => 0
    66	  | _, .succ S₁ L₁ _ rest =>
    67	      fun x =>
    68	        let x₁ := coordinateRestriction S₁ x

    70	
    71	/-- The support invariant for a conditionally-linear syntax term.  This is a
    72	Lean-only companion to `def:cl-func`, blueprint
    73	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch12_qpbt_games.tex:453-463`, paper origin
    74	`references/qpbt-paper/05_conditionally_linear_functions.tex:35-57`.
    75	-/
    76	def CondLinearTerm.supportedOn {ι : Type*} [Fintype ι] [DecidableEq ι]
    77	    {K : Type*} [Field K] :
    78	    {ell : ℕ} → CondLinearTerm K (ι := ι) ell → Finset ι → Prop
    79	  | _, .zero, _ => True
    80	  | _, .succ S₁ _ _ rest, S =>
    81	      S₁ ⊆ S ∧ ∀ y, CondLinearTerm.supportedOn (rest y) (S \ S₁)
    82	
    83	/-- The public conditionally-linear predicate.  Its positive syntax-tree
    84	encoding is the Lean representation of `def:cl-func`, blueprint
    85	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch12_qpbt_games.tex:453-463`, paper origin
    86	`references/qpbt-paper/05_conditionally_linear_functions.tex:35-57`.
    87	-/

    89	    [DecidableEq ι] (S : Finset ι) (ell : ℕ)

    93	
    94	/--
    95	`IsCondLinear` abbreviates the full-coordinate predicate.  Blueprint
    96	`def:cl-func`, `blueprint/src/chapter/ch12_qpbt_games.tex:453-463`; paper
    97	`references/qpbt-paper/05_conditionally_linear_functions.tex:35-57`.
    98	-/
    99	def IsCondLinear (ell : ℕ) (L : (ι → K) → (ι → K)) : Prop :=
   100	  IsCondLinearOn K Finset.univ ell L
   101	
   102	/--
   103	The distribution obtained by applying two conditionally linear maps to a common
   104	uniform seed.  This is `def:cl-dist` in
   105	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch12_qpbt_games.tex:467-470`, paper origin
   106	`references/qpbt-paper/05_conditionally_linear_functions.tex:132-138`.

   109	    (L R : (ι → K) → (ι → K)) :
   110	    Distribution ((ι → K) × (ι → K)) :=
   111	  (uniformDistribution (ι → K)).map (fun z => (L z, R z))
   112	
   113	/-- The direct-sum map used to encode the paper's CL concatenation.  The left
   114	coordinates carry `L`, while the right coordinates carry the family member
   115	`R u v` selected by the left input `u`.  This is Lean-only coordinate

   120	def condLinearConcat {ιU ιV : Type*} [Fintype ιU] [DecidableEq ιU]
   121	    [Fintype ιV] [DecidableEq ιV] (L : (ιU → K) → (ιU → K))
   122	    (R : (ιU → K) → (ιV → K) → (ιV → K))
   123	    (x : ιU ⊕ ιV → K) : ιU ⊕ ιV → K :=
   124	  let u : ιU → K := fun i => x (.inl i)
   125	  let v : ιV → K := fun j => x (.inr j)

   127	
   128	/--
   129	Concatenating an outer and an indexed inner CL map adds their levels.  This is
   130	`lem:cl-concat` in `blueprint/src/chapter/ch12_qpbt_games.tex:498-505`, with
   131	paper origin `references/qpbt-paper/05_conditionally_linear_functions.tex:315-364`.
   132	The direct-sum coordinate bookkeeping is represented by `condLinearConcat`; the
   133	level proof remains deferred in this skeleton.
   134	-/
   135	theorem IsCondLinearOn.concat {ιU ιV : Type*} [Fintype ιU] [DecidableEq ιU]
   136	    [Fintype ιV] [DecidableEq ιV] {ell k : ℕ}
   137	    {L : (ιU → K) → (ιU → K)}
   138	    {R : (ιU → K) → (ιV → K) → (ιV → K)}
   139	    (hL : IsCondLinearOn K (Finset.univ : Finset ιU) k L)
   140	    (hR : ∀ u : ιU → K, u ∈ Set.range L →
   141	      IsCondLinearOn K (Finset.univ : Finset ιV) ell (R u)) :
   142	    IsCondLinearOn K (Finset.univ : Finset (ιU ⊕ ιV)) (k + ell)
   143	      (condLinearConcat L R) := by
   144	  sorry

   151	The underlying graph-distribution definition is
   152	`references/qpbt-paper/07_types.tex:65-82`.
   153	-/
   154	noncomputable def graphDistribution {T : Type*} [Fintype T] [DecidableEq T]
   155	    (E : Finset (Sym2 T)) (_hE : E.Nonempty) : Distribution (T × T) :=
   156	  Distribution.uniformOnFinset
   157	    (Finset.univ.filter fun ab : T × T => Sym2.mk ab.1 ab.2 ∈ E)
   158

   161	    (E : Finset (Sym2 T)) (hE : E.Nonempty) :

     7	The blueprint uses asymptotic `approx` notation.  The skeleton records the
     8	corresponding squared norm functionals explicitly, leaving universal-constant
     9	estimates to later proof stages.

    11	## References
    12	
    13	These are `def:state-distance` and `def:povm-distance` in
    14	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch12_qpbt_games.tex:171-220`; the paper origin is

    25	/--
    26	Squared Euclidean distance between pure states.  Blueprint `def:state-distance`
    27	(`blueprint/src/chapter/ch12_qpbt_games.tex:171-179`), paper origin
    28	`references/qpbt-paper/06_nonlocal_games_and_mipstar.tex:219-271`.
    29	-/
    30	noncomputable def stateDistSq {ι : Type*} [Fintype ι]
    31	    [DecidableEq ι]
    32	    (ψ φ : EuclideanSpace ℂ ι) : ℝ :=
    33	  ‖ψ - φ‖ ^ 2
    34	
    35	/--
    36	Average squared state-dependent distance between two operator families.  This
    37	is `def:povm-distance` in `blueprint/src/chapter/ch12_qpbt_games.tex:203-210`,
    38	with paper origin `references/qpbt-paper/06_nonlocal_games_and_mipstar.tex:219-271`.

    40	noncomputable def opFamilyDistSq {X α ι : Type*}
    41	    [Fintype α] [Fintype ι] [DecidableEq ι]
    42	    (μ : Distribution X) (M N : X → α → Op ι)
    43	    (ψ : EuclideanSpace ℂ ι) : ℝ :=

    27

    36	  QuestionB : Type
    37	  AnswerA : Type
    38	  AnswerB : Type
    39	  [questionAFintype : Fintype QuestionA]

    41	  [answerAFintype : Fintype AnswerA]

    92	  ιB : Type
    93	  [ιAFintype : Fintype ιA]
    94	  [ιBFintype : Fintype ιB]
    95	  [ιADecidableEq : DecidableEq ιA]
    96	  [ιBDecidableEq : DecidableEq ιB]
    97	  ψ : EuclideanSpace ℂ (ιA × ιB)
    98	  ψ_norm : ‖ψ‖ = 1
    99	  A : G.QuestionA → Measurement G.AnswerA ιA
   100	  B : G.QuestionB → Measurement G.AnswerB ιB
   101	
   102	attribute [instance] Strategy.ιAFintype Strategy.ιBFintype
   103	  Strategy.ιADecidableEq Strategy.ιBDecidableEq

   108	`references/qpbt-paper/06_nonlocal_games_and_mipstar.tex:26-38`.

   110	def heteroKron {ιA ιB : Type*} (A : Op ιA) (B : Op ιB) : Op (ιA × ιB) :=

   118	`references/qpbt-paper/06_nonlocal_games_and_mipstar.tex:219-271`. -/

   149	`references/qpbt-paper/06_nonlocal_games_and_mipstar.tex:40-57`; attainment is
   150	intentionally not asserted here.
   151	-/
   152	noncomputable def Game.value (G : Game) : ℝ :=
   153	  sSup (Set.range (fun S : Strategy G => S.value))

    12	  A \emph{two-player one-round game} $\game$ is specified by a tuple
    13	  $(\cal{X}, \cal{Y}, \cal{A}, \cal{B}, \mu, D)$ where
    14	  \begin{enumerate}
    15	  \item $\cal{X}$ and $\cal{Y}$ are finite sets (called the \emph{question
    16	      alphabets}),
    17	  \item $\cal{A}$ and $\cal{B}$ are finite sets (called the \emph{answer
    18	      alphabets}),
    19	  \item $\mu$ is a probability distribution over $\cal{X} \times \cal{Y}$
    20	    (called the \emph{question distribution}), and
    21	  \item $D: \cal{X} \times \cal{Y} \times \cal{A} \times \cal{B} \to \{0,1\}$ is
    22	    a function (called the \emph{decision predicate}).
    23	  \end{enumerate}
    24	\end{definition}
    25	
    26	\begin{definition}[Tensor product strategies]
    27	  \label{def:tensor-product-strategy}
    28	  A \emph{tensor product strategy} $\strategy$ for a game $\game = (\cal{X},
    29	  \cal{Y}, \cal{A}, \cal{B}, \mu, D)$ is a tuple $(\ket{\psi}, A, B)$ where
    30	  \begin{itemize}
    31		\item $\ket{\psi}$ is a pure quantum state, i.e.\ a unit vector in $\mH_A \otimes \mH_B$ for finite
    32	    dimensional complex Hilbert spaces $\mH_A, \mH_B$,
    33		\item $A$ is a set $\{A^x\}$ such that for every $x \in \cal{X}$, $A^x =
    34	    \{A^x_a \}_{a \in \cal{A}}$ is a POVM over $\mH_A$, and
    35		\item $B$ is a set $\{B^y\}$ such that for every $y \in \cal{Y}$, $B^y =
    36	    \{B^y_b \}_{b \in \cal{B}}$ is a POVM over $\mH_B$.
    37	\end{itemize}
    38	\end{definition}
    39	
    40	\begin{definition}[Tensor product value]
    41	  \label{def:tensor-product-value}
    42		The \emph{tensor product value} of a tensor product strategy $\strategy =
    43	  (\ket{\psi}, A, B)$  with respect to a game $\game=(\cal{X}, \cal{Y}, \cal{A},
    44	  \cal{B}, \mu, D)$ is defined as
    45	  \begin{equation*}
    46			\val^*(\game, \strategy) = \sum_{x,\, y,\, a,\, b} \, \mu(x,y)\, D(x,y,a,b)\,
    47	    \bra{\psi} A^x_a \otimes B^y_b\, \ket{\psi}\;.
    48	  \end{equation*}
    49		For $v\in[0,1]$ we say that the strategy $\strategy$ \emph{passes (or wins)
    50	    $\game$ with probability $v$ if} $\val^*(\game, \strategy) \geq v$.
    51	  The \emph{tensor product value} of $\game$ is defined as
    52	  \begin{equation*}
    53			\val^*(\game) = \sup_\strategy \val^*(\game, \strategy)\;,
    54	  \end{equation*}
    55		where the supremum is taken over all tensor product strategies $\strategy$ for
    56	  $\game$.
    57	\end{definition}
    58	
    59	
    60	\begin{remark}
    61	  Unless specified otherwise, all strategies considered in this paper are tensor
    62	  product strategies, and we simply call them \emph{strategies}.
    63	  Similarly, we refer to $\val^*(\game)$ as the \emph{value} of the game
    64	  $\game$.
    65	\end{remark}
    66	
    67	
    68	\begin{definition}[Projective strategies]
    69	  \label{def:projective-strategy}
    70	  We say that a strategy $\strategy = (\ket{\psi}, A, B)$ is \emph{projective} if
    71	  all the measurements $\{A^x_a\}_a$ and $\{B^y_b\}_b$ are projective.
    72	\end{definition}
    73	
    74	\begin{definition}\label{rem:symmetric-games}
    75		A game $\game = (\cal{X}, \cal{Y}, \cal{A}, \cal{B}, \mu, D)$ is
    76	  \emph{symmetric} if the question and answer alphabets are the same for both
    77	  players (i.e.\
    78	  $\cal{X} = \cal{Y}$ and $\cal{A} = \cal{B}$), the distribution $\mu$ is
    79	  symmetric (i.e.\
    80	  $\mu(x,y) = \mu(y,x)$), and the decision predicate $D$ treats both players
    81	  symmetrically (i.e.\ for all $x,y,a,b$, $D(x,y,a,b) = D(y,x,b,a)$).
    82	 
    83	We call a strategy $\strategy = (\ket{\psi}, A, B)$
    84	  \emph{symmetric} if $\ket{\psi}$ is a (pure) state in $\mH \otimes \mH$, for some
    85	  Hilbert space $\mH$, that is invariant under permutation of the two factors,
    86	  and the measurement operators of both players are identical.
    87	\end{definition}
    88	
    89	We often specify symmetric games $\game$ and symmetric strategies $\strategy$ using
    90	  a compact notation: we write $\game = (\cal{X}, \cal{A}, \mu, D)$ and
    91	  $\strategy = (\ket{\psi}, M)$ where $M$ denotes the set of measurement
    92	  operators for both players.
    93	
    94	\begin{lemma}\label{lem:symmetric-strat}
    95	  Let $\game = (\cal{X}, \cal{A},  \mu, D)$ be a symmetric game
    96	  such that $\val^*(\game) = 1-\eps$ for some $\eps\geq 0$.
    97	  Then there exists a symmetric and projective strategy
    98	  $\strategy=(\ket{\psi},M)$ such that $\val^*(\game,\strategy)\geq 1-\eps$.
    99	\end{lemma}
   100	
   101	\begin{proof}
   102	  By definition for any $\eps'>\eps$ there exists a strategy $\strategy'= (\ket{\psi'},A,B)$ such
   103	  that $\val^*(\game,\strategy')\geq 1-\eps'$.
   104	Using Naimark's theorem (Theorem~\ref{thm:naimark}) we can assume
   105	without loss of generality that $\ket{\psi'}\in\C_{\alice'}^d\otimes \C_{\bob'}^d$ for some integer $d$
   106	  and that for every $x$, $A^x$ and $B^x$ are projective measurements.
   107	Let
   108	  \[
   109	    \ket{\psi} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \big( \ket{0}_\alice \ket{1}_\bob
   110	    \ket{\psi'}_{\alice'\bob'} + \ket{1}_\alice \ket{0}_\bob
   111	    \ket{\psi'_\tau}_{\alice'\bob'}\big) \in (\C_{\alice}^2 \otimes
   112	    \C_{\alice'}^d) \otimes (\C_\bob^2 \otimes \C_{\bob'}^d)\;,
   113	  \]
   114	  where $\ket{\psi'_\tau}$ is obtained from $\ket{\psi}$ by permuting the two
   115	  players' registers.
   116	  Observe that $\ket{\psi}$ is invariant under permutation of $\alice\alice'$
   117	  and $\bob\bob'$.
   118	
   119	  For any question $x\in \cal{X}$ define the measurement $M^x = \{M^x_a\}_{a \in \cal{A}}$
   120	  acting on the Hilbert space $\C^2 \otimes \C^d$ as follows:
   121	  \[
   122	  	M^x_a = \ketbra{0}{0} \otimes A^x_a + \ketbra{1}{1} \otimes B^x_a \;,
   123	  \]
   124		i.e.\ for $\ket{\varphi} \in \C^d$, $M^x_a(\ket{0}\ket{\varphi})=\ket{0}A^x_a\ket{\varphi}$ and $M^x_a(\ket{1}\ket{\varphi})=\ket{1}B^x_a\ket{\varphi}$.
   125	  When Alice receives question $x$, she measures $M^x$ on registers $\alice \alice'$, and when Bob receives 
   126	  question $y$, he measures $M^y$ on registers $\bob \bob'$.
   127	Using that by assumption the decision predicate $D$ for $\game$ is symmetric,
   128	  it is not hard to verify that $\val^*(\game,\strategy) =
   129	  \val^*(\game,\strategy')$.
   130	\end{proof}

   132	\begin{definition}
   133	  \label{def:comm-strategy}
   134	  Let $\game = (\cal{X}, \cal{Y}, \cal{A}, \cal{B}, \mu, D)$ be a game, and let
   135	  $\strategy = (\ket{\psi}, A, B)$ be a strategy for $\game$ such that  $\mH_A = \mH_B$.
   136	  Let $S \subseteq \cal{X} \times \cal{Y}$ denote the support of the question
   137	  distribution $\mu$, i.e.\ the set of $(x,y)$ such that $\mu(x,y)>0$.
   138	  We say that $\strategy$ is a \emph{commuting strategy for $\game$} if for all
   139	  question pairs $(x, y) \in S$, we have $[A^x_a, B^y_b] = 0$ 
   140	  for all $a
   141	  \in \cal{A}, b \in \cal{B}$, where $[A, B] = AB - BA$ denotes the commutator.
   142	\end{definition}
   143	
   144	\begin{definition}[Consistent measurements]
   145	  \label{def:consistent-measurement}
   146	  Let $\cal{A}$ be a finite set, let $\ket{\psi} \in \mH \otimes \mH$ be a
   147	  state, and let $\{ M_a \}_{a \in \cal{A}}$ be a projective measurement on
   148	  $\mH$.
   149	  We say that \emph{$\{M_a\}_{a \in \cal{A}}$ is consistent on $\ket{\psi}$} if
   150	  and only if
   151	  \begin{equation*}
   152	    \forall a \in \mA\;,\quad M_a \otimes \Id_\bob\, \ket{\psi}
   153	    = \Id_\alice \otimes M_a\, \ket{\psi}\;.
   154	  \end{equation*}
   155		When the state $\ket{\psi}$ is clear from context we simply say that \emph{$\{M_a\}_{a \in \cal{A}}$ is consistent}.
   156	\end{definition}
   157	
   158	The terminology ``consistent'' arises from the fact that when the measurement $\{M_a\}$ is performed on both registers of $\ket{\psi}$, the probability of obtaining twice the same outcome is 
   159	\[ \sum_a \bra{\psi} M_a \otimes M_a \ket{\psi}\,=\, \sum_a \bra{\psi} \Id_\alice \otimes (M_a)^2 \ket{\psi} \,=\, \sum_a \bra{\psi} \Id_\alice \otimes M_a \ket{\psi} \,=\,1\;,\]
   160	where the first equality is by definition of consistency, the second uses that $\{M_a\}$ is projective, and the last uses $\sum_a M_a=\Id$. 
   161	
   162	\begin{definition}[Consistent strategies]
   163	  \label{def:consistent-strategy}
   164		Let $\strategy = (\ket{\psi}, A, B)$ be a projective strategy with state
   165	  $\ket{\psi} \in \mH \otimes \mH$, for some Hilbert space~$\mH$, which is
   166	  defined on question alphabets $\cal{X}$ and~$\cal{Y}$ and answer alphabets
   167	  $\cal{A}$ and~$\cal{B}$, respectively.
   168	  We say that the strategy $\strategy$ is \emph{consistent} if for all $x \in
   169	  \cal{X}$, the measurement $\{A^x_a\}_{a \in \cal{A}}$ is consistent on
   170	  $\ket{\psi}$ and if for all $y \in \cal{Y}$, the measurement $\{B^y_b\}_{b \in
   171	    \cal{B}}$ is consistent on $\ket{\psi}$.
   172	\end{definition}
   173	
   174	We almost always restrict our attention to symmetric strategies. In this case, consistency implies that whenever both players are sent the same question, they provide the same answer. 
   175	
   176	\begin{definition}
   177	  \label{def:spcc}
   178	  We say that a strategy $\strategy$ for a game $\game$ is \emph{PCC} if it is projective, consistent, and commuting for $\game$.
   179	  Additionally, we say that a PCC strategy $\strategy$ is \emph{SPCC} if it is furthermore symmetric.
   180	\end{definition}
   181	
   182	
   183	Recall that for a (pure) state $\ket{\psi}\in \mH_\alice \otimes \mH_\bob$, the \emph{Schmidt rank} of $\ket{\psi}$ is the smallest integer $k$ such that 
   184	\[ \ket{\psi} = \sum_{i=1}^k\, \alpha_i \ket{u_i}\otimes \ket{v_i}\;,\]
   185	for some orthonormal families $\{\ket{u_i}\}\subset \mH_\alice$ and $\{\ket{v_i}\}\subset\mH_\bob$ and $\alpha_i>0$. The coefficients $\alpha_i$ are uniquely defined by $\ket{\psi}$ and called \emph{Schmidt coefficients}. The state $\ket{\psi}$ is called \emph{maximally entangled} if $\alpha_i=\frac{1}{\sqrt{k}}$ for all $i=1,\ldots,k$.  
   186	
   187	
   188	\begin{definition}[Entanglement requirements of a game]
   189	  \label{def:ent}
   190		For all games $\game$ and $\nu \in [0, 1]$, let $\Ent(\game, \nu)$ denote the
   191	  minimum integer $d$ such that there exists a finite dimensional tensor product
   192	  strategy $\strategy$ that achieves success probability at least $\nu$ in the
   193	  game $\game$ with a state $\ket{\psi}$ whose Schmidt rank is at most $d$.
   194	  If there is no finite dimensional strategy that achieves success probability
   195	  $\nu$, then define $\Ent(\game, \nu)$ to be $\infty$.
   196	\end{definition}
   197	
   198	
   199	
   200	\begin{remark}
   201	  A strategy $\strategy = (\ket{\psi},A,B)$ for a symmetric game $\game =
   202	  (\cal{X}, \cal{X}, \cal{A}, \cal{A}, \mu, D)$ is called \emph{synchronous} if
   203	  it holds that for every $x\in \cal{X}$ and $a\neq b \in \cal{A}$, $\bra{\psi}
   204	  A^x_a \otimes B^x_b \ket{\psi} = 0$; in other words,
   205	  the players never return different answers when simultaneously asked the same
   206	  question.
   207	  As shown in~\cite{paulsen2016estimating} the condition for a
   208	  finite-dimensional strategy of being synchronous is equivalent to the
   209	  condition that it is projective, consistent, and moreover $\ket{\psi}$ is a
   210	  maximally entangled state.
   211	  (The equivalence is extended to infinite-dimensional strategies, as well as
   212	  correlations induced by limits of finite-dimensional strategies,
   213	  in~\cite{kim2018synchronous}.)
   214	\end{remark}
   215	\subsection{Distance measures}
   216	
   217	We introduce several distance measures that are used throughout.
   218	
   219	\begin{definition}[Distance between states]
   220	  \label{def:state-distance}
   221	
   222		Let $\{\ket{\psi_n}\}_{n\in \N}$ and $\{\ket{\psi'_n}\}_{n\in \N}$ be two
   223	  families of states in the same space $\mH$.
   224	  For some function $\delta : \N \to [0,1]$ we say that $\{ \ket{\psi_n} \}$ and
   225	  $\{ \ket{\psi'_n} \}$ are \emph{$\delta$-close}, denoted as $\ket{\psi}
   226	  \approx_\delta \ket{\psi'}$, if $ \norm{\ket{\psi_n} - \ket{\psi'_n}}^2 =
   227	  O(\delta(n))$.
   228	  (For convenience we generally leave the dependence of the states and $\delta$
   229	  on the indexing parameter $n$ implicit, writing e.g.\ $\ket{\psi}$ for $\ket{\psi_n}$.)
   230	\end{definition}
   231	
   232	\begin{definition}[Consistency between POVMs]
   233	  \label{def:consistency}
   234		Let $\mX$ be a finite set and $\mu$ a distribution on $\mX$.
   235	  Let $\ket{\psi} \in \cal{H}_A \otimes \cal{H}_B$ be a quantum state, and for
   236	  all $x\in \mX$, $\{A^x_a\}$ and $\{B^x_a\}$ POVMs.
   237	  We write
   238	  \begin{equation*}
   239	    A^x_a \otimes I_\bob \simeq_\delta I_\alice \otimes B^x_a
   240	  \end{equation*}
   241	  on state $\ket{\psi}$ and distribution $\mu$ if
   242	  \begin{equation*}
   243	    \E_{x\sim \mu} \sum_{a\ne b} \bra{\psi} A^x_a \otimes B^x_b \ket{\psi}
   244	    = O(\delta)\;.\footnote{Here the use of the $O(\cdot)$ notation refers to the fact that the notation will often be used to measure consistency for \emph{famillies} of POVM and states indexed by an implicit parameter $n\in \mathbb{N}$, which will always be clear from context but omitted for legibility, see Definition~\ref{def:state-distance}. The $O(\cdot)$ is taken as $n\to\infty$.}
   245	  \end{equation*}
   246	  In this case, we say that $\{A^x_a\}$ and $\{B^x_a\}$ are
   247	  \emph{$\delta$-consistent} on $\ket{\psi}$.
   248	\end{definition}
   249	
   250	Note that a consistent measurement on $\ket{\psi}$ according to
   251	Definition~\ref{def:consistent-measurement} is $0$-consistent with itself on the same $\ket{\psi}$ and under
   252	the singleton distribution, according to Definition~\ref{def:consistency} (and
   253	vice-versa). This is because 
   254	\[ \sum_a \bra{\psi} M_a \otimes M_a \ket{\psi} =1 \,\implies \, \forall a\;,\;\Id\otimes M_a \ket{\psi} = M_a \otimes \Id \ket{\psi}\;,\]
   255	because using that $\{M_a\}$ is a POVM there must be equality in the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality
   256	\[ 1 = \sum_a \bra{\psi} M_a \otimes M_a \ket{\psi}\, \leq\, \Big(\sum_a \|\Id\otimes M_a \ket{\psi}\|^2 \Big)\Big(\sum_a \|M_a\otimes \Id \ket{\psi}\|^2 \Big)^{1/2} \,\leq\,1 \;.\]
   257	
   258	\begin{definition}[Distance between POVMs]
   259	  \label{def:povm-distance}
   260		Let $\mX$ be a finite set and $\mu$ a distribution on $\mX$. 
   261	  Let $\ket{\psi} \in \cal{H}$ be a quantum state, and for all $x\in \mX$,
   262	  $\{M^x_a\}$ and $\{N^x_a\}$ two POVMs on $\mH$.
   263	  We say that \emph{$\{M^x_a\}$ and $\{N^x_a\}$ are $\delta$-close on state
   264	    $\ket{\psi}$ and under distribution $\mu$} if
   265	  \begin{equation*}
   266	    \E_{x\sim \mu} \sum_a \norm{ (M^x_a - N^x_a) \ket{\psi} }^2 \leq O(\delta)\;,
   267	  \end{equation*}
   268	  and we write $M^x_a \approx_\delta N^x_a$ to denote this when the state
   269	  $\ket{\psi}$ and distribution $\mu$ are clear from context.
   270	  This distance is referred to as the \emph{state-dependent} distance.
   271	\end{definition}
   272	
   273	\begin{definition}[Distance between strategies]
   274	  \label{def:strategy-distance}
   275	  Let $\game = (\cal{X}, \cal{Y}, \cal{A}, \cal{B}, \mu, D)$ be a nonlocal game
   276	  and let $\strategy = (\psi, A, B)$, $\strategy' = (\psi', A', B')$ be 
   277	  strategies for $\game$.
   278	  For $\delta\in[0,1]$ we say that \emph{$\strategy$ is $\delta$-close to
   279	    $\strategy'$} if the following conditions hold.
   280	  \begin{enumerate}
   281		\item The states $\ket{\psi}, \ket{\psi'}$ are states in the same
   282	    Hilbert space $\mH_A \otimes \mH_B$ and are $\delta$-close.
   283		\item For all $x \in \cal{X}, y \in \cal{Y}$, we have $A^x_a \approx_\delta
   284	    (A')^x_a$ and $B^y_b \approx_\delta (B')^y_b$, with the approximations
   285	    holding under the distribution $\mu$, and on either $\ket{\psi}$ or
   286	    $\ket{\psi'}$.
   287	  \end{enumerate}
   288	\end{definition}
   289	
   290	We record several useful facts about the consistency measure and the
   291	state-dependent distance without proof.

     1	\section{Types}
     2	\label{sec:types}
     3	
     4	We augment the definition of conditionally linear functions with a construct
     5	we call \emph{types}.
     6	A type~$\tvar$ is an element of a \emph{type set} $\type$, and a $\type$-typed
     7	family of conditionally linear functions is a collection
     8	$\{L_\tvar\}_{\tvar\in\type}$ containing a CL function $L_\tvar$ for each
     9	type~$\tvar\in\type$.
    10	The utility of this definition is that it allows us to define another object,
    11	namely conditionally linear distributions parameterized by an undirected graph
    12	$G = (\type, E)$ on the set of types known as a \emph{type graph}.
    13	Given two $\type$-typed families of conditionally linear functions
    14	$\{L_\lvar\}_{\lvar\in\type}, \{R_\rvar\}_{\rvar\in\type}$, the $(\type,
    15	G)$-typed conditionally linear distribution corresponding to them is the
    16	distribution which samples a pair of types $(\lvar, \rvar)$ uniformly at random
    17	from the edges of~$G$ (with each endpoint having equal probability as being
    18	chosen for $\lvar$ or $\rvar$, respectively) and then samples $(x, y)$ from
    19	$\mu_{L_\lvar,\, R_\rvar}$.
    20	The output is the pair $( (\lvar, x), (\rvar, y) )$.
    21	
    22	The normal form verifiers we present in the paper frequently use typed CL
    23	distributions to sample their questions, rather than untyped CL distributions.
    24	Types allow us to model the parts of their question distributions which are
    25	unstructured and unsuitable for being sampled from CL distributions.
    26	A common use of types is to allow the verifier to use previously defined games
    27	as subroutines.
    28	Here, the type helps indicate which subroutine the verifier selects, and an edge
    29	in the type graph between two different types allows us to introduce a test that
    30	cross-checks the results of one subroutine with the results of another.
    31	
    32	Finally, we show how to convert any typed CL distribution into an equivalent (in
    33	the precise sense defined below) untyped CL distribution with two additional
    34	levels, a technique we call \emph{detyping}.
    35	This entails showing how to ``simulate'' the \emph{graph distribution} of $G =
    36	(\type, E)$, i.e.\ the uniform distribution on its edges, using an untyped CL
    37	distribution.
    38	The simulation we give is based on rejection sampling and is only approximate:
    39	its quality degrades exponentially with the number of types in~$\type$.
    40	As a result, we will ensure throughout the paper that all type sets we consider
    41	are of a small, in fact generally constant, size.
    42	
    43	This section is organized as follows.
    44	In \cref{sec:typed-samplers} we define typed variants of CL distributions,
    45	samplers, deciders, and verifiers.
    46	In \cref{sec:graph-dist} we define a CL distribution which samples from the
    47	graph distribution of a given graph $G = (\type, E)$.
    48	In \cref{sec:detype} we define a canonical way to detype typed samplers,
    49	deciders, and verifiers using the graph sampler from \cref{sec:graph-dist}.
    50	We then prove the main result of the section, \cref{lem:detyping-verifiers},
    51	which relates the value of the detyped normal form verifier to the value of
    52	the original typed verifier.

    54	\subsection{Typed samplers, deciders, and verifiers}
    55	\label{sec:typed-samplers}
    56	
    57	\begin{definition}[Typed conditionally linear functions]
    58	  Let $\type$ be a finite set and $V$ be $\F^n$ for some integer $n \geq 0$.
    59	  A \emph{$\type$-typed family of $\ell$-level conditionally linear functions}
    60	  (implicitly, \emph{on $V$}) is a collection $\{L_\tvar\}_{\tvar \in \type}$
    61	  such that, for each $\tvar \in \type$, $L_\tvar$ is an $\ell$-level
    62	  conditionally linear function on~$V$.
    63	\end{definition}
    64	
    65	\begin{definition}[Graph distribution]
    66	  \label{def:graph-distribution}
    67	  Let $G = (U, E)$ be an undirected graph with vertex set $U$ and edge set~$E$.
    68	  Edges in~$E$ are written as multisets $\{u, v\}$ of two vertices; the case $u
    69	  = v$ represents a self-loop.
    70	  Suppose there are $m$ edges, $k$ of which are self-loops.
    71	  Then the \emph{graph distribution $\mu_G$ of~$G$} is the distribution over
    72	  $U\times U$ such that for every $(u, v)\in U\times U$,
    73	  \begin{equation*}
    74	    \mu_G(u, v) =
    75	    \begin{cases}
    76	      1/(2m-k) & \text{if $\{u, v\} \in E$},\\
    77	      0 & \text{otherwise}.
    78	    \end{cases}
    79	  \end{equation*}
    80	  This is identical to the uniform distribution over pairs $(u, v)\in U\times U$
    81	  such that $\{u, v\} \in E$.
    82	\end{definition}
    83	
    84	\begin{definition}[Typed conditionally linear distributions]
    85	  Let $\type$ be a type set and
    86	  $L=\{L_\lvar\}_{\lvar\in\type},R=\{R_\rvar\}_{\rvar\in\type}$ be $\type$-typed
    87	  families of conditionally linear functions on~$V$.
    88	  Let $G = (\type, E)$ be a graph with vertex set $\type$.
    89	  The \emph{$(\type, G)$-typed conditionally linear distribution $\mu_{L,\,
    90	      R}^G$ corresponding to~$(L, R)$} is the distribution over pairs $( (\lvar,
    91	  x), (\rvar, y) )$, where $(\lvar, \rvar)$ is drawn from $\mu_G$ and $(x,y)$ is
    92	  drawn from $\mu_{L_\lvar,\, R_\rvar}$.
    93	\end{definition}
    94	
    95	\begin{definition}[Typed conditionally linear samplers]
    96	  \label{def:typed-sampler}
    97		Let $q:\N \to \N$ be an admissible field size function and $s: \N \to \N$ be a
    98	  function.
    99	  Let $\type$ be a finite type set and let $G = (\type, E)$ be a graph with vertex set $\type$.
   100	  A $7$-input Turing machine $\sampler$ is a \emph{$(\type, G)$-typed, $\ell$-level
   101	    conditionally linear sampler with field size $q(n)$ and dimension $s(n)$} if
   102	  for all $n \in \N$, letting $q = q(n)$ and $s = s(n)$, there exist
   103	  $\type$-typed families of $\ell$-level conditionally linear functions
   104	  $\{L^{\alice,\, n}_{\tvar}\}_{\tvar \in \type}$ and $\{L^{\bob,\,
   105	    n}_{\tvar}\}_{\tvar \in \type}$ on $V = \F_q^s$ where $\tvar \in \type, w\in
   106	  \AB$, the conditionally linear function $L^{w,\, n}_{\tvar}$ has marginal
   107	  functions $\{L^{w,\, n}_{\tvar,\, \leq j}\}$ and factor spaces $\{V^{w,\,
   108	    n}_{\tvar,\, j,\, u}\}$ satisfying the conditions of Lemma~\ref{lem:cl-kth},
   109	  and for all $\tvar \in \type$, $w \in \ab$, $j \in \{1, \ldots, \ell\}$, and
   110	  $z \in V$:
   111	  \begin{itemize}
   112	  \item On input $(n, \gamestyle{dimension})$, the sampler $\sampler$ returns
   113	    the dimension $s(n)$.
   114		
   115		\item On input $(n, w, \gamestyle{marginal}, j, z, \tvar)$, the sampler
   116	    $\sampler$ returns the binary representation of $L^{w,\, n}_{\tvar,\, \le
   117	      j}(z)$.
   118				
   119				\item On input $(n, w, \gamestyle{linear}, j, u, y, \tvar)$, the sampler $\sampler$
   120	    outputs the binary representation of $L^{w,\, n}_{\tvar,\, j,\, u}(y)$,
   121	
   122		\item On input $(n, w, \gamestyle{factor}, j, u, \tvar)$, the sampler
   123	    $\sampler$ returns the factor space $V^{w,\, n}_{\tvar,\, j,\, u}$ of
   124	    $L^{w,\, n}_{\tvar}$, represented as an indicator vector in $\{0,1\}^s$.
   125	  \end{itemize}
   126	  We call $\F_{q(n)}^{s(n)}$ the \emph{ambient space of $\sampler$}.
   127	  We call $\{ L^{\alice,\, n}_{\tvar} \}, \{ L^{\bob,\, n}_{\tvar} \}$ the
   128	  \emph{CL functions of $\sampler$ on index $n$}.
   129	  The \emph{time complexity} of $\sampler$, denoted $\TIME_\sampler(n)$, is the
   130	  number of steps before $\sampler$ halts for index $n$.
   900	\label{sec:qld-game}
   901	
   902	We start by discussing parameter settings.
   903	The game $\game^\pauli$ is parametrized by a tuple
   904	\[\qldparams = (q,m,d)\;,\] where $q,m,d \in \N$ are integers. 
   905	We sometimes write $\game^\pauli_\qldparams$ to emphasize the dependence of the
   906	Pauli basis test on the parameters.
   907	
   908	Informally, the test is meant to certify that the players share a state of the
   909	form $\ket{\EPR_q}^{\otimes M}$, where $M=2^m$.
   910	Its question set includes questions that are axis-parallel/diagonal lines and points in $\F_q^m$,
   911	which are meant to correspond to questions in the classical low-degree test, and questions
   912	of the form $(\Pauli, W)$, for $W \in \{X, Z\}$.
   913	Upon receipt of a question of the latter form, the players are expected to
   914	perform the POVM $\{\tau_h^W\}_{h \in \F_q^{M}}$ and report the outcome $h$ as
   915	their answer.
   916	
   917	The key idea behind the test
   918	is for the provers to encode their outcomes using the \emph{low-degree encoding} from Section~\ref{sec:ld-encoding}.
   919	Given an outcome $h \in \F_q^M$, the low-degree encoding of~$h$ is the polynomial $g_h:\F_q^m \rightarrow \F_q$.
   920	Rather than asking the provers to always return the entire string~$h$,
   921	many of the subtests in the game $\game^\pauli$ will ``probe'' limited information about~$h$ as follows:
   922	the verifier provides the provers with a string $u_W \in \F_q^m$,
   923	and using this they are expected to evaluate $g_h(u_W) \in \F_q$ and return it to the verifier.
   924	For a fixed value of~$W$, then, the prover's responses to these ``probes'' should be consistent with some low-degree polynomial in the input~$u_W$.
   925	To check this, the verifier can perform the classical low-degree test from Section~\ref{sec:ld-verifier}.
   926	This ensures that the prover's responses for the $W = X$ basis are consistent with each other,
   927	as well as their responses for the $W = Z$ basis, although it does not test consistency between the $X$ and $Z$ responses.
   928	
   929	The next set of subtests the verifier performs ensure that the provers' $X$ and $Z$ measurements are consistent with each other.
   930	On the $X$ side, consider the measurement in which the prover performs the $\{\tau_h^X\}$ POVM,
   931	receives outcome $h_X$, and outputs $g_{h_X}(u_X) \in \F_q$.
   932	For technical reasons that will become clear shortly,
   933	it will be convenient for the prover's measurement to have two outcomes rather than~$q$ outcomes.
   934	To accomplish this, the verifier also provides the prover with an element $r_X \in \F_q$;
   935	given this, the prover should output not $g_{h_X}(u_X) \in \F_q$ but $\tr(g_{h_X}(u_X) \cdot r_X)$, which is an element of $\F_2$.
   936	Similarly, on the $Z$ side, suppose the prover is provided $r_Z \in \F_q$,
   937	performs $\{\tau_h^Z\}$ to receive $h_Z$, and outputs $\tr(g_{h_Z}(u_Z) \cdot r_Z) \in \F_2$.
   938	Together, these two are a pair of two-outcome measurements, one in the~$X$ basis and one in the~$Z$ basis,
   939	and as it turns out, this pair of measurements either commutes with each other or anticommutes with each other
   940	(this is why we modified the measurements to have only two outcomes).
   941	The key quantity to determine which of these is the case is the following complicated-looking expression:
   942	\begin{equation*}
   943	\gamma = \tr \bigl( (\ind_{m}(u_\xpt) \cdot r_\xpt) \cdot
   944	      (\ind_{m}(u_\zpt) \cdot r_\zpt) \bigr)\;.
   945	\end{equation*}
   946	If $\gamma = 0$, then these two measurements commute, and if $\gamma = 1$, then these two measurements anticommute
   947	(this fact is established in the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:pauli-completeness} below).
   948	In the $\gamma = 0$ case, the verifier can check whether these two measurements commute by performing the ``commutation check'',
   949	which asks the provers to simultaneously measure both $\tr(g_{h_X}(u_X) \cdot r_X)$ and $\tr(g_{h_Z}(u_Z) \cdot r_Z)$ and report their values.
   950	In the $\gamma = 1$ case, on the other hand, the measurements anticommute, which implies that they cannot simultaneously be measured.
   951	In spite of this, the verifier can still check that the measurements anticommute by using the Magic Square game from Section~\ref{sec:ms} above.
   952	As was shown in Theorem~\ref{thm:ms-from-ac}, any pair of anticommuting measurements
   953	can be used to form a perfect strategy for the Magic Square game
   954	(and indeed the reverse is true as well: any perfect strategy for the Magic Square game entails a pair of anticommuting measurements).
   955	
   956	Together, these give the main subtests for the game $\game^\pauli$.
   957	
   958	\begin{definition}[Admissible parameters]\label{def:admissible}
   959	  We say that the tuple $\qldparams=(q, m, d)$ is \emph{admissible} if $q$ is
   960	  an admissible field size (Definition~\ref{def:admissible-size}) and $m | q$.
   961	\end{definition}
   962	
   963	
   964	\paragraph{Question distribution.}
   965	We now describe the question distribution of the game $\game^\pauli$, and show
   966	that it is a (typed) CL distribution.
   967	The question types in the game $\game^\pauli$ are
   968	\begin{equation}
   969	  \label{eq:pauli-type}
   970	  \type^\pauli= \bigl( \{\Point, \ALine, \DLine, \Pauli, \Pair \} \times \{X,Z\} \bigr)
   971	  \cup \type^\ms \cup \{\Pair\}\;,
   972	\end{equation}
   973	where $\type^\ms$ is the question type set of the Magic Square game defined in
   974	Section~\ref{sec:ms}.
   975	
   976	
   977	
   978	
   979	Before presenting the CL functions of the Pauli basis test, we first give an
   980	intuitive description of the question distribution of the Pauli basis test: a
   981	pair of questions $((\tvar_\alice, x_\alice), (\tvar_\bob, x_\bob))$ in
   982	$\game^\pauli$ can be sampled via the following procedure:
   983	
   984	\begin{enumerate}
   985	\item Sample a pair of types by sampling an edge $(\tvar_\alice, \tvar_\bob)$ of
   986	  the graph $G^\pauli$ given in Figure~\ref{fig:type-graph-pauli} uniformly at
   987	  random (including the self-loops).
   988	\item Sample the following uniformly at random:
   989		\begin{enumerate}
   990		\item (\emph{Points}) $u_\xpt,u_\zpt \in \F_q^m$,
   991		\item (\emph{Directions}) $s \in \F_q$, $v \in \F_q^m$,
   992	  \item (\emph{Qubit basis for (anti-)commutation}) $r_\xpt,r_\zpt \in \F_q$.
   993		\end{enumerate}
   994	\item For $w \in \AB$ and $W\in\{X,Z\}$,
   995		\begin{enumerate}
   996	  \item If $\tvar_w = (\Point, W)$, then set $x_w = u_W$,
   997	  \item If $\tvar_w = (\ALine, W)$, then set $x_w = (u_0,s)$, where $u_0 =
   998	    L^\lnf_{e_i}(u_W)$, with $i = \chi(s)$ (see \Cref{sec:ld-game} for
   999	    definition of $L^\lnf$ and $\chi(s)$),
  1000	  \item If $\tvar_w = (\DLine,W)$, then set $x_w = (u_0,s,v')$, where $i =
  1001	    \chi(s)$, $v' = \pi_{i-1}(v)$, and $u_0 = L^\lnf_{v'}(u_W)$,
  1002	  \item If $\tvar_w = \Constraint_i$ for some $i\in\{1,\ldots,6\}$, then set
  1003	    $x_w = (u_\xpt, u_\zpt, r_\xpt, r_\zpt)$,
  1004	  \item If $\tvar_w = \Variable_j$ for some $j\in\{1,\ldots,9\}$, then set $x_w
  1005	    = (u_\xpt, u_\zpt, r_\xpt, r_\zpt)$,
  1006	  \item If $\tvar_w = \Pair$, then set $x_w = (u_\xpt, u_\zpt, r_\xpt, r_\zpt)$,
  1007	  \item If $\tvar_w = (\Pair, W)$, then set $x_w = (u_\xpt, u_\zpt, r_\xpt, r_\zpt)$,
  1008	  \item If $\tvar_w = (\Pauli, W)$, then set $x_w = 0$.
  1009		\end{enumerate}
  1010	\end{enumerate}

178	\paragraph{Question distribution.}
   179	We now present the question distribution of the game $\game^\ld$ as a typed CL
   180	distribution (see \Cref{sec:types} for the definition of typed CL functions and
   181	typed CL distributions).
   182	The type set $\type^\ld$ of the game $\game^\ld$ we use is
   183	\[
   184		\type^\ld = \{ \Point, \ALine, \DLine \}\;.
   185	\]
   186	The distribution over question types is uniform over $\type^\ld \times \type^\ld$. 
   187	
   188	We introduce the corresponding typed CL functions $L_\Point$, $L_\ALine$,
   189	$L_\DLine$ where the corresponding CL distributions $\mu_{L_\ALine,L_\Point}$
   190	and $\mu_{L_\DLine,L_\Point}$ implement the axis line-versus-point and diagonal
   191	line-versus-point distributions, respectively.
   192	The functions are parametrized by a field size $q$, a dimension $m$, and three
   193	complementary register subspaces $V_\xpt,V_{\coord}, V_{\dir{}}$ of some ambient
   194	space.
   195	The register $V_\xpt$ (which is isomorphic to $\F_q^m$) is called the
   196	\emph{point register}, $V_\coord$ (which is isomorphic to $\F_q$) is called the
   197	\emph{coordinate register}, and $V_{\dir{}}$ (which is isomorphic to $\F_q^m$)
   198	is called the \emph{direction register}, respectively.
   199	We let $V$ denote the direct sum $V_\xpt \oplus V_{\coord} \oplus V_{\dir{}}$.
   200	We identify elements of $V$ as triples $(u,s,v) \in \F_q^m \times \F_q \times
   201	\F_q^m$.
   202	
   203	Define $L_\Point$ to be the $1$-level CL function that projects onto $V_\xpt$: for every $(u,s,v) \in V$,
   204	\begin{equation}
   205	  \label{eq:cl-ptf}
   206		L_\Point(u,s,v) = (u,0,0) \;.
   207	\end{equation}
   208	Define $L_\ALine$ to be the following $2$-level CL function:
   209	\begin{equation}
   210	  \label{eq:cl-alnf}
   211		L_\ALine(u,s,v) = (L^\lnf_{e_i}(u), s, 0)\ \text{for all } (u,s,v) \in V,
   212	\end{equation}
   213	where $L^\lnf$ is the linear function used to compute the canonical
   214	representative of lines (see \Cref{def:line-representative}), and $i = \chi(s)$
   215	where we define $\chi(s)$ to be the unique integer such that
   216	\begin{equation}
   217	\label{eq:chi-func}
   218		s = (\chi(s) - 1) \frac{q}{m} + r
   219	\end{equation}
   220	for some $0 \leq r < q/m$, and we interpret the field element $s \in \F_q$ as an
   221	integer between $0$ and $q - 1$).
   222	The function $L_\ALine$ is the concatenation of the $1$-level CL function that
   223	projects the subspaces $V_{\coord} \oplus V_{\dir{}}$ down to $V_\coord$ (i.e.
   224	zeroes out the entire $V_{\dir{}}$ register), and the family of $1$-level CL
   225	functions $\{L^\lnf_{e_i} \}$ acting on $V_\xpt$, indexed by $i \in
   226	\{1,2,\ldots,m\}$.
   227	(See \Cref{lem:cl-concat} for definition of CL function concatenation.)
   228	Thus $L_\ALine$ is a $2$-level CL function.
   229	
   230	Define $L_\DLine$ to be the following $3$-level CL function: for all $(u,s,v) \in
   231	V$,
   232	\begin{equation}
   233	\label{eq:cl-dlnf}
   234		L_\DLine(u,s,v) = (L^\lnf_{\pi_{i-1}(v)}(u),s,\pi_{i-1}(v))
   235	\end{equation}
   236	where $i = \chi(s)$.
   237	The function $L_\DLine$ is the concatenation of the following CL functions (again, see \Cref{lem:cl-concat} for definition of CL function concatenation): (i) the identity function on $V_{\coord}$ (which is a $1$-level CL function); (ii) for every $i \in \{1,2,\ldots,m\}$ the $1$-level CL function on $V_{\dir{}}$ that maps $v \mapsto \pi_{i-1}(v)$ (i.e.~it zeroes out the first $i-1$ coordinates of $v$), and (iii) for every pair $(s,v') \in V_\coord \oplus V_{\dir{}}$, the $1$-level CL function $L^\lnf_{v'}$ acting on $V_\xpt$. Thus $L_\DLine$ is a $3$-level CL function.
   238

   240	The following two lemmas establish that the CL functions
   241	$L_\Point,L_\ALine,L_\DLine$ give rise to the axis-parallel line-versus-point and
   242	diagonal line-versus-point distributions.
   243	\begin{lemma}
   244		\label{lem:alnf}
   245		Consider the pair $(\line, u)$ sampled in the following way: first, sample the
   246	  tuple $((u_0,s,0),(u,0,0))$ from the CL distribution $\mu_{L_\ALine,L_\Point}$,
   247	  and let $\line = \line(u_0,e_i)$ where $i = \chi(s)$.
   248	  Then $u$ is a uniformly random point in $\F_q^m$ and $\line$ is a line that
   249	  goes through $u$ and is parallel to a uniformly random axis $i \in
   250	  \{1,2,\ldots,m\}$.
   251	\end{lemma}
   252	\begin{proof}
   253		Since $s$ is uniformly random in $\F_q$ and $m$ divides $q$ by assumption, we
   254	  have that $i$ is uniformly random between $\{1,2,\ldots,m\}$ and therefore
   255	  $(u_0,s)$ specifies a uniformly random axis-parallel line $\line(u_0,e_i)$.
   256	  Since $u_0 = L^{\lnf}_{e_i}(u)$, we have that $u \in \line(u_0,e_i)$.
   257	\end{proof}
   258	
   259	
   260	
   261	\begin{lemma}
   262		\label{lem:dlnf}
   263		Consider the pair $(\line,u)$ sampled in the following way: first, sample the
   264	  tuple $((u_0,s,v),(u,0,0))$ from the CL distribution $\mu_{L_\DLine,L_\Point}$,
   265	  and let $\line = \line(u_0,v)$ where $i = \chi(s)$.
   266	  Then $u$ is a uniformly random point in $\F_q^m$ and $\line$ is a random
   267	  diagonal line that goes through $u$ and shares the first $i-1$ coordinates
   268	  with $u$, for uniformly random $i$.
   269	\end{lemma}
   270	\begin{proof}
   271		The proof of this follows identically to \Cref{lem:alnf}.
   272	\end{proof}

   276	\begin{definition}[Line-point distributions]
   277	        \label{def:line-point-dist}
   278	 The \emph{axis line-point distribution} $D_{\ALine}$ is the
   279	 distribution $\mu_{L_\ALine,L_\Point}$ over pairs $(\ell=(u_0,e_i),u)$
   280	 (we omit the $0$ elements for simplicity). The \emph{diagonal
   281	   line-point distribution} $D_{\DLine}$ is the distribution
   282	 $\mu_{L_\DLine,L_\Point}$  over $(\ell=(u_0,s,v),u)$. The
   283	 \emph{line-point distribution} $D_{\Line}$ is the equal mixture of the axis-parallel line-point distribution and the diagonal line-point distribution.
   284	 In other words, a sample from $D_{\Line}$ is distributed as follows:
   285	 with probability $\tfrac{1}{2}$, output a sample from $D_{\ALine}$,
   286	 and with probability $\tfrac{1}{2}$, output a sample from $D_{\DLine}$.
   287	\end{definition}

   320	\paragraph{Decision procedure} The decision procedure $\decider^\ld$ for the
   321	game $\game^\ld$ is presented in Figure~\ref{fig:ld-decider}.
   322	The table at the top specifies a parsing scheme for the questions and answers,
   323	depending on the type of question.
   324	For example, when a player receives a question with type $\Point$, the question
   325	content $x$, a bit string of length $m \log q$, should be interpreted by the
   326	decision procedure and the players as an element of the vector space $\F_q^m$,
   327	as indicated in Section~\ref{sec:ff-representations}.
   328	Similarly the answer to a question with type $\Point$ is expected to be a bit
   329	string of length $\ldc \log q$, and is interpreted as an element of $\F_q^\ldc$.
   330	For questions with type $\ALine$, the question content is a $(m \log q + \log
   331	q)$-bit string, which is parsed as a pair $(u_0, s) \in \F_q^m \times \F_q$,
   332	which in turn can be interpreted as a specification for an axis-parallel line
   333	$\line(u_0,e_i)$ in $\F_q^m$ where $i = \chi(s)$, as described in
   334	\Cref{lem:alnf}.
   335	The answer is interpreted as the description of $\ldc$ degree-$d$ univariate
   336	polynomials defined on the line $\line(u_0,e_i)$, each polynomial given by a
   337	list of $d+1$ coefficients.
   338	For questions with type $\DLine$, the question content is a $(2m \log q + \log
   339	q)$-bit string, which is parsed as a triple $(u_0, s, v) \in \F_q^m \times \F_q
   340	\times \F_q^m$ that specifies a diagonal line $\line(u_0,v')$ where $v' =
   341	\pi_{i-1}(v)$ as described in \Cref{lem:dlnf}.
   342	The answer is interpreted as the description of $\ldc$ degree-$md$ univariate
   343	polynomials defined on the line $\line(u_0,v')$.
   344	If the answers returned by the players do not fit this format the decision
   345	procedure rejects.

   394	We define a special class of measurements that are relevant to the soundness
   395	properties of the low-degree test.
   396	
   397	\begin{definition}[Low-degree polynomial measurements]
   398	  \label{def:ld-meas}
   399	  Define $\polymeas{m}{d}{q}$ to be the set of POVM measurements whose outcomes
   400	  correspond to (individual) degree-$d$ polynomials of $m$ variables over
   401	  $\F_q$.
   402	  More generally, for an integer $\ldc$ and tuples $m=(m_1, m_2, \ldots,
   403	  m_\ldc)$, $d=(d_1, d_2, \ldots, d_\ldc)$ and $q=(q_1, q_2, \ldots, q_\ldc)$,
   404	  we let $\simulpolymeas{m}{d}{q}{\ldc}$ be the set of measurements $G =
   405	  \{G_{g_1,\, g_2,\, \ldots\,,\, g_\ldc}\}$ such that for $i\in\{1, 2, \ldots,
   406	  \ldc\}$, $g_i$ is a polynomial $g_i:\F_{q_i}^{m_i} \rightarrow
   407	  \F_{q_i}$ with individual degree $d_i$ (see \Cref{sec:ld-encoding} for a definition of individual degree). 
   408	\end{definition}
   409	
   410	Quantum soundness of a version of the classical low-degree test for polynomials of low \emph{total} degree was claimed
   411	in~\cite{natarajan2018low}, building on an analysis of a three-prover version of the test in~\cite{vidick2016three}. Unfortunately there is a gap in the soundness analysis of this test. For our construction we use the low individual degree test, whose quantum soundness is shown in~\cite{ML20} and generalized in~\cite{ji2021quantum}. We state the result in the form that is most directly useful for us, and show how the stated result follows from~\cite{ji2021quantum}.

   413	\begin{theorem}[Quantum soundness of the simultaneous classical low-degree test]

   240	The following two lemmas establish that the CL functions
   241	$L_\Point,L_\ALine,L_\DLine$ give rise to the axis-parallel line-versus-point and
   242	diagonal line-versus-point distributions.
   243	\begin{lemma}
   244		\label{lem:alnf}
   245		Consider the pair $(\line, u)$ sampled in the following way: first, sample the
   246	  tuple $((u_0,s,0),(u,0,0))$ from the CL distribution $\mu_{L_\ALine,L_\Point}$,
   247	  and let $\line = \line(u_0,e_i)$ where $i = \chi(s)$.
   248	  Then $u$ is a uniformly random point in $\F_q^m$ and $\line$ is a line that
   249	  goes through $u$ and is parallel to a uniformly random axis $i \in
   250	  \{1,2,\ldots,m\}$.
   251	\end{lemma}
   252	\begin{proof}
   253		Since $s$ is uniformly random in $\F_q$ and $m$ divides $q$ by assumption, we
   254	  have that $i$ is uniformly random between $\{1,2,\ldots,m\}$ and therefore
   255	  $(u_0,s)$ specifies a uniformly random axis-parallel line $\line(u_0,e_i)$.
   256	  Since $u_0 = L^{\lnf}_{e_i}(u)$, we have that $u \in \line(u_0,e_i)$.
   257	\end{proof}

   261	\begin{lemma}
   262		\label{lem:dlnf}
   263		Consider the pair $(\line,u)$ sampled in the following way: first, sample the
   264	  tuple $((u_0,s,v),(u,0,0))$ from the CL distribution $\mu_{L_\DLine,L_\Point}$,
   265	  and let $\line = \line(u_0,v)$ where $i = \chi(s)$.
   266	  Then $u$ is a uniformly random point in $\F_q^m$ and $\line$ is a random
   267	  diagonal line that goes through $u$ and shares the first $i-1$ coordinates
   268	  with $u$, for uniformly random $i$.
   269	\end{lemma}

   276	\begin{definition}[Line-point distributions]
   277	        \label{def:line-point-dist}
   278	 The \emph{axis line-point distribution} $D_{\ALine}$ is the
   279	 distribution $\mu_{L_\ALine,L_\Point}$ over pairs $(\ell=(u_0,e_i),u)$
   280	 (we omit the $0$ elements for simplicity). The \emph{diagonal
   281	   line-point distribution} $D_{\DLine}$ is the distribution
   282	 $\mu_{L_\DLine,L_\Point}$  over $(\ell=(u_0,s,v),u)$. The
   283	 \emph{line-point distribution} $D_{\Line}$ is the equal mixture of the axis-parallel line-point distribution and the diagonal line-point distribution.
   284	 In other words, a sample from $D_{\Line}$ is distributed as follows:
   285	 with probability $\tfrac{1}{2}$, output a sample from $D_{\ALine}$,
   286	 and with probability $\tfrac{1}{2}$, output a sample from $D_{\DLine}$.
   287	\end{definition}

   320	\paragraph{Decision procedure} The decision procedure $\decider^\ld$ for the
   321	game $\game^\ld$ is presented in Figure~\ref{fig:ld-decider}.
   322	The table at the top specifies a parsing scheme for the questions and answers,
   323	depending on the type of question.
   324	For example, when a player receives a question with type $\Point$, the question
   325	content $x$, a bit string of length $m \log q$, should be interpreted by the
   326	decision procedure and the players as an element of the vector space $\F_q^m$,
   327	as indicated in Section~\ref{sec:ff-representations}.
   328	Similarly the answer to a question with type $\Point$ is expected to be a bit
   329	string of length $\ldc \log q$, and is interpreted as an element of $\F_q^\ldc$.
   330	For questions with type $\ALine$, the question content is a $(m \log q + \log
   331	q)$-bit string, which is parsed as a pair $(u_0, s) \in \F_q^m \times \F_q$,
   332	which in turn can be interpreted as a specification for an axis-parallel line
   333	$\line(u_0,e_i)$ in $\F_q^m$ where $i = \chi(s)$, as described in
   334	\Cref{lem:alnf}.
   335	The answer is interpreted as the description of $\ldc$ degree-$d$ univariate
   336	polynomials defined on the line $\line(u_0,e_i)$, each polynomial given by a
   337	list of $d+1$ coefficients.
   338	For questions with type $\DLine$, the question content is a $(2m \log q + \log
   339	q)$-bit string, which is parsed as a triple $(u_0, s, v) \in \F_q^m \times \F_q
   340	\times \F_q^m$ that specifies a diagonal line $\line(u_0,v')$ where $v' =
   341	\pi_{i-1}(v)$ as described in \Cref{lem:dlnf}.
   342	The answer is interpreted as the description of $\ldc$ degree-$md$ univariate
   343	polynomials defined on the line $\line(u_0,v')$.
   344	If the answers returned by the players do not fit this format the decision
   345	procedure rejects.

blueprint/src/chapter/ch13_qpbt_test.tex:108:	The source states the two line-versus-point clauses with ``the'' $t \in \F_q$ such that $x_{\overline w} = u_0 + t v$. When the direction is nonzero and $x_{\overline w}$ lies on the line, exactly one such $t$ exists and the formulation above agrees with the source. But zero directions occur: Definition~\ref{def:line} explicitly permits them, and the question distribution of Definition~\ref{def:ld-question-distribution} produces $\mathsf{DLine}$ questions with $v' = \pi_{i-1}(v) = 0$ with positive probability, namely whenever the last $m - i + 1$ coordinates of $v$ vanish. In that case $\ell(u_0, 0) = \{u_0\}$, every $t \in \F_q$ satisfies $x_{\overline w} = u_0 + t v'$ when $x_{\overline w} = u_0$, and the source clause does not determine acceptance for a nonconstant answer polynomial. The universal quantification over $t$ adopted in Definition~\ref{def:ld-win-predicate} makes the predicate a well-defined function of its arguments; it accepts vacuously when no such $t$ exists, a case the question distribution never produces. Completeness is unaffected: the restriction of a polynomial $g$ to the singleton line $\ell(u_0,0)$, expressed through the parameterization $t \mapsto u_0 + t \cdot 0$, is the constant polynomial with value $g(u_0)$, which passes the check for every $t$. Soundness is likewise unaffected: zero directions occur with probability at most $2/(mq)$, so any acceptance convention on this event changes success probabilities by at most that amount; the game-correspondence obligation enumerated in the proof of Theorem~\ref{lem:ld-soundness} accounts for this event explicitly, and an error of this shape is absorbed into the universal constants of $\delta_{\mathrm{ld}}$.

blueprint/src/chapter/ch13_qpbt_test.tex:172:		\item (\emph{Game correspondence.}) The source asserts that the two games are identical; they are not. In the cited test, the subcube commutation and pair-synchronicity branches send an ordered pair of points of a \emph{hidden} subcube and receive a pair of field values --- a question type that $\mathfrak{G}^{\mathrm{ld}}$ does not have --- its line questions carry no analogue of the seed $s$, its nontrivial cross-tests have mass $1/3$ where the present ones have $2/9$, and it fixes no acceptance convention on the zero-direction event of Remark~\ref{rem:ld-win-zero-direction}, whose probability is at most $\frac1m \sum_{j=1}^m q^{-j} \le \frac{1}{m(q-1)} \le \frac{2}{mq}$ over uniform $(s,v)$. What must be proved is a reduction converting any projective strategy for $\mathfrak{G}^{\mathrm{ld}}$ with success probability $1-\eps$ into a two-prover strategy for the tensor-code test with rejection probability at most $\tfrac32\,\eps + O(1/(mq))$ --- the factor $\tfrac32$ being the target bookkeeping constant from the branch weights, and the $O(1/(mq))$ the zero-direction term. A deficit of this shape is then absorbed into $\delta_{\mathrm{ld}}$ by enlarging the universal constant $a$, since $(x+y)^b \le x^b + y^b$ for $0 < b \le 1$ and $(2/(mq))^b \le 2\,q^{-b}$ for $m \ge 1$, using $dmk \ge 1$.
blueprint/src/chapter/ch13_qpbt_test.tex:328:	The question distribution of $\mathfrak{G}^{\mathrm{Pauli}}$ is the typed CL distribution on $\mathcal T^{\mathrm{pauli}} \times V^{\mathrm{pauli}} \times \mathcal T^{\mathrm{pauli}} \times V^{\mathrm{pauli}}$ obtained by sampling the type pair $(t_{\mathrm A}, t_{\mathrm B})$ from the graph distribution $\mu_{G^{\mathrm{pauli}}}$ of Definition~\ref{def:graph-distribution}, that is, uniformly at random among all ordered pairs of types whose underlying unordered pair $\{t_{\mathrm A}, t_{\mathrm B}\}$ is an edge of $G^{\mathrm{pauli}}$, self-loops included; sampling $z \in V^{\mathrm{pauli}}$ uniformly at random; and setting $x_w = L_{t_w}(z)$ for $w \in \{\mathrm A,\mathrm B\}$. Explicitly, if $z = (u_X,u_Z,s,v,r_X,r_Z)$, then a player whose type is $(\mathsf{Point},W)$ receives $u_W$; a player whose type is $(\mathsf{ALine},W)$ receives $(u_0, s)$ with $u_0 = L^{\mathrm{Ln}}_{e_i}(u_W)$ and $i = \chi(s)$; a player whose type is $(\mathsf{DLine},W)$ receives $(u_0, s, v')$ with $i = \chi(s)$, $v' = \pi_{i-1}(v)$, and $u_0 = L^{\mathrm{Ln}}_{v'}(u_W)$; a player whose type lies in $\mathcal T^{\mathrm{ms}} \cup \{\mathsf{Pair}, (\mathsf{Pair},X), (\mathsf{Pair},Z)\}$ receives $(u_X, u_Z, r_X, r_Z)$; and a player whose type is $(\mathsf{Pauli},W)$ receives $0$.

   512	\subsection{The Magic Square game}
   513	\label{sec:ms}
   514	
   515	We recall the \emph{Magic Square game} of Mermin and
   516	Peres~\cite{mermin1990simple,peres1990incompatible,aravind2002simple}.
   517	The Magic Square game is a simple self-test for EPR pairs (it tests for two of
   518	them). In addition, it allows one to test that a pair of observables
   519	\emph{anticommutes}.
   520	Here we use it as a building block to construct the quantum low-degree test. 
   521	
   522	There are several formulations of the Magic Square game; here we present it as a
   523	\emph{binary constraint satisfaction} game~\cite{cleve2014characterization}.
   524	In this formulation of the game (denoted by $\game_\MS$) there are $6$ linear
   525	equations defined over $9$ variables that take values in $\F_2$.
   526	The variables correspond to the cells of a $3 \times 3$ grid, as depicted in
   527	Figure~\ref{fig:ms}.
   528	Five of the equations correspond to the constraint that the sum of the variables
   529	in each row and the first two columns must be equal to $0$, and the last
   530	equation requires that the sum of the variables in the last column must be equal
   531	to $1$.
   532	
   533	\begin{figure}[ht!]
   534		\begin{center}
   535	    \renewcommand{\arraystretch}{1.6}
   536			\begin{tabular}{|c|c|c|}
   537				\hline
   538				$x_1$ & $x_2$ & $x_3$ \\
   539				\hline 
   540				$x_4$ & $x_5$ & $x_6$ \\	
   541				\hline
   542				$x_7$ & $x_8$ & $x_9$ \\
   543				\hline
   544			\end{tabular}
   545			\caption{The Magic Square game}
   546			\label{fig:ms}
   547			\end{center}
   548	\end{figure}
   549	
   550	The question set $\type^\ms$ of the Magic Square game is the following:
   551	\begin{equation*}
   552	  \begin{split}
   553	    \type^\msc & = \{ \Constraint_i : i = 1, 2, \ldots, 6\}\;,\\
   554	    \type^\msv & = \{ \Variable_j : j = 1, 2, \ldots, 9\}\;,\\
   555	    \type^\ms & = \type^\msc \cup \type^\msv\;.
   556	  \end{split}
   557	\end{equation*}
   558	The questions $\Constraint_i$ for $i \in \{1,2,3\}$ correspond to the three row
   559	constraints, the questions $\Constraint_4$, $\Constraint_5$ correspond to the first
   560	two column constraints, and question $\Constraint_6$ corresponds to the third
   561	column constraint.
   562	
   563	In the Magic Square game, the verifier first samples a constraint $\Constraint_i
   564	\in \type^\msc$ uniformly at random, and then samples $\Variable_j$, one of the
   565	three variables in the row or column corresponding to $\Constraint_i$, uniformly
   566	at random.
   567	One player is randomly assigned to be the $\Constraint$ player, and the other is
   568	assigned to be the $\Variable$ player.
   569	The $\Constraint$ player is sent the question $\Constraint_i$ and is expected to
   570	respond with three bits $(\beta_{v_1}, \beta_{v_2}, \beta_{v_3}) \in \F_2^3$,
   571	where $(v_1,v_2,v_3)$ are the indices of the three variables corresponding to
   572	$\Constraint_i$.
   573	The $\Variable$ player is given question $\Variable_j$ and is expected to
   574	respond with a single bit $\gamma \in \F_2$.
   575	The players win if the $\Constraint$ player's answers satisfy the equation
   576	associated with $\Constraint_i$, and $\gamma = \beta_j$.
   577	More precisely, the verifier samples an edge of the type graph (see Section~\ref{sec:types}) $G^\ms$
   578	in Fig.~\ref{fig:type-graph-ms}, sends one endpoint to a random player, and the
   579	other endpoint to the other player.
   580

   582	  \centering

    89	    | .bit γ => .inr γ

    91	    | .inl β => .triple β
    92	    | .inr γ => .bit γ

   103	/-- The Magic Square consistency predicate.  Constructor mismatches are
   104	rejected, as required by `def:ms-game` (blueprint lines 188-203; paper
   105	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:512-610`).
   106	-/
   107	def msWinPredicate :
   108	    MsType → MsType → MsAnswer → MsAnswer → Bool
   109	  | .constraint i, .constraint j, .triple β, .triple β' =>
   110	      decide (i = j ∧ β = β')
   111	  | .var i, .var j, .bit γ, .bit γ' =>
   112	      decide (i = j ∧ γ = γ')
   113	  | .constraint i, .var j, .triple β, .bit γ =>
   114	      decide
   115	        ((∑ k : Fin 3, β k) = msParity i ∧
   116	          ∃ k : Fin 3, msConstraintVars i k = j ∧ β k = γ)
   117	  | .var j, .constraint i, .bit γ, .triple β =>
   118	      decide
   119	        ((∑ k : Fin 3, β k) = msParity i ∧
   120	          ∃ k : Fin 3, msConstraintVars i k = j ∧ β k = γ)
   121	  | _, _, _, _ => false
   122	
   123	/-- The Magic Square game as a finite `Game`.  This is `def:ms-game` in
   124	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch13_qpbt_test.tex:188-203`, paper origin
   125	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:512-610`.
   126	-/
   127	noncomputable def msGame : Game where
   128	  QuestionA := MsType
   129	  QuestionB := MsType
   130	  AnswerA := MsAnswer
   131	  AnswerB := MsAnswer
   132	  μ := graphDistribution msEdges msEdges_nonempty
   133	  μ_prob := by sorry
   134	  decide := msWinPredicate

   358	  | pauliOutcome (a : PauliRegister P)
   359	  deriving DecidableEq
   360	
   361	/-- A finite sum code used only to construct the `Fintype` instance for the
   362	answer alphabet in `def:pauli-win-predicate`, blueprint
   363	`ch13_qpbt_test.tex:331-367`, paper origin
   364	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:1126-1225`.
   365	-/
   366	abbrev PauliAnswerCode (P : AdmissibleParams) :=
   367	  PauliScalar P ⊕
   368	    ((Fin (P.d + 1) → PauliScalar P) ⊕
   369	      ((Fin (P.m * P.d + 1) → PauliScalar P) ⊕
   370	        ((ZMod 2 × ZMod 2) ⊕
   371	          (ZMod 2 ⊕ ((Fin 3 → ZMod 2) ⊕ PauliRegister P)))))
   372	
   373	/-- The constructor-preserving finite-code equivalence for `PauliAnswer`.
   374	Lean-only infrastructure for `def:pauli-win-predicate`, blueprint
   375	`ch13_qpbt_test.tex:331-367`, paper origin
   376	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:1126-1225`.
   377	-/
   378	noncomputable def pauliAnswerEquiv (P : AdmissibleParams) :
   379	    PauliAnswer P ≃ PauliAnswerCode P where
   380	  toFun
   381	    | .value a => .inl a
   382	    | .alinePoly a => .inr (.inl a)
   383	    | .dlinePoly a => .inr (.inr (.inl a))
   384	    | .pairBits a => .inr (.inr (.inr (.inl a)))
   385	    | .bit a => .inr (.inr (.inr (.inr (.inl a))))
   386	    | .msTriple a => .inr (.inr (.inr (.inr (.inr (.inl a)))))
   387	    | .pauliOutcome a => .inr (.inr (.inr (.inr (.inr (.inr a)))))
   388	  invFun
   389	    | .inl a => .value a
   390	    | .inr (.inl a) => .alinePoly a
   391	    | .inr (.inr (.inl a)) => .dlinePoly a
   392	    | .inr (.inr (.inr (.inl a))) => .pairBits a
   393	    | .inr (.inr (.inr (.inr (.inl a)))) => .bit a
   394	    | .inr (.inr (.inr (.inr (.inr (.inl a))))) => .msTriple a
   395	    | .inr (.inr (.inr (.inr (.inr (.inr a))))) => .pauliOutcome a
   396	  left_inv := by
   397	    intro x
   398	    cases x <;> rfl
   399	  right_inv := by
   400	    intro x
   401	    cases x with
   402	    | inl a => rfl
   403	    | inr x =>
   404	        cases x with
   405	        | inl a => rfl
   406	        | inr x =>
   407	            cases x with
   408	            | inl a => rfl
   409	            | inr x =>
   410	                cases x with
   411	                | inl a => rfl
   412	                | inr x =>
   413	                    cases x with
   414	                    | inl a => rfl
   415	                    | inr x =>
   416	                        cases x with
   417	                        | inl a => rfl
   418	                        | inr a => rfl
   419	
   420	noncomputable instance (P : AdmissibleParams) : Fintype (PauliAnswer P) :=
   421	  Fintype.ofEquiv (PauliAnswerCode P) (pauliAnswerEquiv P).symm
   422	
   423	instance (P : AdmissibleParams) : Inhabited (PauliAnswer P) :=
   424	  ⟨.bit 0⟩

   102	/-- The register blocks used by the Pauli question space.  These are the

   107	abbrev PauliIndex (P : AdmissibleParams) :=
   108	  (((((Fin P.m ⊕ Fin P.m) ⊕ Unit) ⊕ Fin P.m) ⊕ Unit) ⊕ Unit)

   110	/-- The ambient Pauli question coefficient space (`def:pauli-question-distribution`,

   122	/- The nested sum is the fixed register order
   123	`V_X ⊕ V_Z ⊕ V_I ⊕ V_V ⊕ V_{R_X} ⊕ V_{R_Z}` from the blueprint. -/
   124	/-- The `V_X` block of an ambient Pauli vector (`def:pauli-question-distribution`,
   125	blueprint `ch13_qpbt_test.tex:285-329`; paper origin
   126	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:964-1120`). -/
   127	def pauliXBlock {P : AdmissibleParams} (z : PauliSpace P) : Fin P.m → PauliScalar P :=
   128	  fun i => z (.inl (.inl (.inl (.inl (.inl i)))))

   130	/-- The `V_Z` block of an ambient Pauli vector in `def:pauli-question-distribution`,

   132	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:964-1120`.

   134	def pauliZBlock {P : AdmissibleParams} (z : PauliSpace P) : Fin P.m → PauliScalar P :=
   135	  fun i => z (.inl (.inl (.inl (.inl (.inr i)))))
   136	
   137	/-- The scalar block `V_I` of an ambient Pauli vector in
   138	`def:pauli-question-distribution`, blueprint `ch13_qpbt_test.tex:285-329`,
   139	paper origin `references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:964-1120`.
   140	-/
   141	def pauliScalarBlock {P : AdmissibleParams} (z : PauliSpace P) : PauliScalar P :=
   142	  z (.inl (.inl (.inl (.inr ()))))
   143	
   144	/-- The direction block `V_V` of an ambient Pauli vector in
   145	`def:pauli-question-distribution`, blueprint `ch13_qpbt_test.tex:285-329`,
   146	paper origin `references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:964-1120`.
   147	-/
   148	def pauliDirectionBlock {P : AdmissibleParams} (z : PauliSpace P) : Fin P.m → PauliScalar P :=
   149	  fun i => z (.inl (.inl (.inr i)))
   150	
   151	/-- The `r_X` scalar block in the Pauli question content from
   152	`def:pauli-question-distribution`, blueprint `ch13_qpbt_test.tex:285-329`,
   153	paper origin `references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:964-1120`.
   154	-/
   155	def pauliRXBlock {P : AdmissibleParams} (z : PauliSpace P) : PauliScalar P :=
   156	  z (.inl (.inr ()))
   157	
   158	/-- The `r_Z` scalar block in the Pauli question content from
   159	`def:pauli-question-distribution`, blueprint `ch13_qpbt_test.tex:285-329`,
   160	paper origin `references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:964-1120`.

   162	def pauliRZBlock {P : AdmissibleParams} (z : PauliSpace P) : PauliScalar P :=

   164	
   165	/-- Select the basis-dependent point block from a Pauli question content in
   166	`def:pauli-question-distribution`, blueprint `ch13_qpbt_test.tex:285-329`,
   167	paper origin `references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:964-1120`.

   169	def pauliPointBlock {P : AdmissibleParams} (W : PauliKind) (z : PauliSpace P) :
   170	    Fin P.m → PauliScalar P :=
   171	  match W with
   172	  | .X => pauliXBlock z
   173	  | .Z => pauliZBlock z
   174	
   175	/-- Read the low-degree register selected by a basis from an ambient Pauli
   176	vector.  Lean-only coordinate plumbing for `def:pauli-question-distribution`,
   177	blueprint `ch13_qpbt_test.tex:285-329`, paper origin
   178	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:964-1120`.
