   102	\paragraph{Axis-parallel lines and diagonal lines.}
   103	Before presenting a formal description of the game $\game^\ld$, we first define
   104	what we mean by lines, and their properties.
   105	
   106	\begin{definition}[Lines]
   107	  \label{def:line}
   108		A \emph{line} $\line$ in $\F^m_q$ specified by a pair $(u,v) \in (\F_q^m)^2$
   109	  is the subset
   110	  \begin{equation}
   111	    \label{eq:line-set}
   112	    \line(u,v) = \bigl\{\, u + tv : t \in \F_q \,\bigr\} \subseteq \F_q^m \;.
   113	  \end{equation}
   114	  We call the vector $v$ a \emph{direction} of line
   115	  $\line(u,v)$.\footnote{For convenience we explicitly allow
   116	    $v=0$, in which case the line is reduced to a singleton.}
   117	  
   118	  A line $\line(u,v)$ is \emph{axis-parallel} if there is a coordinate $i \in
   119	  \{1,2,\ldots,m\}$ for which $v$ is equal to $e_i$, the $i$-th elementary basis
   120	  vector in $\F_q^m$.
   121	  We say that such a line $\line$ is \emph{parallel to the $i$-th direction}.
   122	  A line $\line(u,v)$ is \emph{diagonal} if there exists an $i \in
   123	  \{0,1,\ldots,m-1\}$ for which $v_1 = v_2 = \cdots = v_i = 0$.
   124	\end{definition}
   125	
   126	The following Proposition establishes that, for a fixed direction, a line
   127	$\line$ is an equivalence class of points on the line.
   128	\begin{proposition}
   129	  \label{prop:line-equiv}
   130	  Let $u,v \in \F_q^m$.
   131	  Then for all $u' \in \line(u,v)$, we have that $\line(u,v) = \line(u',v)$.
   132	\end{proposition}
   133	\begin{proof}
   134		Fix $u' \in \line(u,v)$.
   135	  We have that $u' = u + tv$ for some $t \in \F_q$.
   136	  Let $a \in \line(u,v)$.
   137	  This means that $a = u + sv$ for some $s\in \F_q$.
   138	  We also have that $a = u + (s - t + t)v = u + tv + (s - t)v = u' + (s - t)v$,
   139	  so $\line(u,v) \subseteq \line(u',v)$.
   140	  A similar argument shows that $\line(u',v) \subseteq \line(u,v)$.
   141	\end{proof}
   142	
   143	We now specify a canonical representation of lines $\line = \line(u,v)$ as pairs $(u_0,v)$
   144	where $u_0$ is a \emph{canonical representative} of $\line$ specified as
   145	follows.
   146	Let $L_v^{\lnf}: \F_q^m \to \F_q^m$ denote the canonical linear map with the
   147	one-dimensional kernel basis $\{v\}$ (see \Cref{def:cl-canonical} for a
   148	definition of canonical linear map).
   149	Note that for all $u \in \line$, we have that $L_v^{\lnf}(u)$ is a point in
   150	$\line$.
   151	This is because since the image and kernel of $L_v^{\lnf}$ are complementary
   152	subspaces by definition (see \Cref{def:cl-canonical}), any $u \in \F_q^m$ has a
   153	unique decomposition $u = u_0 + u_1$ where $u_0$ is in the image of $L_v^{\lnf}$
   154	and $u_1 \in \ker(L_v^{\lnf})$, which by definition is the subspace spanned by
   155	$v$.
   156	Thus $u_1 = tv$ for some $t \in \F_q$ and we have that $u_0 = u - tv \in \line$.
   157	In particular, if $u\in \line$ then $u_0 = L_v^{\lnf}(u) \in \line$ as well. 
   158	Furthermore, since $L_v^{\lnf}$ is a projection onto its image by definition, we
   159	have $L_v^{\lnf}(u_0) = u_0$.
   160	
   161	Next, note that for any $u,u' \in \line$, since $u-u' = sv$ for some $s\in \F_q$
   162	it follows that $L_v^\lnf(u) = L_v^\lnf(u')$.
   163	Thus $u_0 = u_0'$ and this shows that $L_v^\lnf$ gives a means to compute a
   164	canonical representative of lines.
   165	
   166	\begin{definition}[Canonical representative of a line]
   167	  \label{def:line-representative}
   168	  Let $\line$ be a line in direction $v$.
   169	  A canonical representative of $\line$ is the point $u_0 \in \F_q^m$ such that
   170	  \[
   171	    u_0 = L_v^\lnf(u)
   172	  \]
   173	  for all $u \in \line$.
   174	\end{definition}

   151	## (d) Statement sketch of `MIPStarRE.QPBT.pauli_soundness`
   152	
   153	```lean
   154	/-- Soundness function of the Pauli basis test; argument order (ε, m, d, q)
   155	everywhere, per rem:delta-qld-argument-order. Real rpow throughout. -/
   156	noncomputable def deltaQld (a b ε : ℝ) (m d q : ℕ) : ℝ :=
   157	  a * ((m * d : ℕ) : ℝ) ^ a *
   158	    (ε ^ b + (q : ℝ) ^ (-b) + (2 : ℝ) ^ (-(b * ((m * d : ℕ) : ℝ))))
   159	
   160	/-- thm:pauli (qpbt-paper 08_…tex:1426-1447): soundness of the Pauli basis test. -/
   161	theorem pauli_soundness :
   162	    ∃ a b : ℝ, 1 ≤ a ∧ 0 < b ∧ b < 1 ∧
   163	      ∀ (P : AdmissibleParams) [FieldModel P.q] (ε : ℝ), 0 < ε →
   164	        ∀ S : Strategy (pauliBasisTest P), 1 - ε ≤ S.value →
   165	          ∃ (ιA' ιB' : Type) (_ : Fintype ιA') (_ : DecidableEq ιA')
   166	            (_ : Fintype ιB') (_ : DecidableEq ιB')
   167	            (φA : EuclideanSpace ℂ S.ιA →ₗᵢ[ℂ]
   168	                    EuclideanSpace ℂ (ιA' × PauliRegister P))
   169	            (φB : EuclideanSpace ℂ S.ιB →ₗᵢ[ℂ]
   170	                    EuclideanSpace ℂ (ιB' × PauliRegister P))
   171	            (aux : EuclideanSpace ℂ (ιA' × ιB')), ‖aux‖ = 1 ∧
   172	            -- item 1: ‖φA ⊗ φB ψ − aux ⊗ EPR_q^{⊗M}‖ ≤ δ_qld  (squared distance,
   173	            -- via stateDistSq and deltaQld²; or state with ‖·‖ directly — either
   174	            -- form is acceptable, document the choice)
   175	            ‖isometryTensor φA φB S.ψ - idealState P aux‖
   176	                ≤ deltaQld a b ε P.m P.d P.q ∧
   177	            -- item 2, for both players and both bases, summation over u ∈ F_q^M,
   178	            -- w.r.t. the ideal state; O(·) constants absorbed into a (see (e)8)
   179	            ∀ W : PauliKind,
   180	              (∑ u : PauliRegister P,
   181	                ‖(heteroKron
   182	                    (conjIsometry φA ((S.A (pauliQuestion P W)).effect
   183	                      (PauliAnswer.pauliOutcome u) ...decoded))
   184	                    (1 : Op (ιB' × PauliRegister P))
   185	                  - pauliProjOnA'' P W u).mulVec (idealState P aux)‖ ^ 2)
   186	                ≤ deltaQld a b ε P.m P.d P.q ∧
   187	              (symmetric B-side bound)
   188	```
   189	
   190	Supporting definitions in Soundness.lean (all NEW, Lean-only):
   191	`idealState P aux := reindexState prodShuffle (vecTensor aux (eprState (PauliRegister P)))`;
   192	`pauliQuestion P W : (pauliBasisTest P).QuestionA := (PauliType.pauli W, 0)` (the
   193	`(Pauli, W)` question has content `0`, image of the 0-level CL function);
   194	`pauliProjOnA'' P W u : Op ((ιA' × Reg) × (ιB' × Reg))` places `pauliProj W u` on the
   195	`A''` factor, identity elsewhere (and the `B''` analogue). The A-side measurement
   196	outcome family is the sub-family of `S.A` at outcomes `PauliAnswer.pauliOutcome u`
   197	(other constructors carry no mass in the ideal comparison; define the family by
   198	pattern-matching `PauliAnswer → Op` with `0` on the other constructors — this is the
   199	faithful reading of "answer summation over `u ∈ F_q^M`").

   201	## (e) Settled encoding decisions (do not re-derive)
   202	
   203	1. **Polynomials — representative convention** (issue #0004, `def:polynomials-degree`):
   204	   polynomial-valued objects are representatives, not function classes. Reuse
   205	   `MIPStarRE.LDT.Preliminaries.polyFunc` where a polynomial *class* is quantified.
   206	   Game *answers* are finite coefficient tuples exactly as printed in the paper
   207	   ("given by its d+1 coefficients"): `Fin (d+1) → K`, resp. `Fin (m*d+1) → K`.
   208	   Do not reuse `LDT.AxisLinePolynomial`/`DiagonalLineAnswer` (the LDT diagonal answer
   209	   is function-encoded and `Parameters`-bundled; a bridge can come later).
   210	   `def:ld-meas`/`PolyMeas` are NOT in this closure — do not build them now.
   211	2. **Distributions — match LDT, not PMF**: the LDT question distributions use
   212	   `MIPStarRE.LDT.Distribution` (Finset-supported, real weights, `Error := ℝ`) with
   213	   `IsProbability`, `avgOver`, `map`, `uniformDistribution`, `uniformOnFinset`
   214	   (`LDT/Basic/Distribution.lean`, `DistributionUniform.lean`; product combinators in
   215	   `DistributionProduct.lean` — verify the exact name before use). All QPBT question
   216	   distributions are `Distribution` values; `PMF` only ever via the existing
   217	   `DistributionPMF` bridge, never in game-facing statements.
   218	3. **Measurements**: use `MIPStarRE.Quantum.Measurement`/`Submeasurement`
   219	   (`Quantum/Measurement.lean`) as the POVM carrier; marginals and the bracket
   220	   notation are `Measurement.postprocess` (already `\leanok` for ch12 `def:bracket`).
   221	   Projectivity via `MIPStarRE.Quantum.IsProj`.
   222	4. **States**: pure states as unit vectors of `EuclideanSpace ℂ ι` (the theorem's
   223	   conclusion needs vector norms, isometries `→ₗᵢ[ℂ]` — reuse
   224	   `Quantum/FiniteHilbert.lean` patterns — and `eprState`). The density-matrix
   225	   `LDT.QuantumState` layer is NOT used in the QPBT games layer.
   226	5. **Field model**: reuse `MIPStarRE.LDT.FieldModel q` (bundled `K ≃ Fin q`). The χ
   227	   map (eq:chi-func) interprets `s : K` as an integer through `FieldModel.equiv`;
   228	   the finite-field trace is the basis-independent `Algebra.trace (ZMod 2) K`
   229	   (= Tr of `Algebra.leftMulMatrix`, i.e. eq:def-trace). The self-dual normal basis
   230	   and `def:binary-representation` are NOT in the statement closure and are deferred
   231	   (see OPEN-6). `canonicalComplement` is defined basis-freely by the pivot
   232	   characterization — `j` is a pivot of `W` iff restricting to coordinates `≤ j`
   233	   increases rank — which agrees with the source's RREF construction by the
   234	   basis-independence noted in `def:canonical-complement` (equivalence proof deferred).
   235	6. **Qudit indexing**: the `M = 2^m` qudits and the vectors `F_q^M` are indexed by
   236	   `Cube m := Fin m → Bool`. Never introduce `Fin (2^m)`; `M` appears only as
   237	   `Fintype.card (Cube m)` in docstrings.
   238	7. **Prose claims inside blueprint definitions become companion lemmas**: CL-level
   239	   assertions ("`L_ALine` is a 2-level CL function"), uniformity of `χ(s)`,
   240	   well-definedness remarks — each a named `sorry` lemma next to the definition, not
   241	   a definitional obligation. Definitions themselves are direct and computable-shaped.
   242	8. **Asymptotic `≈`/O(·) → quantitative functionals**: `def:state-distance` /
   243	   `def:povm-distance` are encoded as explicit real error quantities (`stateDistSq`,
   244	   `opFamilyDistSq`), mirroring how the LDT track already quantifies `≃`/`≈`
   245	   (cf. rem:asymptotic-distance). The implicit universal constants of the blueprint's
   246	   `≈_δ` are absorbed into the existentially quantified constant `a` of
   247	   `pauli_soundness`; record this in the theorem docstring.
   248	9. **Win predicates are `Bool`-valued**, answer alphabets are sum types, and
   249	   "answers not of the prescribed form are rejected" is a predicate clause (match on
   250	   constructor shape). Question alphabets are `Type × ambient-space` pairs — contents
   251	   are full ambient vectors `ι → K` (images of the CL maps), not per-type refined
   252	   types; this matches the blueprint's `(t, L_t(z))` format.
   253	10. **`deltaQld` argument order** is `(ε, m, d, q)` with `0 < b < 1` strict and

   178	\paragraph{Question distribution.}
   179	We now present the question distribution of the game $\game^\ld$ as a typed CL
   180	distribution (see \Cref{sec:types} for the definition of typed CL functions and
   181	typed CL distributions).
   182	The type set $\type^\ld$ of the game $\game^\ld$ we use is
   183	\[
   184		\type^\ld = \{ \Point, \ALine, \DLine \}\;.
   185	\]
   186	The distribution over question types is uniform over $\type^\ld \times \type^\ld$. 
   187	
   188	We introduce the corresponding typed CL functions $L_\Point$, $L_\ALine$,
   189	$L_\DLine$ where the corresponding CL distributions $\mu_{L_\ALine,L_\Point}$
   190	and $\mu_{L_\DLine,L_\Point}$ implement the axis line-versus-point and diagonal
   191	line-versus-point distributions, respectively.
   192	The functions are parametrized by a field size $q$, a dimension $m$, and three
   193	complementary register subspaces $V_\xpt,V_{\coord}, V_{\dir{}}$ of some ambient
   194	space.
   195	The register $V_\xpt$ (which is isomorphic to $\F_q^m$) is called the
   196	\emph{point register}, $V_\coord$ (which is isomorphic to $\F_q$) is called the
   197	\emph{coordinate register}, and $V_{\dir{}}$ (which is isomorphic to $\F_q^m$)
   198	is called the \emph{direction register}, respectively.
   199	We let $V$ denote the direct sum $V_\xpt \oplus V_{\coord} \oplus V_{\dir{}}$.
   200	We identify elements of $V$ as triples $(u,s,v) \in \F_q^m \times \F_q \times
   201	\F_q^m$.
   202	
   203	Define $L_\Point$ to be the $1$-level CL function that projects onto $V_\xpt$: for every $(u,s,v) \in V$,
   204	\begin{equation}
   205	  \label{eq:cl-ptf}
   206		L_\Point(u,s,v) = (u,0,0) \;.
   207	\end{equation}
   208	Define $L_\ALine$ to be the following $2$-level CL function:
   209	\begin{equation}
   210	  \label{eq:cl-alnf}
   211		L_\ALine(u,s,v) = (L^\lnf_{e_i}(u), s, 0)\ \text{for all } (u,s,v) \in V,
   212	\end{equation}
   213	where $L^\lnf$ is the linear function used to compute the canonical
   214	representative of lines (see \Cref{def:line-representative}), and $i = \chi(s)$
   215	where we define $\chi(s)$ to be the unique integer such that
   216	\begin{equation}
   217	\label{eq:chi-func}
   218		s = (\chi(s) - 1) \frac{q}{m} + r
   219	\end{equation}
   220	for some $0 \leq r < q/m$, and we interpret the field element $s \in \F_q$ as an
   221	integer between $0$ and $q - 1$).
   222	The function $L_\ALine$ is the concatenation of the $1$-level CL function that
   223	projects the subspaces $V_{\coord} \oplus V_{\dir{}}$ down to $V_\coord$ (i.e.
   224	zeroes out the entire $V_{\dir{}}$ register), and the family of $1$-level CL
   225	functions $\{L^\lnf_{e_i} \}$ acting on $V_\xpt$, indexed by $i \in
   226	\{1,2,\ldots,m\}$.
   227	(See \Cref{lem:cl-concat} for definition of CL function concatenation.)
   228	Thus $L_\ALine$ is a $2$-level CL function.
   229	
   230	Define $L_\DLine$ to be the following $3$-level CL function: for all $(u,s,v) \in
   231	V$,
   232	\begin{equation}
   233	\label{eq:cl-dlnf}
   234		L_\DLine(u,s,v) = (L^\lnf_{\pi_{i-1}(v)}(u),s,\pi_{i-1}(v))
   235	\end{equation}
   236	where $i = \chi(s)$.
   237	The function $L_\DLine$ is the concatenation of the following CL functions (again, see \Cref{lem:cl-concat} for definition of CL function concatenation): (i) the identity function on $V_{\coord}$ (which is a $1$-level CL function); (ii) for every $i \in \{1,2,\ldots,m\}$ the $1$-level CL function on $V_{\dir{}}$ that maps $v \mapsto \pi_{i-1}(v)$ (i.e.~it zeroes out the first $i-1$ coordinates of $v$), and (iii) for every pair $(s,v') \in V_\coord \oplus V_{\dir{}}$, the $1$-level CL function $L^\lnf_{v'}$ acting on $V_\xpt$. Thus $L_\DLine$ is a $3$-level CL function.
   238	
   239	
   240	The following two lemmas establish that the CL functions
   241	$L_\Point,L_\ALine,L_\DLine$ give rise to the axis-parallel line-versus-point and
   242	diagonal line-versus-point distributions.
   243	\begin{lemma}
   244		\label{lem:alnf}
   245		Consider the pair $(\line, u)$ sampled in the following way: first, sample the
   246	  tuple $((u_0,s,0),(u,0,0))$ from the CL distribution $\mu_{L_\ALine,L_\Point}$,
   247	  and let $\line = \line(u_0,e_i)$ where $i = \chi(s)$.
   248	  Then $u$ is a uniformly random point in $\F_q^m$ and $\line$ is a line that
   249	  goes through $u$ and is parallel to a uniformly random axis $i \in
   250	  \{1,2,\ldots,m\}$.
   251	\end{lemma}
   252	\begin{proof}
   253		Since $s$ is uniformly random in $\F_q$ and $m$ divides $q$ by assumption, we
   254	  have that $i$ is uniformly random between $\{1,2,\ldots,m\}$ and therefore
   255	  $(u_0,s)$ specifies a uniformly random axis-parallel line $\line(u_0,e_i)$.
   256	  Since $u_0 = L^{\lnf}_{e_i}(u)$, we have that $u \in \line(u_0,e_i)$.
   257	\end{proof}
   258	
   259	
   260	
   261	\begin{lemma}
   262		\label{lem:dlnf}
   263		Consider the pair $(\line,u)$ sampled in the following way: first, sample the
   264	  tuple $((u_0,s,v),(u,0,0))$ from the CL distribution $\mu_{L_\DLine,L_\Point}$,
   265	  and let $\line = \line(u_0,v)$ where $i = \chi(s)$.
   266	  Then $u$ is a uniformly random point in $\F_q^m$ and $\line$ is a random
   267	  diagonal line that goes through $u$ and shares the first $i-1$ coordinates
   268	  with $u$, for uniformly random $i$.
   269	\end{lemma}
   270	\begin{proof}
   271		The proof of this follows identically to \Cref{lem:alnf}.
   272	\end{proof}
   273	
   274	For later convenience we make the following definition. 
   275	
   276	\begin{definition}[Line-point distributions]
   277	        \label{def:line-point-dist}
   278	 The \emph{axis line-point distribution} $D_{\ALine}$ is the
   279	 distribution $\mu_{L_\ALine,L_\Point}$ over pairs $(\ell=(u_0,e_i),u)$
   280	 (we omit the $0$ elements for simplicity). The \emph{diagonal
   281	   line-point distribution} $D_{\DLine}$ is the distribution
   282	 $\mu_{L_\DLine,L_\Point}$  over $(\ell=(u_0,s,v),u)$. The
   283	 \emph{line-point distribution} $D_{\Line}$ is the equal mixture of the axis-parallel line-point distribution and the diagonal line-point distribution.
   284	 In other words, a sample from $D_{\Line}$ is distributed as follows:
   285	 with probability $\tfrac{1}{2}$, output a sample from $D_{\ALine}$,
   286	 and with probability $\tfrac{1}{2}$, output a sample from $D_{\DLine}$.
   287	\end{definition}

   320	\paragraph{Decision procedure} The decision procedure $\decider^\ld$ for the
   321	game $\game^\ld$ is presented in Figure~\ref{fig:ld-decider}.
   322	The table at the top specifies a parsing scheme for the questions and answers,
   323	depending on the type of question.
   324	For example, when a player receives a question with type $\Point$, the question
   325	content $x$, a bit string of length $m \log q$, should be interpreted by the
   326	decision procedure and the players as an element of the vector space $\F_q^m$,
   327	as indicated in Section~\ref{sec:ff-representations}.
   328	Similarly the answer to a question with type $\Point$ is expected to be a bit
   329	string of length $\ldc \log q$, and is interpreted as an element of $\F_q^\ldc$.
   330	For questions with type $\ALine$, the question content is a $(m \log q + \log
   331	q)$-bit string, which is parsed as a pair $(u_0, s) \in \F_q^m \times \F_q$,
   332	which in turn can be interpreted as a specification for an axis-parallel line
   333	$\line(u_0,e_i)$ in $\F_q^m$ where $i = \chi(s)$, as described in
   334	\Cref{lem:alnf}.
   335	The answer is interpreted as the description of $\ldc$ degree-$d$ univariate
   336	polynomials defined on the line $\line(u_0,e_i)$, each polynomial given by a
   337	list of $d+1$ coefficients.
   338	For questions with type $\DLine$, the question content is a $(2m \log q + \log
   339	q)$-bit string, which is parsed as a triple $(u_0, s, v) \in \F_q^m \times \F_q
   340	\times \F_q^m$ that specifies a diagonal line $\line(u_0,v')$ where $v' =
   341	\pi_{i-1}(v)$ as described in \Cref{lem:dlnf}.
   342	The answer is interpreted as the description of $\ldc$ degree-$md$ univariate
   343	polynomials defined on the line $\line(u_0,v')$.
   344	If the answers returned by the players do not fit this format the decision
   345	procedure rejects.

   394	We define a special class of measurements that are relevant to the soundness
   395	properties of the low-degree test.
   396	
   397	\begin{definition}[Low-degree polynomial measurements]
   398	  \label{def:ld-meas}
   399	  Define $\polymeas{m}{d}{q}$ to be the set of POVM measurements whose outcomes
   400	  correspond to (individual) degree-$d$ polynomials of $m$ variables over
   401	  $\F_q$.
   402	  More generally, for an integer $\ldc$ and tuples $m=(m_1, m_2, \ldots,
   403	  m_\ldc)$, $d=(d_1, d_2, \ldots, d_\ldc)$ and $q=(q_1, q_2, \ldots, q_\ldc)$,
   404	  we let $\simulpolymeas{m}{d}{q}{\ldc}$ be the set of measurements $G =
   405	  \{G_{g_1,\, g_2,\, \ldots\,,\, g_\ldc}\}$ such that for $i\in\{1, 2, \ldots,
   406	  \ldc\}$, $g_i$ is a polynomial $g_i:\F_{q_i}^{m_i} \rightarrow
   407	  \F_{q_i}$ with individual degree $d_i$ (see \Cref{sec:ld-encoding} for a definition of individual degree). 
   408	\end{definition}

   109	noncomputable def chiIndex (P : LdParams) (s : ScalarQ P) : Fin P.m := by

   111	    exact Nat.ne_of_gt (lt_of_lt_of_le Nat.zero_lt_one P.hm)⟩

   114	/-- The projection used in the diagonal-line map zeroes coordinates before the

   118	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:31-391`.

   120	def prefixProjection {P : LdParams} (i : Fin P.m) (v : Fin P.m → ScalarQ P) :
   121	    Fin P.m → ScalarQ P :=
   122	  fun j => if j.val < i.val then 0 else v j

   124	/-- The point CL map, retaining the point block and clearing the auxiliary
   125	blocks.  It is the map `L_point` of `def:ld-question-distribution`, blueprint
   126	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch13_qpbt_test.tex:38-49`, paper origin
   127	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:31-391`.

   129	def ldPointCL (P : LdParams) (z : LdSpace P) : LdSpace P :=
   130	  fun i => match i with
   131	  | .inl (.inl j) => z (.inl (.inl j))
   132	  | .inl (.inr _) => 0
   133	  | .inr _ => 0
   134	
   135	/-- The affine-line CL map.  The direction block is put through the canonical
   136	line representative map from `def:line-representative`, while the point block
   137	is retained (blueprint `blueprint/src/chapter/ch13_qpbt_test.tex:38-49`; paper
   138	origin `references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:31-391`).

   140	noncomputable def ldALineCL (P : LdParams) (z : LdSpace P) : LdSpace P :=
   141	  let i := chiIndex P (z.seed)
   142	  let rep := lineRepMap (coordinateDirection i)
   143	  fun i => match i with
   144	  | .inl (.inl j) => (rep (z.point)) j
   145	  | .inl (.inr _) => z (.inl (.inr ()))
   146	  | .inr _ => 0
   147	
   148	/-- The diagonal-line CL map, using the same canonical representative interface
   149	for the direction block.  This is the `L_DLine` clause of
   150	`def:ld-question-distribution` (blueprint
   151	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch13_qpbt_test.tex:38-49`; paper origin
   152	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:31-391`).
   153	-/
   154	noncomputable def ldDLineCL (P : LdParams) (z : LdSpace P) : LdSpace P :=
   155	  let i := chiIndex P (z.seed)
   156	  let direction := prefixProjection i (z.direction)
   157	  let rep := lineRepMap direction
   158	  fun i => match i with
   159	  | .inl (.inl j) => (rep (z.point)) j
   160	  | .inl (.inr _) => z (.inl (.inr ()))
   161	  | .inr j => direction j
   162

   166	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:31-391`.

   168	noncomputable def ldCL (P : LdParams) : LdType → LdSpace P → LdSpace P
   169	  | .point => ldPointCL P

   171	  | .dline => ldDLineCL P

   180	  sorry

   184	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch13_qpbt_test.tex:38-49`, paper origin

   191	/-- The question alphabet for the low-degree game (`def:ld-game`, blueprint
   192	`ch13_qpbt_test.tex:17-31`; paper origin
   193	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:31-391`).

   197	/-- The support of the typed CL question distribution, obtained by pushing a
   198	uniform seed through the type-indexed maps.  This is the construction in
   199	`def:ld-question-distribution`, blueprint
   200	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch13_qpbt_test.tex:38-49`, paper origin

   203	noncomputable def ldQuestionSupport (P : LdParams) :
   204	    Finset (LdQuestion P × LdQuestion P) :=
   205	  (Finset.univ : Finset ((LdType × LdType) × LdSpace P)).image (fun s =>
   206	    ((s.1.1, ldCL P s.1.1 s.2), (s.1.2, ldCL P s.1.2 s.2)))
   207	
   208	/-- The typed CL question distribution.  This is the inlined construction in
   209	`def:ld-question-distribution`, blueprint `ch13_qpbt_test.tex:38-49`; paper
   210	origin `references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:31-391`.
   211	-/
   212	noncomputable def ldQuestionDistribution (P : LdParams) :
   213	    Distribution (LdQuestion P × LdQuestion P) :=
   214	  Distribution.map
   215	    (uniformDistribution ((LdType × LdType) × LdSpace P))
   216	    (fun s =>
   217	      ((s.1.1, ldCL P s.1.1 s.2), (s.1.2, ldCL P s.1.2 s.2)))

   219	/-- The coefficient-tuple answer alphabet of the low-degree game.  Polynomial
   220	answers are representatives with exactly the coefficient lengths printed in
   221	the paper, as required by `def:ld-win-predicate` (blueprint
   222	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch13_qpbt_test.tex:56-105`; paper
   223	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:31-391`).
   224	-/
   225	inductive LdAnswer (P : LdParams) where
   226	  | pointVals (a : Fin P.k → ScalarQ P)
   227	  | alinePolys (a : Fin P.k → Fin (P.d + 1) → ScalarQ P)
   228	  | dlinePolys (a : Fin P.k → Fin (P.m * P.d + 1) → ScalarQ P)
   229	  deriving DecidableEq
   230	
   231	/-- A finite sum code used only to provide the answer alphabet's `Fintype`
   232	instance; the public constructors are those of `def:ld-win-predicate`,
   233	blueprint `ch13_qpbt_test.tex:56-105`, paper origin
   234	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:31-391`.
   235	-/
   236	abbrev LdAnswerCode (P : LdParams) :=
   237	  (Fin P.k → ScalarQ P) ⊕
   238	    ((Fin P.k → Fin (P.d + 1) → ScalarQ P) ⊕
   239	      (Fin P.k → Fin (P.m * P.d + 1) → ScalarQ P))
   240	
   241	/-- The constructor-preserving code equivalence for `LdAnswer` (Lean-only
   242	finite-carrier infrastructure for `def:ld-win-predicate`, blueprint
   243	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch13_qpbt_test.tex:56-105`, paper origin
   244	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:31-391`).
   245	-/
   246	noncomputable def ldAnswerEquiv (P : LdParams) :
   247	    LdAnswer P ≃ LdAnswerCode P where
   248	  toFun
   249	    | .pointVals a => .inl a
   250	    | .alinePolys a => .inr (.inl a)
   251	    | .dlinePolys a => .inr (.inr a)
   252	  invFun
   253	    | .inl a => .pointVals a
   254	    | .inr (.inl a) => .alinePolys a
   255	    | .inr (.inr a) => .dlinePolys a
   256	  left_inv := by intro x; cases x <;> rfl
   257	  right_inv := by
   258	    intro x
   259	    cases x with
   260	    | inl a => rfl
   261	    | inr x =>
   262	        cases x with
   263	        | inl a => rfl
   264	        | inr a => rfl
   265	
   266	instance (P : LdParams) : Inhabited (LdAnswer P) :=
   267	  ⟨.pointVals (fun _ => 0)⟩
   268	
   269	noncomputable instance (P : LdParams) : Fintype (LdAnswer P) :=
   270	  Fintype.ofEquiv (LdAnswerCode P) (ldAnswerEquiv P).symm
   271	
   272	/-- Evaluation of a coefficient tuple at a field element.  This is the
   273	representative convention used by the line answers in `def:ld-win-predicate`,
   274	blueprint `blueprint/src/chapter/ch13_qpbt_test.tex:56-105`, paper origin
   275	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:31-391`.
   276	-/
   277	def evalCoefficient {K : Type*} [Semiring K] {n : ℕ}
   278	    (c : Fin n → K) (t : K) : K :=
   279	  ∑ i : Fin n, c i * t ^ i.val
   280	
   281	/-- Check that an answer has the constructor prescribed by its question type;
   282	Lean encoding of the rejection clause in `def:ld-win-predicate`, blueprint
   283	`ch13_qpbt_test.tex:56-105`, paper origin
   284	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:31-391`.
   285	-/
   286	def validLdAnswer {P : LdParams} (t : LdType) (a : LdAnswer P) : Bool :=
   287	  match t, a with
   288	  | .point, .pointVals _ => true
   289	  | .aline, .alinePolys _ => true
   290	  | .dline, .dlinePolys _ => true
   291	  | _, _ => false
   292	
   293	/-- The axis-parallel line/point relation in `def:ld-win-predicate`, blueprint
   294	`ch13_qpbt_test.tex:56-105`, paper origin
   295	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:31-391`.
   296	-/
   297	def alinePointCondition (P : LdParams) (line point : LdSpace P)
   298	    (f : Fin P.k → Fin (P.d + 1) → ScalarQ P)
   299	    (a : Fin P.k → ScalarQ P) : Prop :=
   300	  -- Universal quantification follows the zero-direction convention in
   301	  -- `rem:ld-win-zero-direction`.
   302	  ∀ t : ScalarQ P,
   303	    point.point = line.point + t • coordinateDirection (chiIndex P line.seed) →
   304	      ∀ j : Fin P.k, evalCoefficient (f j) t = a j
   305	
   306	/-- The diagonal line/point relation in `def:ld-win-predicate`, blueprint
   307	`ch13_qpbt_test.tex:56-105`, paper origin
   308	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:31-391`.
   309	-/
   310	def dlinePointCondition (P : LdParams) (line point : LdSpace P)
   311	    (f : Fin P.k → Fin (P.m * P.d + 1) → ScalarQ P)
   312	    (a : Fin P.k → ScalarQ P) : Prop :=
   313	  ∀ t : ScalarQ P,
   314	    point.point = line.point + t • line.direction →
   315	      ∀ j : Fin P.k, evalCoefficient (f j) t = a j
   316	
   317	/-- The low-degree consistency predicate, rejecting answers of the wrong
   318	constructor shape.  This is `def:ld-win-predicate` in
   319	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch13_qpbt_test.tex:56-105`, paper origin
   320	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:31-391`.
   321	-/
   322	noncomputable def ldWinPredicate (P : LdParams) :
   323	    LdQuestion P → LdQuestion P → LdAnswer P → LdAnswer P → Bool :=
   324	  open Classical in
   325	  fun (tA, xA) (tB, xB) a b =>
   326	      if validLdAnswer tA a && validLdAnswer tB b then
   327	        match tA, tB, a, b with
   328	        | .point, .point, .pointVals u, .pointVals v => decide (u = v)
   329	        | .aline, .point, .alinePolys f, .pointVals u =>
   330	            decide (alinePointCondition P xA xB f u)
   331	        | .point, .aline, .pointVals u, .alinePolys f =>
   332	            decide (alinePointCondition P xB xA f u)
   333	        | .dline, .point, .dlinePolys f, .pointVals u =>
   334	            decide (dlinePointCondition P xA xB f u)
   335	        | .point, .dline, .pointVals u, .dlinePolys f =>
   336	            decide (dlinePointCondition P xB xA f u)
   337	        | .aline, .aline, .alinePolys f, .alinePolys g => decide (f = g)
   338	        | .dline, .dline, .dlinePolys f, .dlinePolys g => decide (f = g)
   339	        | _, _, _, _ => true
   340	      else false
   341	
   342	/-- The low-degree game packaged as a `Game`.  This is `def:ld-game` in
   343	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch13_qpbt_test.tex:17-105`, paper origin
   344	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:31-391`.
   345	-/
   346	noncomputable def ldGame (P : LdParams) : Game where
   347	  QuestionA := LdQuestion P
   348	  QuestionB := LdQuestion P
   349	  AnswerA := LdAnswer P
   350	  AnswerB := LdAnswer P
   351	  μ := ldQuestionDistribution P
   352	  μ_prob := by sorry
   353	  decide := ldWinPredicate P
   354	
   355	end
   356	
   357	end MIPStarRE.QPBT

     5	/-!
     6	# The Magic Square game
     7	
     8	The Magic Square component is represented by finite constraint and variable
     9	question types, the incidence graph, and the two corresponding answer forms.
    10	Its rigidity theorem is outside the stage-4.1 statement closure; only the game
    11	carrier is needed here.
    12	
    13	## References
    14	
    15	This file formalizes `def:ms-game` in
    16	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch13_qpbt_test.tex:188-203`, from
    17	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:512-610`.
    18	-/
    19	
    20	namespace MIPStarRE.QPBT
    21	
    22	open MIPStarRE.LDT
    23	
    24	/-- A Magic Square question is either a row/column constraint or a cell
    25	variable.  This is `def:ms-game`, blueprint lines 188-203, paper origin
    26	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:512-610`.
    27	-/
    28	inductive MsType where
    29	  | constraint (i : Fin 6)
    30	  | var (j : Fin 9)
    31	  deriving DecidableEq, Repr, Inhabited, Fintype
    32	
    33	/-- The cell incident to a constraint and one of its three positions in
    34	`def:ms-game`, blueprint `ch13_qpbt_test.tex:188-203`, paper origin
    35	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:512-610`.
    36	-/
    37	def msConstraintVars (i : Fin 6) (j : Fin 3) : Fin 9 :=
    38	  ⟨if i.val < 3 then i.val * 3 + j.val else i.val - 3 + j.val * 3, by
    39	    by_cases h : i.val < 3 <;> simp [h] <;> omega⟩
    40	
    41	/-- The exceptional Magic Square parity, equal to one only on the final
    42	constraint.  Blueprint `blueprint/src/chapter/ch13_qpbt_test.tex:188-203`; paper
    43	origin `references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:512-610`.
    44	-/
    45	def msParity (i : Fin 6) : ZMod 2 :=
    46	  if i.val = 5 then 1 else 0
    47	
    48	/-- The 18 constraint-variable incidence edges of the Magic Square graph in
    49	`def:ms-game`, blueprint `ch13_qpbt_test.tex:188-203`, paper origin
    50	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:512-610`.
    51	-/
    52	def msEdges : Finset (Sym2 MsType) :=
    53	  (Finset.univ : Finset (Fin 6 × Fin 3)).image (fun ij =>
    54	    Sym2.mk (.constraint ij.1) (.var (msConstraintVars ij.1 ij.2)))
    55	
    56	/-- The Magic Square incidence graph has an edge, as required by the
    57	nonempty-support API of `graphDistribution`.  This is the finite carrier fact
    58	used to instantiate `def:ms-game`, blueprint `ch13_qpbt_test.tex:188-203`,
    59	paper origin `references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:512-610`.
    60	-/
    61	theorem msEdges_nonempty : msEdges.Nonempty := by
    62	  refine ⟨Sym2.mk (.constraint 0) (.var (msConstraintVars 0 0)), ?_⟩
    63	  exact Finset.mem_image.mpr ⟨(0, 0), Finset.mem_univ _, rfl⟩
    64	
    65	/-- A Magic Square answer is a parity triple or a single cell bit, as prescribed
    66	by `def:ms-game`, blueprint `blueprint/src/chapter/ch13_qpbt_test.tex:188-203`,
    67	paper origin `references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:512-610`.
    68	-/
    69	inductive MsAnswer where
    70	  | triple (β : Fin 3 → ZMod 2)
    71	  | bit (γ : ZMod 2)
    72	  deriving DecidableEq
    73	
    74	/-- A finite code for the two Magic Square answer constructors.  This is
    75	Lean-only carrier infrastructure for `def:ms-game`, blueprint
    76	`ch13_qpbt_test.tex:188-203`, paper origin
    77	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:512-610`.
    78	-/
    79	abbrev MsAnswerCode := (Fin 3 → ZMod 2) ⊕ ZMod 2
    80	
    81	/-- The constructor-preserving code equivalence for `MsAnswer`; Lean-only
    82	finite-carrier infrastructure for `def:ms-game`, blueprint
    83	`ch13_qpbt_test.tex:188-203`, paper origin
    84	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:512-610`.
    85	-/
    86	noncomputable def msAnswerEquiv : MsAnswer ≃ MsAnswerCode where
    87	  toFun
    88	    | .triple β => .inl β
    89	    | .bit γ => .inr γ
    90	  invFun
    91	    | .inl β => .triple β
    92	    | .inr γ => .bit γ
    93	  left_inv := by intro x; cases x <;> rfl
    94	  right_inv := by
    95	    intro x
    96	    cases x <;> rfl
    97	
    98	noncomputable instance : Fintype MsAnswer :=
    99	  Fintype.ofEquiv MsAnswerCode msAnswerEquiv.symm
   100	
   101	instance : Inhabited MsAnswer := ⟨.bit 0⟩
   102	
   103	/-- The Magic Square consistency predicate.  Constructor mismatches are
   104	rejected, as required by `def:ms-game` (blueprint lines 188-203; paper
   105	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:512-610`).
   106	-/
   107	def msWinPredicate :
   108	    MsType → MsType → MsAnswer → MsAnswer → Bool
   109	  | .constraint i, .constraint j, .triple β, .triple β' =>
   110	      decide (i = j ∧ β = β')
   111	  | .var i, .var j, .bit γ, .bit γ' =>
   112	      decide (i = j ∧ γ = γ')
   113	  | .constraint i, .var j, .triple β, .bit γ =>
   114	      decide
   115	        ((∑ k : Fin 3, β k) = msParity i ∧
   116	          ∃ k : Fin 3, msConstraintVars i k = j ∧ β k = γ)
   117	  | .var j, .constraint i, .bit γ, .triple β =>
   118	      decide
   119	        ((∑ k : Fin 3, β k) = msParity i ∧
   120	          ∃ k : Fin 3, msConstraintVars i k = j ∧ β k = γ)
   121	  | _, _, _, _ => false
   122	
   123	/-- The Magic Square game as a finite `Game`.  This is `def:ms-game` in
   124	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch13_qpbt_test.tex:188-203`, paper origin
   125	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:512-610`.
   126	-/
   127	noncomputable def msGame : Game where
   128	  QuestionA := MsType
   129	  QuestionB := MsType
   130	  AnswerA := MsAnswer
   131	  AnswerB := MsAnswer
   132	  μ := graphDistribution msEdges msEdges_nonempty
   133	  μ_prob := by sorry
   134	  decide := msWinPredicate
   135	
   136	end MIPStarRE.QPBT

   492	\begin{proof}
   493		Finite field arithmetic over $\F_q$ can be performed in time $\polylog q$, by
   494	  Lemma~\ref{lem:efficient_arithmetic}.
   495		The most expensive step in $\decider^\ld$ is to evaluate a univariate
   496	  polynomial $f: \F_q \to \F_q^k$ at some point $t_u \in \F_q$ that corresponds
   497	  to a point $u \in \F_q^m$, which takes time $\poly(m,d,k,\log q)$.
   498	  The function $L_\Point$ is a projection onto $V_\xpt$, which takes time
   499	  $\poly(m,\log q)$ to compute (it just involves ``zeroing out'' the registers
   500	  outside of $V_\xpt$).
   501	  The functions $L_\ALine$ and $L_\DLine$ require computing a canonical linear
   502	  map, which requires performing Gaussian elimination and can be done in time
   503	  $\poly(m,\log q)$.
   504	
   505	  The Turing-machine description of the decision procedure $\decider^\ld$ can be
   506	  uniformly computed from the integers $(q,m,d,k)$ expressed in binary; the
   507	  complexity of computing the description comes from describing the parameter
   508	  tuple $\ldparams$, which takes time that is at most polynomial in the bit
   509	  length of $(q,m,d,k)$.
   510	\end{proof}

   512	\subsection{The Magic Square game}
   513	\label{sec:ms}
   514	
   515	We recall the \emph{Magic Square game} of Mermin and
   516	Peres~\cite{mermin1990simple,peres1990incompatible,aravind2002simple}.
   517	The Magic Square game is a simple self-test for EPR pairs (it tests for two of
   518	them). In addition, it allows one to test that a pair of observables
   519	\emph{anticommutes}.
   520	Here we use it as a building block to construct the quantum low-degree test. 
   521	
   522	There are several formulations of the Magic Square game; here we present it as a
   523	\emph{binary constraint satisfaction} game~\cite{cleve2014characterization}.
   524	In this formulation of the game (denoted by $\game_\MS$) there are $6$ linear
   525	equations defined over $9$ variables that take values in $\F_2$.
   526	The variables correspond to the cells of a $3 \times 3$ grid, as depicted in
   527	Figure~\ref{fig:ms}.
   528	Five of the equations correspond to the constraint that the sum of the variables
   529	in each row and the first two columns must be equal to $0$, and the last
   530	equation requires that the sum of the variables in the last column must be equal
   531	to $1$.
   532	
   533	\begin{figure}[ht!]
   534		\begin{center}
   535	    \renewcommand{\arraystretch}{1.6}
   536			\begin{tabular}{|c|c|c|}
   537				\hline
   538				$x_1$ & $x_2$ & $x_3$ \\
   539				\hline 
   540				$x_4$ & $x_5$ & $x_6$ \\	
   541				\hline
   542				$x_7$ & $x_8$ & $x_9$ \\
   543				\hline
   544			\end{tabular}
   545			\caption{The Magic Square game}
   546			\label{fig:ms}
   547			\end{center}
   548	\end{figure}
   549	
   550	The question set $\type^\ms$ of the Magic Square game is the following:
   551	\begin{equation*}
   552	  \begin{split}
   553	    \type^\msc & = \{ \Constraint_i : i = 1, 2, \ldots, 6\}\;,\\
   554	    \type^\msv & = \{ \Variable_j : j = 1, 2, \ldots, 9\}\;,\\
   555	    \type^\ms & = \type^\msc \cup \type^\msv\;.
   556	  \end{split}
   557	\end{equation*}
   558	The questions $\Constraint_i$ for $i \in \{1,2,3\}$ correspond to the three row
   559	constraints, the questions $\Constraint_4$, $\Constraint_5$ correspond to the first
   560	two column constraints, and question $\Constraint_6$ corresponds to the third
   561	column constraint.
   562	
   563	In the Magic Square game, the verifier first samples a constraint $\Constraint_i
   564	\in \type^\msc$ uniformly at random, and then samples $\Variable_j$, one of the
   565	three variables in the row or column corresponding to $\Constraint_i$, uniformly
   566	at random.
   567	One player is randomly assigned to be the $\Constraint$ player, and the other is
   568	assigned to be the $\Variable$ player.
   569	The $\Constraint$ player is sent the question $\Constraint_i$ and is expected to
   570	respond with three bits $(\beta_{v_1}, \beta_{v_2}, \beta_{v_3}) \in \F_2^3$,
   571	where $(v_1,v_2,v_3)$ are the indices of the three variables corresponding to
   572	$\Constraint_i$.
   573	The $\Variable$ player is given question $\Variable_j$ and is expected to
   574	respond with a single bit $\gamma \in \F_2$.
   575	The players win if the $\Constraint$ player's answers satisfy the equation
   576	associated with $\Constraint_i$, and $\gamma = \beta_j$.
   577	More precisely, the verifier samples an edge of the type graph (see Section~\ref{sec:types}) $G^\ms$
   578	in Fig.~\ref{fig:type-graph-ms}, sends one endpoint to a random player, and the
   579	other endpoint to the other player.
   580

   582	  \centering
   583	  \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=.8]
   584

   588	      }}
   589	
   590	
   591	
   592	    \foreach \i in {1,...,6} \draw (0,8-9/8*\i)
   593	    coordinate (Constraint-\i)
   594	    node[type={[180]$\Constraint_\i$}] {};
   595	
   596	    \foreach \i in {1,...,9} \draw (2.5,9-\i)
   597	    coordinate (Variable-\i)
   598	    node[type={[0]$\Variable_\i$}] {};
   599	
   600	    \foreach \i in {1,...,3} \foreach \j in {1,...,3}
   601	    \pgfmathsetmacro{\k}{(\i-1)*3+\j}
   602	    \draw (Constraint-\i) -- (Variable-\k);
   603	
   604	    \foreach \i in {4,...,6} \foreach \j in {1,...,3}

   941	The key quantity to determine which of these is the case is the following complicated-looking expression:
   942	\begin{equation*}
   943	\gamma = \tr \bigl( (\ind_{m}(u_\xpt) \cdot r_\xpt) \cdot
   944	      (\ind_{m}(u_\zpt) \cdot r_\zpt) \bigr)\;.
   945	\end{equation*}
   946	If $\gamma = 0$, then these two measurements commute, and if $\gamma = 1$, then these two measurements anticommute
   947	(this fact is established in the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:pauli-completeness} below).
   948	In the $\gamma = 0$ case, the verifier can check whether these two measurements commute by performing the ``commutation check'',
   949	which asks the provers to simultaneously measure both $\tr(g_{h_X}(u_X) \cdot r_X)$ and $\tr(g_{h_Z}(u_Z) \cdot r_Z)$ and report their values.
   950	In the $\gamma = 1$ case, on the other hand, the measurements anticommute, which implies that they cannot simultaneously be measured.
   951	In spite of this, the verifier can still check that the measurements anticommute by using the Magic Square game from Section~\ref{sec:ms} above.
   952	As was shown in Theorem~\ref{thm:ms-from-ac}, any pair of anticommuting measurements
   953	can be used to form a perfect strategy for the Magic Square game
   954	(and indeed the reverse is true as well: any perfect strategy for the Magic Square game entails a pair of anticommuting measurements).
   955	
   956	Together, these give the main subtests for the game $\game^\pauli$.

  1073	\paragraph{Conditional linear functions for the Pauli basis test.}
  1074	The CL functions corresponding to the Pauli basis test question distribution are
  1075	parameterized by the parameter tuple $\qldparams = (q,m,d)$.
  1076	Let $V^\pauli$ denote the linear space $(\F_q^m)^2 \times \F_q \times \F_q^m
  1077	\times (\F_q)^2$.
  1078	The space $V^\pauli$ is decomposed into a direct sum of the following register
  1079	subspaces: $V_\xpt,V_\zpt$ (which are $m$-dimensional), $V_\coord$ (which is
  1080	$1$-dimensional), $V_{\dir{}}$ (which is $m$-dimensional), and
  1081	$V_{\rxpt},V_{\rzpt}$ (which are $1$-dimensional).
  1082	We identify elements of $V^\pauli$ as tuples $(u_\xpt,u_\zpt,s,v,r_\xpt,r_\zpt)
  1083	\in (\F_q^m)^2 \times \F_q \times \F_q^m \times (\F_q)^2$.
  1084	We define CL functions $L_\tvar: V^\pauli \to V^\pauli$ for every type $\tvar
  1085	\in \type^\pauli$:
  1086	\begin{enumerate}
  1087	\item For $W \in \{X,Z\}$, define $L_{\Point,W}(u_\xpt,u_\zpt,s,v,r_\xpt,r_\zpt)
  1088	  = L_\Point(u_W,s,v)$ where $L_\Point$ is the $1$-level CL function defined in
  1089	  \Cref{eq:cl-ptf}.\footnote{The range $V_{\xpt} \oplus V_\coord \oplus
  1090	    V_{\dir{}}$ or $V_{\zpt} \oplus V_\coord \oplus V_{\dir{}}$ of $L_\Point$ is
  1091	    embedded in $V^\pauli$ in the natural way.
  1092	    The same convention is used also in Item 2 and 3 for $L_\ALine$ and
  1093	    $L_\DLine$.}
  1094	\item For $W \in \{X,Z\}$, define $L_{\ALine,W}(u_\xpt,u_\zpt,s,v,r_\xpt,r_\zpt)
  1095	  = L_\ALine(u_W,s,v)$ where $L_\ALine$ is the $2$-level CL function defined in
  1096	  \Cref{eq:cl-alnf}.
  1097	\item For $W \in \{X,Z\}$, define $L_{\DLine,W}(u_\xpt,u_\zpt,s,v,r_\xpt,r_\zpt)
  1098	  = L_\DLine(u_W,s,v)$ where $L_\DLine$ is the $3$-level CL function defined in
  1099	  \Cref{eq:cl-dlnf}.
  1100	\item For $\tvar \in \type^\ms \cup \{\Pair, (\Pair,X), (\Pair,Z) \}$,
  1101	  $L_{\tvar}(u_\xpt,u_\zpt,s,v,r_\xpt,r_\zpt) =
  1102	  (u_\xpt,u_\zpt,0,0,r_\xpt,r_\zpt)$, i.e., it projects onto $V_\xpt \oplus
  1103	  V_\zpt \oplus V_{\rxpt} \oplus V_{\rzpt}$.
  1104	  Thus $L_{\tvar}$ is a $1$-level CL function.
  1105	  
  1106	\item For $W \in \{X,Z\}$, define $L_{\Pauli,W} = 0$ as the identically $0$
  1107	  function.
  1108	  Thus it is a $0$-level CL function.
  1109	
  1110	\end{enumerate}
  1111	We note that the maps $L_{\Point,W}, L_{\ALine,W}, L_{\DLine,W}$ act as the zero function
  1112	on $V_{\overline{W}} \oplus V_{\rxpt} \oplus V_{\rzpt}$ where $\overline{W} = X$
  1113	if $W = Z$ and $\overline{W} = Z$ if $W = X$.
  1114	
  1115	The question distribution of $\game^\pauli$ is thus a typed CL distribution on
  1116	$\type^\pauli \times V^\pauli \times \type^\pauli \times V^\pauli$ where
  1117	$(\tvar_\alice,x_\alice,\tvar_\bob,x_\bob)$ is sampled by first uniformly
  1118	sampling an edge $(\tvar_\alice,\tvar_\bob)$ from the graph $G^\pauli$ defined
  1119	in Figure~\ref{fig:type-graph-pauli}, sampling a uniformly random $z \in
  1120	V^\pauli$, and then setting $x_w = L_{\tvar_w}(z)$ for $w \in \AB$.

  1169	    On input $(\tvar_\alice,x_\alice, \tvar_\bob, x_\bob, a_\alice, a_\bob)$,
  1170	    the decision procedure $\decider^\pauli$ performs the following checks for
  1171	    $w \in \AB$:
  1172	    \begin{enumerate}[itemsep=2pt,parsep=2pt]
  1173	    \item (\textbf{Consistency check}).
  1174	      \label{item:same-type}
  1175	      If $\tvar_\alice = \tvar_\bob$, accept iff $a_\alice = a_\bob$.
  1176	
  1177	    \item (\textbf{Low-degree}).
  1178	      \label{item:low-degree}
  1179	      Let $\ldparams = (q,m,d,1)$. 
  1180	      \begin{enumerate}
  1181	      	\item If $\tvar_w = (\Point, W), \tvar_{\overline{w}} = (\ALine, W)$, accept if
  1182	      $\decider^\ld_{\ldparams}$ accepts $(\Point, x_w, \ALine, x_{\overline{w}}, a_w,
  1183	      a_{\overline{w}})$.
  1184	      	\item If $\tvar_w = (\Point, W), \tvar_{\overline{w}} = (\DLine, W)$, accept if
  1185	      $\decider^\ld_{\ldparams}$ accepts $(\Point, x_w, \DLine, x_{\overline{w}}, a_w,
  1186	      a_{\overline{w}})$.
  1187			\end{enumerate}
  1188	    \item (\textbf{Consistency check}).
  1189	      \label{item:low-degree-consistency}
  1190	      If $\tvar_w = (\Point, W), \tvar_{\overline{w}} = (\Pauli, W)$, accept if
  1191	      $g_{a_{\overline{w}}}(x_w) = a_w$, where $g_{a_{\overline{w}}}$ is
  1192	      the low-degree encoding of $a_{\overline{w}} \in \F_q^M$ defined in
  1193	      Section~\ref{sec:ld-encoding}.
  1194	    \end{enumerate}
  1195	    In the remaining four cases, the decision procedure first computes the
  1196	    number
  1197	    \begin{equation}
  1198	      \label{eq:gamma-value}
  1199	      \gamma = \tr \bigl( (\ind_{m}(u_\xpt) \cdot r_\xpt) \cdot
  1200	      (\ind_{m}(u_\zpt) \cdot r_\zpt) \bigr)\;,
  1201	    \end{equation}
  1202	    where we recall the $\ind_{m}(\cdot)$ vector from Section~\ref{sec:ld-encoding}.
  1203	    \begin{enumerate}[itemsep=2pt,parsep=2pt]
  1204	      \setcounter{enumi}{3}
  1205	    \item (\textbf{Commutation check}).
  1206	      \label{item:commutation} If $\tvar_w = (\Pair, W), \tvar_{\overline{w}} =
  1207	      \Pair$, accept if $a_w = \beta_W$ or $\gamma \neq 0$.
  1208	    \item (\textbf{Consistency check}).
  1209	      \label{item:commutation-consistency} If $\tvar_w = (\Point,W), \tvar_{\overline{w}} =
  1210	      (\Pair,W)$, accept if $\tr (a_w r_W) = a_{\overline{w}}$ or $\gamma \neq 0$.
  1211	      
  1212	    \item (\textbf{Magic square check}).
  1213	      \label{item:magic-square} If $\tvar_w = \Constraint_i,
  1214	      \tvar_{\overline{w}} = \Variable_j$, accept if $\gamma = 0$, or $a_w$
  1215	      satisfies constraint $\Constraint_i$ and $ \alpha_j = a_{\overline{w}}$.
  1216	
  1217	    \item (\textbf{Consistency check}).
  1218	      \label{item:magic-square-consistency}
  1219	      If $\tvar_w = (\Point,W), \tvar_{\overline{w}} = \Variable_j$, accept if
  1220	      $\gamma = 0$ or if $j = 1$, $W = X$, and $\tr(a_w r_\xpt) =
  1221	      a_{\overline{w}}$ or if $j = 5$, $W = Z$, and $\tr(a_w r_\zpt) =
  1222	      a_{\overline{w}}$.
  1223	    \end{enumerate}

Blueprint\n  links are intentionally unchanged in this repair; the known missing `\\\\uses`\n  edges and QPBT chapter links are tracked for the Stage 4.2 synchronization.\n\nAll remaining `sorry`s are proof-level obligations explicitly allowed by the\nStage 4.1 skeleton brief; no definition body or axiom was added.  The fixed\nbasis fields are source-facing data, while the finite serialization equivalence\nand Euclidean coordinate helpers are Lean-only representation infrastructure.\n\n### Statement Integrity\n\n- **Paper assumptions:** admissible `q = 2^k` with odd `k`, `m | q`, a fixed\n  self-dual normal field representation, and a finite-dimensional tensor-product\n  strategy passing the Pauli basis test with probability at least `1 - epsilon`.\n- **Lean assumptions:** `AdmissibleParams` carries `q`, `m`, `d`, the admissibility\n  and divisibility proofs, and the fixed `FixedFieldModel` basis/algebra data;\n  `Strategy` carries finite Euclidean registers and a unit state; the theorem\n  assumes `0 <= epsilon` and the same success inequality. The model is fixed in `AdmissibleParams`, as the\n  paper requires; no fresh field identification is added to `pauli_soundness`.\n- Define `tauObservable` independently from the single-qudit shift and phase\n  operators, retaining the Fourier expansion identities as proof obligations.\n- Correct conditional-linear concatenation, require nonempty graph support,\n  remove the unused low-degree edge set, and provide the proved Magic Square\n  nonemptiness witness.\n- Correct Point/Pair orientation, add both supported Magic Square orientations,\n  make same-type consistency unconditional, and accept unsupported total cases\n  as prescribed by the decider.\n- Use `Matrix.toEuclideanLin` for the shared Hilbert-space action and the\n  state-dependent operator distances; allow the source's `epsilon = 0` boundary.\n- Add the missing helper docstrings and replace stale paper anchors.  Blueprint\n  links are intentionally unchanged in this repair; the known missing `\\\\uses`\n  edges and QPBT chapter links are tracked for the Stage 4.2 synchronization.\n\nAll remaining `sorry`s are proof-level obligations explicitly allowed by the\nStage 4.1 skeleton brief; no definition body or axiom was added.  The fixed\nbasis fields are source-facing data, while the finite serialization equivalence\nand Euclidean coordinate helpers are Lean-only representation infrastructure.\n\n### Statement Integrity\n\n- **Paper assumptions:** admissible `q = 2^k` with odd `k`, `m | q`, a fixed\n  self-dual normal field representation, and a finite-dimensional tensor-product\n  strategy passing the Pauli basis test with probability at least `1 - epsilon`.\n- **Lean assumptions:** `AdmissibleParams` carries `q`, `m`, `d`, the admissibility\n  and divisibility proofs, and the fixed `FixedFieldModel` basis/algebra data;\n  `Strategy` carries finite Euclidean registers and a unit state; the theorem\n  assumes `0 <= epsilon` and the same success inequality.  These are faithful\n  finite-type and boundary hypotheses, not a residual or repair package.\n- **Paper conclusion:** universal constants and a quantitative error scale,\n  local isometries into auxiliary registers tensored with Pauli registers, a\n  unit auxiliary state, and state-dependent closeness of the state and both\n  Pauli POVM families.\n- **Lean conclusion:** existential `a,b` with the stated bounds and a\n  `PauliSoundnessWitness` containing finite auxiliary types, local isometries,\n  and a unit auxiliary vector; it states the Euclidean state inequality and the\n  two explicit squared operator-distance inequalities using `deltaQld`.\n- **Verdict:** faithful finite-dimensional encoding with ordinary typeclass and\n  nonemptiness boundary hypotheses.  No extra bridge, residual, producer, or\n  assumptions bundle is present.  The analytic arguments remain intentional\n  Stage 4.1 proof obligations, and the explicit inequalities make the paper's\n  asymptotic distance convention concrete.\n\n### Testing\n\n- `lake env lean` passed for all twelve edited QPBT modules in dependency order.\n- `git diff --check` and the QPBT line-length audit passed.\n- The proof-hole scan reports only the intentional Stage 4.1 `sorry` sites; no\n  `axiom`, `native_decide`, or kernel-bypass declaration was introduced.\n- The repository pre-commit statement-integrity, proof-debt, faithful-boundary,\n  and conclusion-shaped-hypothesis checks all passed.\n- The direct full build was attempted, but this repair worktree's copied package\n  source cache is incomplete; the authoritative local CI gate is run separately\n  through `local/bin/ci.sh` with the hot cache.\n\n---\nAddresses #4\n",

All CI workflows and review prompts should reference this file\nrather than duplicating the rules inline.\n\n> **Lean version**: 4.x (Lean 3 keywords like `constant` do not apply)\n\n> **Companion document:** [`anti_patterns.md`](./anti_patterns.md) catalogues\n> subtler proof-evasion patterns that pass every blocker check below yet still\n> fail to prove the claimed mathematics (conclusion-shaped hypotheses,\n> definitional sleight-of-hand, zero-fallback branches, trivial default\n> witnesses, Mathlib-bypass castles, external `*Statement` smuggles).\n> Consult it alongside this file during review.\n\n> **Paper-realignment exception:** When a PR is explicitly realigning a\n> source-labelled declaration with `references/ldt-paper/`, the `sorry`\n> blocker below may be temporarily relaxed for the affected proof bodies.  The\n> PR must restore the source-faithful public statement, name the remaining proof\n> obligation as a theorem or lemma, and cite the paper passage plus the\n> tracking issue or paper-gap note.  A theorem whose proof still depends on a\n> known non-paper bridge, residual, repair input, obligation structure, or\n> conditional helper\n> must carry the `**Unfaithful:**` docstring marker described in `AGENTS.md`.\n> Review such PRs against statement faithfulness and the documented discharge\n> plan, not merely against the temporary `sorry` count.\n\n---\n\n## Blockers\n\nThese patterns **must** be resolved before merging.\n\n### Direct proof holes\n\n| Pattern | Risk |\n|---------|------|\n| `sorry` | Axiomatically closes any goal — the proof is incomplete |\n| `admit` | Tactic alias for `sorry` |\n\n### Kernel / type system bypasses\n\n| Pattern | Risk |\n|---------|------|\n| `native_decide` | Relies on trusted native evaluation / compiler; banned in Mathlib for soundness and process reasons |\n| `unsafeCast`, `unsafeCoerce` | Type system bypass — can fabricate any proof term |\n| `lcProof` | Low-level proof fabrication primitive — can prove `False` |\n| `ofReduceBool`, `ofReduceNat` | Kernel reduction primitives exploitable for unsound proofs |\n\n### Axiom smuggling\n\n| Pattern | Risk |\n|---------|------|\n| `axiom` declarations | Introduces unproven assumptions that could be inconsistent; must be explicitly justified |\n\nWhen an external mathematical result must remain unformalized temporarily,\nprefer a caller-supplied `Prop` hypothesis over a global `axiom`\ndeclaration, and add a regression check (for example a\n`Lean.collectAxioms`-based assertion, as in\n`MIPStarRE.LDT.Test.AxiomAudit`) so later refactors cannot silently widen\nthe axiomatic base.\n\nThis preference does not license proposition inputs on source-labelled paper\ntheorems.  If the cited paper theorem does not assume the proposition, a\ncaller-supplied `Prop` hypothesis is an additional theorem hypothesis, not a\nproof of the paper statement.  Use such hypotheses only for explicitly\nconditional auxiliary results, and keep the source-labelled theorem statement\nfaithful to the paper.\n\n### Circular reasoning\n\nLean's kernel forbids literal declaration cycles, so focus on **mathematical\ncircularity**:\n\n- Proofs that assume (or trivially reintroduce) the statement being proved as a\n  local hypothesis, then immediately close the goal from that hypothesis\n- Helper lemmas in the same file that essentially restate the main goal and are\n  only used to prove that goal\n- Local `have`/`let` bindings that are just the goal rephrased, used to solve\n  the goal without any real argument\n- Newly introduced `axiom` that makes a difficult statement trivially provable\n  without connecting to existing Mathlib / core theorems\n- Abuse of `unsafe` features to fabricate proofs instead of giving a genuine\n  derivation\n- `by exact h` where `h` came from an unjustified assumption identical to the\n  goal\n\n### Castle-in-the-air (ungrounded proofs)\n\nProofs that avoid grounding in Mathlib:\n\n- Custom re-declarations of standard Mathlib lemmas (e.g., re-proving\n  `add_comm` instead of importing it)\n- `axiom` or `sorry`-based helper lemmas for facts that already exist in\n  Mathlib\n- Chains of custom lemmas that never bottom out in Mathlib or Lean core\n- `private` helper lemmas that duplicate Mathlib API (e.g., custom matrix\n  transpose lemmas when `Matrix.transpose_*` exists)\n- Overly long proof chains replaceable by a single Mathlib lemma\n\nWhen flagging, perform an actual lookup (grep, `#find?`, `exact?`,\n`library_search`). If an equivalent exists, cite the Mathlib lemma and module\npath. If not, state \"no equivalent found\" with search evidence.\n\n### Scaffolding that blocks real formalization\n\nThis is a subtle but critical failure mode: **scaffolding definitions or\ntheorem statements that do not faithfully represent the actual mathematics**,\nmaking them impossible to connect to real Mathlib-based proofs.\n\nSigns to watch for:\n\n- Custom type definitions for objects that already exist in Mathlib (e.g.,\n  defining a custom `Measurement` type instead of using Mathlib's\n  `MeasureTheory` or operator algebra API)\n- Theorem statements whose hypotheses or conclusions use project-local types\n  that are not definitionally equal to or coercible from the Mathlib versions\n- Scaffolded definitions that compile but encode the wrong mathematical\n  semantics (e.g., a \"projective measurement\" definition that does not enforce\n  the correct positivity or completeness conditions)\n- Intermediate lemmas stated in terms of scaffolding types that cannot be\n  connected upstream to Mathlib's API without reproving everything\n- Definitions that \"work\" for `sorry`-based proofs but fail when you try to\n  fill in real proofs using Mathlib lemmas (type mismatches, missing instances,\n  incompatible universes)\n\nWhen reviewing scaffolded code, ask: **Can a real proof be built on top of\nthis?** If the types, instances, and API surface don't align with Mathlib, the\nscaffolding is actively harmful — it creates technical debt that blocks\nprogress rather than enabling it.\n\n### Paper-labelled theorem statement drift\n\nA theorem advertised as the Lean formalization of a paper theorem is a blocker\nif its public statement has drifted from the cited paper statement.\nChanging a theorem away from the statement in `references/ldt-paper/` is\nstrongly discouraged unless it is forced by faithful formal encoding or by a\ndocumented mathematical necessity.\n\nThe most common failure mode is replacing an unformalized proof step by an\nextra hypothesis on the theorem itself.  This produces a true conditional\ntheorem, but it is not the theorem stated in the paper.  In particular, do not\nrepair a theorem such as `mainFormal` by adding assumptions named\n`BridgeHypotheses`, `Input`, `Residual`, `Package`, `RepairInput`, `Producer`,\ngeneric `Hypotheses` or `Assumptions` bundles, or similar, unless those\nassumptions are explicitly present in the cited paper statement.\n\nConditional helpers are a last-resort quarantine for proof work that cannot yet\nbe closed.  Before introducing one, state the missing intermediate fact as a\nnamed lemma or theorem to be proved from the paper hypotheses.  A conditional\nhelper is permitted only when it has a paper-gap note or tracking issue, a named\nobligation-discharger target, and an explicit removal plan.  Its name must show\nthat it is conditional, for example with `_of_...`, `_assuming_...`, or\n`conditional...`.  It must not be the declaration used by a source-labelled\nblueprint theorem with `\\leanok`.\n\nExisting bridge hypotheses should be treated as proof debt.  Mine their proofs\nfor reusable arguments, but do not keep a paper-labelled theorem in a\nstrengthened form merely because the conditional version compiles.  If the\nbridge data cannot be derived from the paper hypotheses, the correct repair is\nto restore the paper-aligned theorem statement and leave the missing proof as a\ntracked `sorry`, rather than to keep the extra assumption on the theorem.\n\nNot every explicit Lean hypothesis is statement drift.  Side conditions needed\nto encode the paper's domain, such as nonemptiness, decidability, field-model\ninstances, positivity of parameters, or denominator nonvanishing, may be\nfaithful when the paper uses the corresponding objects without comment.  These\nconditions should still be reviewed.  The issue is whether the hypothesis is\nmathematical domain data implicit in the source, or an unproved intermediate\nstep of the source proof.\n\nFor every paper-labelled theorem change, require a statement integrity audit:\n\n- paper assumptions versus Lean assumptions;\n- paper conclusion versus Lean conclusion;\n- verdict: exact, faithful boundary hypotheses, extra assumptions, weakened\n  conclusion, or strengthened conclusion.\n\n---\n\n## Warnings\n\nThese should be flagged for review but may be acceptable with justification.\n\n### Placeholder tactics\n\n| Pattern | Risk |\n|---------|------|\n| `exact?`, `apply?`, `library_search`, `suggest` | Search tactics left as placeholders — replace with the concrete result |\n\n### Safety / termination bypasses\n\n| Pattern | Risk |\n|---------|------|\n| `unsafe def` | Bypasses Lean safety checks; should not appear in proof-relevant code |\n| `partial def` | No termination proof required; unsound if used to build proof terms |\n| `implemented_by` / `implementedBy` | Decouples runtime behavior from proven specification |\n\n### Suspicious options\n\n| Pattern | Risk |\n|---------|------|\n| `set_option maxHeartbeats 0` | Disables timeout — can hide non-terminating proofs |\n| `set_option maxHeartbeats` with values >= 4,000,000 | 20x the default (200,000) — likely indicates an inefficient proof |\n| `set_option maxRecDepth` with values >= 10,000 | May hide structural issues in proofs |\n\n### Debug artifacts\n\n| Pattern | Risk |\n|---------|------|\n| `dbg_trace` | Debug trace left in code |\n| `stop` | Halts elaboration — development aid only |\n| `#check`, `#eval`, `#print` in proof files | Debug commands that should be removed |\n\n---\n\n## How to use this file\n\n**For source-statement proof gaps**: Read\n[`paper-gaps/proof-gap-protocol.tex`](paper-gaps/proof-gap-protocol.tex) when a\nproof is blocked by a bridge, residual, repair, input, package, or obligation\nstructure.  It explains when to introduce an internal obligation theorem, why\nconditional helpers are exceptional temporary quarantine objects, and why a\ntracked `sorry` is preferable to a strengthened source theorem statement.\n\n**In CI review prompts**: Reference this file instead of inlining the rules:\n```\nRead `docs/PROOF_INTEGRITY.md` for the complete list of proof integrity\nrules. Flag blockers as must-fix issues that should block merge.\nFlag warnings as advisory — note them but acknowledge they may be\nacceptable with justification.\n```\n\n**For manual review**: Use this as a checklist when reviewing Lean PRs.\n\n**Updating rules**: Edit this file and all referencing workflows will\nautomatically pick up the changes.\n","exit_code":0,"status":"completed"}}

Append to `local/protocols/EVOLUTION.md`:\n   `## YYYY-MM-DD — <short title>` with fields **Trigger** (cite events.md\n   entry or telemetry line), **Change** (files + gist), **Expected effect**,\n   and, when known later, **Outcome**.\n4. It complements the individual chapter audits\nin `audits/`, the proof-integrity rules in the lean-conventions skill (addenda:\n`docs/project_conventions.md`), and the\nproof-gap protocol in `docs/paper-gaps/proof-gap-protocol.tex`.\n\n## Table of Contents\n\n1. [Source-faithful statements and internal proof obligations](#pattern-1-source-faithful-statements-and-internal-proof-obligations)\n2. [Blueprint–Lean synchronization](#pattern-2-blueprintlean-synchronization)\n3. [Split-module architecture](#pattern-3-split-module-architecture)\n4. [Public re-export pattern](#pattern-4-public-re-export-pattern)\n5. [Temporary obligation-structure pattern](#pattern-5-temporary-obligation-structure-pattern)\n6. [Paper-gap documentation pattern](#pattern-6-paper-gap-documentation-pattern)\n\n---\n\n## Pattern 1: Source-faithful statements and internal proof obligations\n\n### The rule\n\nA declaration presented as the formalization of a paper theorem, lemma,\nproposition, or corollary must state the paper result, up to faithful formal\nencoding of the mathematical domain.  Its public hypotheses and conclusion are\nboth part of the statement.  Adding a load-bearing bridge, residual, repair,\nobligation-structure input, hypotheses bundle, or assumptions bundle not present\nin the cited statement changes the theorem into a conditional helper.\n\nThe project therefore distinguishes three objects.\n\n| Object | Public statement | Blueprint status |\n|--------|------------------|------------------|\n| Paper theorem | Matches the cited result in `references/ldt-paper/` | May be linked by source-labelled `\\lean{}`; statement-level `\\leanok` only when the statement matches |\n| Internal proof obligation | Proves a missing intermediate mathematical input from paper hypotheses | May contain a tracked `sorry` while the proof is open |\n| Conditional helper | Quarantines an unproved intermediate obligation | Not a paper theorem; no source-labelled `\\leanok` |\n\nIt is never allowed to change the public statement of a declaration presented\nas the formalization of a source-labelled paper theorem.  At the final assembly\npoint, the paper theorem must either discharge the extra hypotheses internally,\nor remain as the paper-aligned statement with an unfinished proof while the\nconditional helper is given a different name.\n\nThe preferred way to expose unfinished work is a named internal theorem or\ndefinition with a precise paper-origin docstring and, if necessary, a tracked\n`sorry`.  This makes the proof frontier visible without weakening the statement\nof a source-labelled theorem.\n\n### Why legacy scaffolding may remain temporarily\n\n| Temporary reason | Explanation |\n|------------------|-------------|\n| **Localizing an obstruction** | A conditional helper can isolate the exact missing mathematical input while the obligation discharger is being proved. |\n| **Recovering useful proof content** | The proof body may contain genuine estimates or constructions that should be extracted into source-faithful lemmas. |\n| **Auditability** | An explicit temporary hypothesis is easier to find than an implicit assumption hidden in prose, provided it is named as proof debt. |\n\nThese reasons do not justify strengthening a paper theorem.  They only explain\nwhy a short-lived helper declaration may exist while its remaining hypotheses\nare being actively removed.\n\n### How to proceed when a proof needs an extra input\n\n1. **Check the source statement.**  Read the corresponding TeX in\n   `references/ldt-paper/` before changing a theorem linked from the blueprint.\n2. **Keep the paper-facing declaration source-faithful.**  Boundary hypotheses\n   such as positivity, nonemptiness, decidability, field-model instances, or\n   type-class assumptions may be faithful encodings when they are needed to\n   state the mathematics in Lean.  Proof data such as `BridgeInputs`,\n   `RepairInput`, `Residual`, `Package`, generic `Hypotheses`, or generic\n   `Assumptions` is different: it is not a paper assumption unless the cited\n   statement says so.\n3. **Name the missing intermediate result.**  If the proof uses a mathematical\n   fact not yet formalized, state it as a separate proof obligation.  A\n   temporary `sorry` in this declaration is preferable to adding the obligation as\n   a hypothesis on the paper theorem.\n4. **Do not introduce conditional helpers by default.**  A helper whose name\n   ends in `_ofObligations` is a quarantine device, not a normal formalization\n   pattern.  It may remain temporarily only when it preserves substantial proof\n   content that cannot yet be connected to the paper hypotheses, has a tracked\n   discharge or deletion target, and has no source-labelled blueprint\n   `\\leanok`.  If the helper would merely package missing work as an extra\n   hypothesis, restore the theorem with the paper statement and leave a tracked\n   `sorry` instead.\n5. **Audit the final statement.**  Every PR touching a source-labelled theorem\n   should compare paper assumptions and Lean assumptions, paper conclusion and\n   Lean conclusion, and report whether the Lean statement is exact, has only\n   faithful boundary hypotheses, or has extra assumptions.\n\nIf a paper-facing declaration is temporarily proved by calling a conditional\nhelper whose load-bearing input has not yet been produced from the paper\nhypotheses, the proof frontier must be marked explicitly.  The declaration\nshould carry an `**Unfaithful:**` docstring section naming the non-paper\ndependency, citing the paper-gap note or tracking issue, and identifying the\ninternal theorem that will remove the dependency.  A named proof obligation\nwith a tracked `sorry` is preferred whenever possible, because it makes the\nmissing mathematical assertion visible without adding it to the paper theorem\nstatement.\n\n### Required metadata for new proof-obligation declarations\n\nA new declaration whose name contains a proof-debt token such as `Bridge`,\n`Residual`, `Repair`, `Package`, `Producer`, `Input`, `Hypotheses`,\n`Assumptions`, `Obligation`, or `Witness` must explain its mathematical role in\nthe def-site docstring.  A paper citation alone is not enough, because the\nreviewer must be able to tell whether the declaration is part of the paper\nstatement or a Lean-only proof obligation.\n\nUse one of the following markers.\n\n| Marker | Use |\n|--------|-----|\n| `**Source:**`, `**Paper source:**`, or `**Source statement:**` | The declaration is a faithful formal encoding of a cited source statement or a field of that statement |\n| `**Faithful encoding:**` | The declaration records boundary data or domain data that the paper uses implicitly |\n| `**Proof obligation:**` or `**Internal proof obligation:**` | The declaration is a theorem or record that must be proved from the paper hypotheses before a source theorem is complete |\n| `**Conditional:**` | The declaration is a conditional helper; it must not be linked as the source theorem |\n| `**Unfaithful:**` | The declaration or proof currently depends on a load-bearing assumption not yet derived from the paper hypotheses |\n\nProof-obligation, conditional, and unfaithful markers must cite a paper-gap note\nor tracking issue and must state the planned discharge or elimination theorem.\nIf such a declaration would merely package missing work as an added hypothesis\nto a source theorem, do not introduce it; restore the source theorem statement\nand leave the missing proof as a tracked `sorry`.\n\n### Conditional helper boundary\n\n1. **Prefer a source theorem with a tracked `sorry`.**  If a proof requires a\n   construction that is not yet available from the paper hypotheses, the first\n   repair is to restore the source theorem statement and leave the missing proof\n   open.
