The patterns below are the displacement mechanisms we've seen in this\\\\\\\\ncodebase.\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n## Catalogue\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n- [A1 — Conclusion-shaped hypothesis](#a1--conclusion-shaped-hypothesis)\\\\\\\\n- [A2 — Definitional sleight-of-hand](#a2--definitional-sleight-of-hand)\\\\\\\\n- [A3 — Zero-fallback branches hiding preconditions](#a3--zero-fallback-branches-hiding-preconditions)\\\\\\\\n- [A4 — Trivial default witnesses for existentials](#a4--trivial-default-witnesses-for-existentials)\\\\\\\\n- [A5 — Castle-in-the-air / bypassing Mathlib](#a5--castle-in-the-air--bypassing-mathlib)\\\\\\\\n- [A6 — External `*Statement` smuggles](#a6--external-statement-smuggles)\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n---\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n## A1 — Conclusion-shaped hypothesis\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n**Smell.** The theorem takes a hypothesis whose type is the theorem's own\\\\\\\\nconclusion (or an `∃`/function that produces the conclusion). The proof body\\\\\\\\nis a trivial `rcases`/`exact`/`.trans`/`simpa using h` and does no\\\\\\\\nmathematical work. A variant wraps the hypothesis in a named bundle\\\\\\\\n(`*BridgePackage`, `*Statement`); see issues [#449], [#451], [#477] for the\\\\\\\\ncatalogue, and [#493] for the inline-existential mutation triggered by\\\\\\\\nPR [#491].\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n### Why it's bad\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\nThe theorem's named mathematical content is never derived from prior lemmas;\\\\\\\\nthe caller (who supplies the hypothesis) has to discharge it. In practice the\\\\\\\\ncaller then has the same problem, pushing the obligation further up the\\\\\\\\nstack. The theorem is true under a vacuous hypothesis and the `\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\leanok` tag\\\\\\\\nmisrepresents the actual state of the proof.\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n### How to spot it\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n- The hypothesis type contains, up to `∃` / `∧` / a coercion, the theorem's\\\\\\\\n  conclusion.\\\\\\\\n- The proof body is one of:\\\\\\\\n  - `rcases h with ⟨...⟩; exact ⟨...⟩`\\\\\\\\n  - `exact h.fieldName` / `exact h.a.trans h.b`\\\\\\\\n  - `by simpa using h.fieldName`\\\\\\\\n- The hypothesis is a bundle named `*BridgePackage`, `*Witness`, `*Package`,\\\\\\\\n  `*Output`, with a field whose type matches the conclusion structure.\\\\\\\\n- Consumers of the bundle are trivial (field projection + return).\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n### Concrete example\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\nHistorical example (before the MainInductionStep cleanup):\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n```lean\\\\\\\\ntheorem mainInduction\\\\\\\\n    (params : Parameters) [FieldModel params.q]\\\\\\\\n    (strategy : SymStrat params ι)\\\\\\\\n    (eps delta gamma : Error) (k : ℕ)\\\\\\\\n    (hbridge : MainInductionBridgePackage params strategy eps delta gamma k) :\\\\\\\\n    ∃ G : Measurement (Polynomial params) ι,\\\\\\\\n      ConsRel strategy.state ...\\\\\\\\n        (mainInductionError params k eps delta gamma) := by\\\\\\\\n  rcases hbridge.witness with ⟨error, G, hG, herror⟩\\\\\\\\n  refine ⟨G, ?_⟩\\\\\\\\n  exact ⟨le_trans hG.offDiagonalBound herror⟩\\\\\\\\n```\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\nHere `MainInductionBridgePackage.witness` has type\\\\\\\\n`∃ error, ∃ G, ConsRel ... error ∧ error ≤ mainInductionError ...` — literally\\\\\\\\nthe conclusion. The code has since been refactored to remove both this\\\\\\\\nspecific MainInductionStep bridge and the interim theorem alias that exposed\\\\\\\\nthe same witness shape under the paper theorem's name, but the snippet remains\\\\\\\\nthe archetypal example of the anti-pattern.\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\nPR [#491] proposed to delete the `*BridgePackage` by **inlining** the bundle's\\\\\\\\nfields as explicit hypotheses. That only scatters the same pattern across\\\\\\\\nindividual signatures without producing any proof — it's strictly worse\\\\\\\\nbecause the named bundle at least shows up in one tracker. Do not accept PRs\\\\\\\\nthat discharge an ungrounded bridge by flattening it into conclusion-shaped\\\\\\\\nexistential hypotheses, or by reintroducing the same shape under a theorem name\\\\\\\\nthat suggests the paper result has been proved.\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n### How to fix it\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\nPrefer **proving a real intermediate lemma** — one that the paper also uses\\\\\\\\n— and stating its signature with the paper's hypotheses (not the theorem's\\\\\\\\nconclusion). Then use it inside the larger theorem. If the missing content\\\\\\\\ncannot be formalized yet, state the missing assertion as a named obligation\\\\\\\\nto be proved from the paper hypotheses, and leave the corresponding proof open\\\\\\\\nunder a tracker. Do not put that obligation on the source-labelled theorem as\\\\\\\\nan extra hypothesis. Existing `BridgePackage`-style declarations are proof\\\\\\\\ndebt to be removed or converted into source-faithful obligations; they are not\\\\\\\\nthe preferred shape for new work.\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\nA signature passes the smell test if:\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n- Every hypothesis is a **named intermediate fact** that also appears in the\\\\\\\\n  paper or blueprint proof, not the theorem's output packaged up, and\\\\\\\\n- Replacing a hypothesis with its negation would produce a *different*\\\\\\\\n  theorem, not a trivially-false one.\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n### Related issues and patterns\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n- [#449] — paper-wide gap tracker\\\\\\\\n- [#451] — the tracked `BridgePackage` producer catalogue\\\\\\\\n- [#595] — resolved the QXP `ProjectiveNonMeasurementBridgePackage` offender by\\\\\\\\n  deleting the bridge and threading `RoundingToProjectorsWitness` directly\\\\\\\\n- [#477] — resolved `QXPLayerData` axiom-field projection (a definitional variant)\\\\\\\\n- [#493] — the inline-existential mutation of this pattern\\\\\\\\n- [#491] — PR that introduced the mutation\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n---\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n## A2 — Definitional sleight-of-hand\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n**Smell.** A `def`/`abbrev` is written so its body is the paper's claim, and\\\\\\\\na nearby `theorem` restates that claim and proves it by `rfl` (or a one-line\\\\\\\\n`simp [foo]` where `foo` is the defining equation). The \\\\\\\\\\\\\\\"mathematical\\\\\\\\ncontent\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\" has been baked into the definition; the theorem is a tautology. See\\\\\\\\nissues [#477], [#494].\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n### Why it's bad\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n`rfl` proves that a definition equals itself. If the definition is chosen\\\\\\\\n*so that* it equals the conclusion, the `rfl` \\\\\\\\\\\\\\\"proof\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\" transports none of the\\\\\\\\npaper's reasoning — it is literally the reflexivity of a shape we invented to\\\\\\\\nmatch the conclusion. The real identity the paper proves (e.g.,\\\\\\\\n`⟨φ_α, φ_β⟩ = δ_αβ` over an actual inner product) is still not stated\\\\\\\\nanywhere in Lean.\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n### How to spot it\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n- A `theorem` whose body is `rfl` / `by rfl` / `by simp [defName]` where\\\\\\\\n  `defName` is the def that unfolds to the conclusion.\\\\\\\\n- A `structure` with a `Prop`-typed field whose *role* in the paper is a\\\\\\\\n  nontrivial identity (SVD, orthonormality, Cauchy–Schwarz), accompanied by a\\\\\\\\n  constructor that discharges that field with `rfl`.\\\\\\\\n- A `def foo := if α = β then 1 else 0` followed by a theorem asserting\\\\\\\\n  `foo α β = if α = β then 1 else 0`.\\\\\\\\n- Bridge-like structures where every field is itself a function\\\\\\\\n  `(precondition) → (conclusion-step)` and the consumer applies the field\\\\\\\\n  directly.\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n### Concrete example\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\nFrom `MIPStarRE/LDT/ExpansionHypercubeGraph/Defs/Fourier.lean`:\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n```lean\\\\\\\\n/-- The exact inner-product formula for the hypercube Fourier basis. -/\\\\\\\\ndef fourierBasisInnerProduct (params : Parameters)\\\\\\\\n    (α β : Point params) : Error :=\\\\\\\\n  if α = β then 1 else 0\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n/-- The exact inner-product formula for the hypercube Fourier basis. -/\\\\\\\\nlemma fourierBasisInnerProduct_eq (params : Parameters)\\\\\\\\n    (α β : Point params) :\\\\\\\\n    fourierBasisInnerProduct params α β = if α = β then 1 else 0 := rfl\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n/-- `prop:eigenvectors`. -/\\\\\\\\ntheorem eigenvectors (params : Parameters) :\\\\\\\\n    (∀ α β : Point params,\\\\\\\\n      fourierBasisInnerProduct params α β = if α = β then 1 else 0) ∧ ... := by\\\\\\\\n  refine ⟨?_, ?_⟩\\\\\\\\n  · intro α β\\\\\\\\n    exact fourierBasisInnerProduct_eq params α β    -- castle: def IS Kronecker delta\\\\\\\\n  ...\\\\\\\\n```\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\nThe paper's orthonormality claim — that the additive characters `φ_α` form an\\\\\\\\northonormal basis under the actual inner product\\\\\\\\n`⟨f, g⟩ := (1/|V|) · ∑_u f(u)^* · g(u)` — requires a genuine character-sum\\\\\\\\nidentity. The Lean theorem states and proves only the trivial fact that the\\\\\\\\ndefinition equals itself.\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n### Not every `rfl` is a castle\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\nDistinguish from legitimate bookkeeping where a named equation is literally\\\\\\\\nhow something was defined. Example: `mainFormalError_eq_envelope` in\\\\\\\\n`Test/ErrorCascade/Definitions.lean` unfolds the definition of\\\\\\\\n`mainFormalError` to its envelope factorization. The mathematical content is\\\\\\\\nelsewhere (the envelope is derived from per-step bounds); the `rfl` theorem is\\\\\\\\na naming convenience only. The test is: **does the `def` body encode a paper\\\\\\\\nidentity, or does it just name a compound expression?**\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n### How to fix it\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n1. Move the paper's real definition to the concrete one: for Fourier, define\\\\\\\\n   the inner product as the actual sum over vertices, and the characters\\\\\\\\n   `φ_α` as functions from `Point params` to `ℂ`.\\\\\\\\n2. State the paper's identity (`⟨φ_α, φ_β⟩ = δ_αβ`) as a theorem over those\\\\\\\\n   concrete objects.\\\\\\\\n3. Prove it via the standard character-sum derivation (or cite the Mathlib\\\\\\\\n   counterpart if one exists — `Matrix.dotProduct` / `Finset.sum_eq_zero_iff`\\\\\\\\n   combined with `ZMod.sum_pow_units` style lemmas).\\\\\\\\n4. If you want to keep the Kronecker shorthand, define it *afterward* as a\\\\\\\\n   consequence, not as the primitive.\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n### Related issues\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n- [#477] — resolved `QXPLayerData` field projections (Ch4 SVD as axiom fields)\\\\\\\\n- [#494] — the Fourier case and other candidates\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n---\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n## A3 — Zero-fallback branches hiding preconditions\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n**Smell.** A total function is defined by `if eligible then real_value else\\\\\\\\ndefault`, where the `default` (usually `0`, `default`, `⊥`, or\\\\\\\\n`Classical.arbitrary`) is a sentinel for \\\\\\\\\\\\\\\"precondition not met.\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\" Downstream\\\\\\\\ntheorems state properties that are only true on the eligible branch, but the\\\\\\\\ntheorem's type signature does not carry the eligibility proof, so the\\\\\\\\nobligation moves silently from the prover to whoever happens to call the\\\\\\\\nfunction. See issue [#495], related to [#307].\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n### Why it's bad\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\nThe signature lies about the domain of validity. A caller passing a\\\\\\\\nnon-eligible input gets `0` back; any theorem proved about \\\\\\\\\\\\\\\"the output\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\" is\\\\\\\\nproved for `0`, which is trivially true and carries no information. When a\\\\\\\\nlater theorem composes the output with another lemma, the composition\\\\\\\\ntype-checks but the conclusion is vacuous on inputs where the original\\\\\\\\nprecondition failed.\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\nThe paper, by contrast, restricts the quantifier in the first place:\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\"Fix a tuple `(x₁, ..., x_k)` with Hamming weight `≥ d+1`.\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\" The Lean should\\\\\\\\nmatch.\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n### How to spot it\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n- `match ... with | some _ => real | none => 0` or `| _ => 0`.\\\\\\\\n- `if hEligible : P then ... else default`.\\\\\\\\n- Identifier names containing `fallback`, `placeholder`, `sentinel`,\\\\\\\\n  `dummy`, `or0`, `orDefault`.\\\\\\\\n- Recursive definitions whose base case unconditionally returns a sentinel.\\\\\\\\n- Functions that return `Polynomial params` but can return the zero polynomial\\\\\\\\n  on inputs that shouldn't be in the domain.\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n### Concrete example (historical; resolved by PR #561)\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\nUntil PR #561, `MIPStarRE/LDT/Pasting/Defs/Interpolation.lean` contained:\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n```lean\\\\\\\\n/-- Extract the polynomial from a completed slice outcome; returns 0 on ⊥. -/\\\\\\\\nnoncomputable def extractSliceOr0 {params : Parameters} [FieldModel params.q]\\\\\\\\n    (g : GHatOutcome params) : PolynomialModel params :=\\\\\\\\n  match g with\\\\\\\\n  | some p => p.poly\\\\\\\\n  | none   => 0\\\\\\\\n```\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\nThe consumer `interpolateCompletedSlicesFromSupport` ran Lagrange\\\\\\\\ninterpolation on `extractSliceOr0`-extracted values. If the support contained\\\\\\\\na `none`, the interpolant silently pretended that slice evaluated to zero.\\\\\\\\nThe paper's Lagrange step is quantified over *eligible* slices only, so the\\\\\\\\nLean API should carry `∀ i ∈ support, (g i).isSome` as a hypothesis; instead\\\\\\\\nit carried nothing, and the theorem technically type-checked on inputs for\\\\\\\\nwhich its conclusion was meaningless.\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n**Current status:** resolved. The live API now removes `extractSliceOr0`,\\\\\\\\nthreads the explicit hypothesis `hσsupport : σ ⊆ gHatTupleSupport gs` into\\\\\\\\n`interpolateCompletedSlicesFromSupport`, and packages the chosen support subset\\\\\\\\nas `InterpolationSupportWitness` so the arbitrary choice and its proof fields\\\\\\\\nare visible at call sites.\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n### Acceptable uses of this pattern\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\nNot every default branch is a castle. `Inhabited` / `Nonempty` instances\\\\\\\\nthat provide a canonical inhabitant (e.g., the zero polynomial for\\\\\\\\n`Nonempty (Polynomial params)`) are plumbing, not proof. The test is: **does\\\\\\\\nany theorem mention the output?** If a theorem says \\\\\\\\\\\\\\\"the output satisfies\\\\\\\\nP\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\", and P is not trivially satisfied by the sentinel, the fallback is\\\\\\\\nsmuggling a precondition.\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n### How to fix it\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\nPick one of:\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n1. **Make the precondition explicit.** Add `(h : eligible input) :` to the\\\\\\\\n   signature. Let Lean's type system enforce that non-eligible inputs cannot\\\\\\\\n   be passed.\\\\\\\\n2. **Return an `Option`.** The `none` result forces every caller to handle\\\\\\\\n   the case, so theorems about \\\\\\\\\\\\\\\"the output\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\" now quantify only over the\\\\\\\\n   `some` branch.\\\\\\\\n3. **Restrict the domain.** Instead of `(x : X) → Y`, take `(x : {x : X //\\\\\\\\n   P x}) → Y`. Common for finite-support Lagrange-style constructions where\\\\\\\\n   the subtype is computable via `Finset.filter`.\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\n### Classical-logic dependencies\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\nA sibling smell in this pattern: `DecidablePred` / `DecidableEq` instances\\\\\\\\nthat silently use `Classical.dec` to fill in decidability that should be\\\\\\\\nconstructive.   1426	\paragraph{Soundness of the Pauli basis test.} 
  1427	We state the soundness properties of the Pauli basis test.
  1428	The following is an adaptation of the self-testing statement in~\cite[Theorem
  1429	6.4]{NW19}.
  1430	
  1431	\begin{theorem}
  1432	  \label{thm:pauli}
  1433	There exists a function 
  1434	\[\delta_{\qld}(\eps,m,d,q) = a(md)^a(\eps^b + q^{-b} + 2^{-bmd})\]
  1435	 for universal constants $a \geq 1$ and $0 < b < 1$ such that the following holds. For all admissible parameter tuples $\qldparams = (q,m,d)$ and for all strategies $\strategy = (\ket{\psi},A,B)$ for the game $\game^\pauli_\qldparams$ that succeed with probability at least $1 - \eps$, there exist local isometries $\phi_\alice: \mH_\alice \to \mH_{\alice'} \otimes \mH_{\alice''},\phi_\bob: \mH_\bob \to \mH_{\bob'} \otimes \mH_{\bob''}$ (where $\ket{\psi} \in \mH_\alice \otimes \mH_\bob$ and $\mH_{\alice''},\mH_{\bob''} \cong (\C^q)^{\otimes M}$ with $M = 2^m$) and a state $\ket{\aux} \in \mH_{\alice'} \otimes \mH_{\bob'}$ such that 
  1436	\begin{enumerate}
  1437	    \item $\left \| \phi_\alice \otimes \phi_B \ket{\psi} - \ket{\aux} \otimes \ket{\EPR_q}^{\otimes M}  \right \| \leq \delta_{\qld}(\eps,m,d,q)$,
  1438	    \item Letting $\tilde{A}^x_a = \phi_A\, A^x_a \, \phi_A^\dagger$ and $\tilde{B}^y_b = \phi_B B^y_b \phi_B^\dagger$, we have for $W \in \{X,Z\}$
  1439	    \begin{gather*}
  1440	        \tilde{A}^{(\pauli,W)}_u \otimes I_{\bob'\bob''} \approx_{\delta_{\qld}} (\tau^W_u)_{\alice''} \otimes I_{\alice' \bob' \bob''} \\
  1441	        I_{\alice'\alice''} \otimes \tilde{B}^{(\pauli,W)}_u    \approx_{\delta_{\qld}} I_{\alice' \alice'' \bob'} \otimes (\tau^W_u)_{\bob''}\;,
  1442	    \end{gather*}
  1443	    where the $\approx_{\delta_{\qld}}$ statement holds with respect to the state $\ket{\aux}_{\alice'\bob'} \otimes \ket{\EPR_q}^{\otimes M}_{\alice''\bob''}$ and the answer summation is over $u \in \F_q^M$.
  1444	\end{enumerate}
  1445	\end{theorem}

  1447	We provide a proof of \Cref{thm:pauli} in \Cref{sec:qld-analysis}.

  1450	The strategies described in the proof of \Cref{lem:pauli-completeness} and in the conclusion of \Cref{thm:pauli} are described in terms of qudit Pauli measurements and maximally entangled states defined over $q$-dimensional qudits. 
  1451	However, it is more convenient for our application of the Pauli basis test to
  1452	instead deal with \emph{qubits}.
  1453	In particular, we use the Pauli basis test in the ``introspection game'' of
  1454	Section~\ref{sec:introspection}, where the players are commanded to sample
  1455	questions according to a sampler $\sampler$ of a normal form verifier.
  1456	By definition of normal form verifier, $\sampler$ is a sampler over $\F_2$, and
  1457	therefore it is natural to use a test for qubit Pauli measurements.
  1458	
  1459	Since we use field sizes $q$ that are powers of $2$, Lemma~\ref{lem:pauli-binary}
  1460	shows that the conclusions of \Cref{thm:pauli} can also be described in terms of
  1461	testing for maximally entangled states over qubits and qubit Pauli measurements.

## 5. Review Checklist

Every PR touching Lean code should be reviewed against these criteria:

1. **Proof correctness** -- No unexplained `sorry`. No `axiom` unless discussed.
   Run `rg -n "sorry|axiom" <file>` to verify.

2. **Mathlib style** -- Follow the lean-conventions `MATHLIB_naming` and
   `MATHLIB_doc` references. See the lean-conventions `MATHLIB_pr-review`
   reference for the full Mathlib review guide.

3. **Paper terminology** -- Public Lean names, module docstrings, declaration
   docstrings, and documentation-visible comments should use terminology from
   the paper and blueprint, not implementation history. See
   [mathematical_language.md](mathematical_language.md) for the project-local
   language rule for Lean documentation and public names. Reviewers should flag
   names that encode historical formalization status rather than mathematical
   content. When an old public identifier cannot be renamed in the current PR,
   record the required migration in the issue, PR description, or an audit file
   under [audits/](../audits/).
   New and substantively updated audit files should follow the term norm and
   format in
   [audits/2026-04-29_audit-document-format.md](../audits/2026-04-29_audit-document-format.md).
   Do not add an empty pass-through abbreviation merely to introduce a second
   public name.
   Review-fix PRs must read the relevant audit files under [audits/](../audits/)
   before changing names or prose. If an audit marks a naming migration or
   historical-formalization term as in scope for the fix, addressing it or
   explicitly updating the audit trail is a merge blocker.

4. **Linter hygiene** -- Linter-warning cleanup must fix warnings, not mask
   them with broad `set_option linter.<name> false` blocks. See
   [project_conventions.md](project_conventions.md#linter-warnings) for the project rule and the narrow
   exception policy.

5. **Type safety** -- No universe mismatches, coercion problems, or unresolved
   metavariables.

6. **Performance** -- Avoid expensive tactics on large types (e.g., `decide` on
   `Fin 1000`). Watch for timeout-prone proof terms.

more chapter-local leaves, the copies should be consolidated into a single
shared helper in an appropriate common module.  This avoids duplication and
ensures that fixes, generalizations, or upstream replacements apply to all
call sites at once.  Issue [#1145] tracks this work across the repository.

Procedure:

1. **Confirm equivalence.**  Compare the statement of each copy.  If the
   types differ only by a chapter-specific parameterization (e.g.,
   `SubMeas (Polynomial params) ι` vs `SubMeas (Point params) ι`),
   parameterize the shared helper over that type via a `variable` or
   explicit argument.
2. **Find the right home.**  Prefer a module that is already imported by
   both call sites.  Typical candidates:
   - `MIPStarRE/LDT/Basic/` for parameter-free operators and bounds,
   - `MIPStarRE/LDT/Preliminaries/` for polynomial/field/character lemmas,
   - The highest chapter that is a common dependency of the two sites.
3. **Name mathematically.**  Give the shared helper a name that describes
   what it states, not which chapter it originally came from.
4. **Replace call sites.**  Delete the chapter-local copies and replace
   their uses with the shared helper.  A thin wrapper is allowed only when it
   preserves a paper-facing or blueprint-facing name that external readers
   need to search for; such wrappers should have a docstring or compatibility
   comment explaining why the alias exists.  Remove the wrapper once that
   paper-facing name is no longer needed for external reference.
5. **Document.**  Add a docstring to the shared helper citing the paper or
   blueprint location it supports.

### Legacy identifier treatment

If a docstring must mention a legacy Lean identifier, cite it in backticks and
describe the mathematical object in paper terminology. If an old public
identifier cannot be renamed in the current PR, record the required migration
in the issue, PR description, or an audit file under `audits/`.

Do not add an empty pass-through abbreviation merely to introduce a second
public name.  This is different from a documented public wrapper allowed in the
shared-helper procedure above: a wrapper must preserve a paper-facing or
blueprint-facing term and must say why the alias exists.

178	\paragraph{Question distribution.}
   179	We now present the question distribution of the game $\game^\ld$ as a typed CL
   180	distribution (see \Cref{sec:types} for the definition of typed CL functions and
   181	typed CL distributions).
   182	The type set $\type^\ld$ of the game $\game^\ld$ we use is
   183	\[
   184		\type^\ld = \{ \Point, \ALine, \DLine \}\;.
   185	\]
   186	The distribution over question types is uniform over $\type^\ld \times \type^\ld$. 
   187	
   188	We introduce the corresponding typed CL functions $L_\Point$, $L_\ALine$,
   189	$L_\DLine$ where the corresponding CL distributions $\mu_{L_\ALine,L_\Point}$
   190	and $\mu_{L_\DLine,L_\Point}$ implement the axis line-versus-point and diagonal
   191	line-versus-point distributions, respectively.
   192	The functions are parametrized by a field size $q$, a dimension $m$, and three
   193	complementary register subspaces $V_\xpt,V_{\coord}, V_{\dir{}}$ of some ambient
   194	space.
   195	The register $V_\xpt$ (which is isomorphic to $\F_q^m$) is called the
   196	\emph{point register}, $V_\coord$ (which is isomorphic to $\F_q$) is called the
   197	\emph{coordinate register}, and $V_{\dir{}}$ (which is isomorphic to $\F_q^m$)
   198	is called the \emph{direction register}, respectively.
   199	We let $V$ denote the direct sum $V_\xpt \oplus V_{\coord} \oplus V_{\dir{}}$.
   200	We identify elements of $V$ as triples $(u,s,v) \in \F_q^m \times \F_q \times
   201	\F_q^m$.
   202	
   203	Define $L_\Point$ to be the $1$-level CL function that projects onto $V_\xpt$: for every $(u,s,v) \in V$,
   204	\begin{equation}
   205	  \label{eq:cl-ptf}
   206		L_\Point(u,s,v) = (u,0,0) \;.
   207	\end{equation}
   208	Define $L_\ALine$ to be the following $2$-level CL function:
   209	\begin{equation}
   210	  \label{eq:cl-alnf}
   211		L_\ALine(u,s,v) = (L^\lnf_{e_i}(u), s, 0)\ \text{for all } (u,s,v) \in V,
   212	\end{equation}
   213	where $L^\lnf$ is the linear function used to compute the canonical
   214	representative of lines (see \Cref{def:line-representative}), and $i = \chi(s)$
   215	where we define $\chi(s)$ to be the unique integer such that
   216	\begin{equation}
   217	\label{eq:chi-func}
   218		s = (\chi(s) - 1) \frac{q}{m} + r
   219	\end{equation}
   220	for some $0 \leq r < q/m$, and we interpret the field element $s \in \F_q$ as an
   221	integer between $0$ and $q - 1$).
   222	The function $L_\ALine$ is the concatenation of the $1$-level CL function that
   223	projects the subspaces $V_{\coord} \oplus V_{\dir{}}$ down to $V_\coord$ (i.e.
   224	zeroes out the entire $V_{\dir{}}$ register), and the family of $1$-level CL
   225	functions $\{L^\lnf_{e_i} \}$ acting on $V_\xpt$, indexed by $i \in
   226	\{1,2,\ldots,m\}$.
   227	(See \Cref{lem:cl-concat} for definition of CL function concatenation.)
   228	Thus $L_\ALine$ is a $2$-level CL function.
   229	
   230	Define $L_\DLine$ to be the following $3$-level CL function: for all $(u,s,v) \in
   231	V$,
   232	\begin{equation}
   233	\label{eq:cl-dlnf}
   234		L_\DLine(u,s,v) = (L^\lnf_{\pi_{i-1}(v)}(u),s,\pi_{i-1}(v))
   235	\end{equation}
   236	where $i = \chi(s)$.
   237	The function $L_\DLine$ is the concatenation of the following CL functions (again, see \Cref{lem:cl-concat} for definition of CL function concatenation): (i) the identity function on $V_{\coord}$ (which is a $1$-level CL function); (ii) for every $i \in \{1,2,\ldots,m\}$ the $1$-level CL function on $V_{\dir{}}$ that maps $v \mapsto \pi_{i-1}(v)$ (i.e.~it zeroes out the first $i-1$ coordinates of $v$), and (iii) for every pair $(s,v') \in V_\coord \oplus V_{\dir{}}$, the $1$-level CL function $L^\lnf_{v'}$ acting on $V_\xpt$. Thus $L_\DLine$ is a $3$-level CL function.
   238	
   239	
   240	The following two lemmas establish that the CL functions
   241	$L_\Point,L_\ALine,L_\DLine$ give rise to the axis-parallel line-versus-point and
   242	diagonal line-versus-point distributions.
   243	\begin{lemma}
   244		\label{lem:alnf}
   245		Consider the pair $(\line, u)$ sampled in the following way: first, sample the
   246	  tuple $((u_0,s,0),(u,0,0))$ from the CL distribution $\mu_{L_\ALine,L_\Point}$,
   247	  and let $\line = \line(u_0,e_i)$ where $i = \chi(s)$.
   248	  Then $u$ is a uniformly random point in $\F_q^m$ and $\line$ is a line that
   249	  goes through $u$ and is parallel to a uniformly random axis $i \in
   250	  \{1,2,\ldots,m\}$.
   251	\end{lemma}
   252	\begin{proof}
   253		Since $s$ is uniformly random in $\F_q$ and $m$ divides $q$ by assumption, we
   254	  have that $i$ is uniformly random between $\{1,2,\ldots,m\}$ and therefore
   255	  $(u_0,s)$ specifies a uniformly random axis-parallel line $\line(u_0,e_i)$.
   256	  Since $u_0 = L^{\lnf}_{e_i}(u)$, we have that $u \in \line(u_0,e_i)$.
   257	\end{proof}
   258	
   259	
   260	
   261	\begin{lemma}
   262		\label{lem:dlnf}
   263		Consider the pair $(\line,u)$ sampled in the following way: first, sample the
   264	  tuple $((u_0,s,v),(u,0,0))$ from the CL distribution $\mu_{L_\DLine,L_\Point}$,
   265	  and let $\line = \line(u_0,v)$ where $i = \chi(s)$.
   266	  Then $u$ is a uniformly random point in $\F_q^m$ and $\line$ is a random
   267	  diagonal line that goes through $u$ and shares the first $i-1$ coordinates
   268	  with $u$, for uniformly random $i$.
   269	\end{lemma}
   270	\begin{proof}
   271		The proof of this follows identically to \Cref{lem:alnf}.
   272	\end{proof}

     3	/-!
     4	# Uniform subset estimates
     5	
     6	This file contains estimates for the total variation distance between the
     7	uniform distribution on a finite type and the uniform distribution on a
     8	nonempty finite subset, together with averaging bounds for `[0,1]`-valued
     9	functions.  The uniform-subset total-variation identity is proved by transport
    10	through Mathlib probability mass functions.
    11	-/
    12	
    13	open scoped BigOperators
    14	
    15	namespace MIPStarRE.LDT
    16	
    17	/-- Total variation between the uniform distribution on a finite ambient type and
    18	the uniform distribution on a nonempty finite subset.
    19	
    20	This is the elementary finite identity
    21	`TV(uniform α, uniform s) = 1 - |s| / |α|`.  The proof transports the project
    22	`Distribution` statement to Mathlib's uniform probability mass functions. -/
    23	theorem totalVariationDistance_uniformDistribution_uniformOnFinset_eq
    24	    {α : Type*} [Fintype α] [DecidableEq α] [Nonempty α]
    25	    (s : Finset α) (hs : s.Nonempty) :
    26	    totalVariationDistance (uniformDistribution α) (Distribution.uniformOnFinset s) =
    27	      1 - (s.card : Error) / (Fintype.card α : Error) := by
    28	  rw [totalVariationDistance_eq_toPMF_sum]
    29	  change PMF.totalVariationDistance
    30	      ((uniformDistribution α).toPMF (uniformDistribution_isProbability α))
    31	      ((Distribution.uniformOnFinset s).toPMF
    32	        (Distribution.uniformOnFinset_isProbability s hs)) =
    33	    1 - (s.card : Error) / (Fintype.card α : Error)
    34	  rw [uniformDistribution_toPMF, Distribution.uniformOnFinset_toPMF]
    35	  exact PMF.totalVariationDistance_uniformOfFintype_uniformOfFinset_eq s hs
    36	
    37	/-- A `[0,1]`-valued function averaged over a nonempty finite subset is bounded
    38	by its ambient uniform average plus the total variation distance between the
    39	two uniform distributions. -/
    40	theorem avgOver_uniformOnFinset_le_uniformDistribution_add_totalVariationDistance
    41	    {α : Type*} [Fintype α] [DecidableEq α] [Nonempty α]
    42	    (s : Finset α) (hs : s.Nonempty)
    43	    (f : α → Error)
    44	    (hf_nonneg : ∀ a, 0 ≤ f a)
    45	    (hf_le_one : ∀ a, f a ≤ 1) :
    46	    avgOver (Distribution.uniformOnFinset s) f
    47	      ≤ avgOver (uniformDistribution α) f
    48	        + totalVariationDistance (uniformDistribution α) (Distribution.uniformOnFinset s) := by
    49	  exact
    50	    avgOver_le_avgOver_add_totalVariationDistance
    51	      (uniformDistribution α) (Distribution.uniformOnFinset s)
    52	      (uniformDistribution_isProbability α)
    53	      (Distribution.uniformOnFinset_isProbability s hs)
    54	      f hf_nonneg hf_le_one

    22	/-- A finite-support weighted distribution with nonnegative real-valued weights. -/
    23	structure Distribution (α : Type*) where
    24	  support : Finset α := ∅
    25	  weight : α → Error := fun _ => 0
    26	  nonnegative : ∀ a, 0 ≤ weight a := by intro _; positivity
    27	  outsideSupport : ∀ a, a ∉ support → weight a = 0 := by intro _ _; rfl
    28	
    29	namespace Distribution
    30	
    31	/-- The total mass carried by the explicit support of a distribution. -/
    32	def totalWeight {α : Type*} (𝒟 : Distribution α) : Error :=
    33	  ∑ a ∈ 𝒟.support, 𝒟.weight a
    34	
    35	/-- A `Distribution` is probabilistic when its total mass is exactly `1`. -/
    36	def IsProbability {α : Type*} (𝒟 : Distribution α) : Prop :=
    37	  𝒟.totalWeight = 1
    38	
    39	/-- Push a finite-support distribution forward along a map.
    40	
    41	This is the project `Distribution` analogue of `PMF.map`.  The support is the
    42	image of the original finite support, and each new weight is the sum of the
    43	weights in the corresponding fiber. -/
    44	noncomputable def map {α β : Type*} [DecidableEq β]
    45	    (𝒟 : Distribution α) (e : α → β) : Distribution β where
    46	  support := 𝒟.support.image e
    47	  weight := fun b => ∑ a ∈ 𝒟.support.filter (fun a => e a = b), 𝒟.weight a
    48	  nonnegative := fun _ => Finset.sum_nonneg fun a _ => 𝒟.nonnegative a
    49	  outsideSupport := fun _ hb =>
    50	    Finset.sum_eq_zero fun a ha =>
    51	      (hb (Finset.mem_image.mpr
    52	        ⟨a, (Finset.mem_filter.mp ha).1, (Finset.mem_filter.mp ha).2⟩)).elim
    53	
    54	@[simp]
    55	theorem map_support {α β : Type*} [DecidableEq β]
    56	    (𝒟 : Distribution α) (e : α → β) :
    57	    (𝒟.map e).support = 𝒟.support.image e := rfl
    58	
    59	@[simp]
    60	theorem map_weight {α β : Type*} [DecidableEq β]
    61	    (𝒟 : Distribution α) (e : α → β) (b : β) :
    62	    (𝒟.map e).weight b =
    63	      ∑ a ∈ 𝒟.support.filter (fun a => e a = b), 𝒟.weight a := rfl
    64	
    65	/-- Push-forward preserves total mass. -/
    66	theorem map_totalWeight {α β : Type*} [DecidableEq β]
    67	    (𝒟 : Distribution α) (e : α → β) :
    68	    (𝒟.map e).totalWeight = 𝒟.totalWeight := by

    72	      (fun a ha => Finset.mem_image.mpr ⟨a, ha, rfl⟩) 𝒟.weight)

55	that is the restriction of $g$ to line $\line$; formally, for $t \in \F_q$,
    56	\[f_\line(t)=g(u_1,u_2,\ldots,u_{i-1},t,u_{i+1},\ldots,u_m)\;.\] It is easy to
    57	see that $f_\line(t)$ has degree at most $d$ in the variable $t$.
    58	Thus in this case the players will pass the low-degree test with probability
    59	$1$.
    60	The low-degree testing theorem states that the converse approximately holds: if
    61	the players pass the low-degree test with probability close to $1$, then their
    62	responses must be approximately consistent (in some sense) with a global
    63	polynomial $g$ with individual degree $d$.
    64	
    65	When $k > 1$, the players are supposed to respond with a \emph{tuple} of
    66	answers; and the test is intended to check that the players' responses are
    67	consistent with a $k$-tuple of functions $g_i: \F_q^m \to \F_q$ that are
    68	polynomials where every variable has degree at most $d$.
    69	
    70	The game that we use is slightly more elaborate than the ``axis-parallel
    71	lines-versus-points'' test just described.
    72	In addition, we have two other subtests.
    73	One is a ``diagonal line-vs-points'' test: here, the points player receives a
    74	point $u \in \F_q^m$ as before, but the lines player receives a line $\line$
    75	that goes through $u$ but is not necessarily axis-aligned.
    76	Instead, it's chosen by first picking an index $i \in \{1,2,\ldots,m\}$
    77	uniformly at random, picking $v \in \F_q^m$ uniformly at random, and letting $v'
    78	= \pi_{i-1}(v) = (0,0,\ldots,0,v_i,v_{i+1},\ldots,v_m)$ (i.e., $\pi_{i-1}$
    79	zeroes out the first $i-1$ coordinates of its input).
    80	Then, the line is defined as the set
    81	\[
    82		\line = \{ u + tv' : t \in \F_q \}\;,
    83	\]
    84	which is a uniformly random line in the affine subspace of $\F^m_q$
    85	corresponding to all points $v$ whose first $(i-1)$ coordinates match those of
    86	$u$.
    87	The points player responds with a value $a \in \F_q$, the lines player responds
    88	with a univariate polynomial $f_\line$ of degree $md$,\footnote{Since $\line$ is
    89	  no longer axis-parallel, the restriction of an individual degree-$d$
    90	  polynomial $g$ to a line $\line$ may yield a degree $md$ polynomial.}
    91	and the verifier checks that $f_\line(t_u) = a$ (where $t_u \in \F_q$ is the
    92	projection of $u$ onto the line $\line$ with respect to a canonical
    93	parameterization of $\line$).
    94	
    95	The other additional test is a ``consistency test'', where both players receive
    96	either the same points question, the same axis-parallel lines question, or the
    97	same diagonal lines question.
    98	In all cases they are expected to respond with the same answer.

  1079	subspaces: $V_\xpt,V_\zpt$ (which are $m$-dimensional), $V_\coord$ (which is
